title: Repeated Failed Domain Logon Against Single Account
description: A single domain account failed authentication repeatedly within a short window, consistent with brute-force guessing against that specific account. Legitimate users occasionally mistype passwords a handful of times; a sustained burst is the signal worth alerting on.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Failed logon events.

detection_logic: Counts 4625 failure events per target account within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count values(src) AS sources by _time, TargetUserName
| where count>=10
tuning_guidance: Exclude known misconfigured service/scheduled-task accounts with stale cached credentials.
investigation_steps: Identify the source(s) of the failures.
Check for a subsequent successful logon (AD-AUTH-006).
response_guidance: Lock the account if externally sourced and unexplained; investigate the source host.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Failed Domain Logons Against Many Distinct Accounts
description: Failed logons occurred against an unusually large number of distinct accounts in a short window, which — regardless of source — indicates a broad credential-guessing campaign against the domain rather than a single targeted account.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Failed logon events aggregated by distinct target account.

detection_logic: Counts distinct TargetUserName values with a 4625 failure within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS distinct_users values(TargetUserName) AS users by _time
| where distinct_users>=20
tuning_guidance: Correlate with a known password-expiration/mass-onboarding event before escalating.
investigation_steps: Determine if this maps to a single source (spray) or many sources (distributed spray/credential stuffing).
response_guidance: Investigate as a domain-wide credential-access campaign.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Password Spray: One Source Against Many Users
description: A single source authenticated against many distinct domain accounts with a low per-account failure count, the classic password-spray pattern that evades per-account lockout thresholds by never failing enough times against any one account to trigger it.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Failed logon events aggregated per source across distinct accounts.

detection_logic: Counts distinct target accounts per source IP within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count dc(TargetUserName) AS distinct_users values(TargetUserName) AS users by _time src
| where distinct_users >= 10 AND count >= 15
tuning_guidance: Exclude known vulnerability-scanner or credential-testing sources with documented authorization.
investigation_steps: Determine whether any targeted account had a subsequent successful logon (AD-AUTH-008).
Block the source.
response_guidance: Block the source and force password resets for any account with a successful logon.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Low-and-Slow Password Spray
description: A source authenticated against many distinct accounts at a low rate sustained over a much longer window (hours to days) than the standard spray-detection window, evading threshold detections tuned to a 15-minute burst while still eventually touching a large population of accounts.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Failed logon events aggregated per source over an extended window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct target accounts per source over a 24-hour rolling window with a low per-hour rate.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=24h
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS distinct_users count by _time src
| where distinct_users>=30 AND (count/24)<5
tuning_guidance: Requires a longer lookback than most real-time searches; run as a scheduled daily search rather than near-real-time.
investigation_steps: Review the full 24-hour source activity pattern.
Check for any successful logon among targeted accounts.
response_guidance: Block the source and investigate for successful compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Distributed Password Spray Across Many Sources
description: Many distinct source IPs each authenticated against a handful of accounts with failures, but the aggregate pattern across all sources targets a broad, overlapping set of accounts — consistent with a distributed spray campaign (e.g. via a botnet or residential-proxy network) designed to evade single-source-IP thresholds entirely.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Failed logon events aggregated by target account across many distinct sources.

detection_logic: Counts distinct source IPs per target account within a rolling window and flags accounts targeted by an unusually high number of distinct sources.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(src) AS source_count by _time, TargetUserName
| where source_count>=5
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS affected_users sum(source_count) AS total_source_touches by _time
| where affected_users>=10
tuning_guidance: Correlate with known cloud/proxy egress ranges; a strong candidate once tuned since single-source thresholds miss this pattern entirely.
investigation_steps: Enumerate every source IP involved.
Check for successful logons across the affected account population.
response_guidance: Block the source ranges where feasible; force password resets for accounts with successful logons.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Successful Domain Logon Following Failure Burst
description: A domain account authenticated successfully immediately following a burst of failed attempts against it — the classic successful-brute-force pattern, and given Active Directory's Tier-0 role, a strong precursor to every other identity-attack detection in this catalogue.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Sequenced failure and success logon events for the same account.

detection_logic: Correlates a failure burst (>=10 in 10m) against a single account followed by a success event for that account within 5 minutes.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count AS fail_count by _time, TargetUserName
| where fail_count>=10
| join TargetUserName [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 | table _time, TargetUserName, src]
| where _time_success>_time AND (_time_success-_time)<=300
tuning_guidance: Low false-positive pattern; investigate all matches.
investigation_steps: Force a password reset on the account.
Review every action taken during the resulting session.
response_guidance: Treat as a confirmed account-compromise incident: reset credentials, terminate active sessions, and review activity.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Failed Logon Against Invalid/Non-Existent Username
description: A logon attempt failed with a bad-username status (as opposed to bad-password), consistent with username enumeration or a spray tool guessing at both usernames and passwords rather than working from a known valid-user list.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Failed logon events with the bad-username substatus.

detection_logic: Filters 4625 events with Sub_Status 0xC0000064 (user name does not exist), aggregated per source.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625 Sub_Status=0xC0000064
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS invalid_user_count values(TargetUserName) AS attempted by _time src
| where invalid_user_count>=10
tuning_guidance: Exclude known legacy application connection strings that legitimately attempt stale usernames.
investigation_steps: Determine the source's intent — automated enumeration vs. misconfiguration.
response_guidance: Block if malicious; low urgency standalone otherwise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Password Spray Followed by Successful Logon
description: A source engaged in a password-spray pattern against many accounts and one of the targeted accounts subsequently authenticated successfully from that same source — confirming the spray campaign actually compromised a credential rather than merely being noise.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation: spray pattern, then success from the same source.

detection_logic: Correlates AD-AUTH-003's spray pattern against a subsequent 4624 success event for the same source and one of the targeted accounts.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS distinct_users values(TargetUserName) AS spray_targets by _time src
| where distinct_users>=10
| join src [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 | table _time, TargetUserName, src]
| where mvfind(spray_targets, TargetUserName)>=0
tuning_guidance: A Tier-1 flagship credential-access confirmation; alert on all matches.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed account-compromise incident.
Reset the compromised account's credential immediately.
response_guidance: Full incident response: reset credentials, terminate sessions, block the spray source.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: VPN Login Followed by AD Password Spray
description: A VPN authentication was followed by a password-spray pattern against Active Directory originating from the VPN-assigned address, consistent with an attacker who compromised or brute-forced VPN access using it as a foothold to then spray the internal domain, bypassing any external-facing rate limiting.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: VPN authentication events followed by an AD-AUTH-003-style spray pattern from the VPN address pool
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlates VPN login events against a subsequent AD spray pattern from an IP within the VPN's assigned address pool.
spl:
index=<vpn_index> sourcetype=<vpn_sourcetype> event=login_success
| eval stage="1_vpn_login"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625 | lookup vpn_address_pool.csv src OUTPUT is_vpn_range | where is_vpn_range=1 | bin _time span=15m | stats dc(TargetUserName) AS distinct_users by _time, src | where distinct_users>=10 | eval stage="2_spray"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by src
| where stage_count>=2 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=3600
tuning_guidance: Requires a VPN address-pool lookup and correlation-search support.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed incident given the VPN-compromise precursor.
Suspend the VPN session and investigate.
response_guidance: Terminate the VPN session, rotate VPN credentials, and investigate any successful AD logons from the source.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: RDP Login Followed by AD Password Spray
description: An RDP session was followed by a password-spray pattern originating from that RDP session's host, consistent with an attacker using a compromised RDP-accessible host as a staging point to spray the domain from inside the network perimeter.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.path: index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=10, followed by a spray pattern originating from that host
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlates an RDP (Logon_Type=10) success event against a subsequent AD spray pattern originating from the same host.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=10
| eval stage="1_rdp_login"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625 | bin _time span=15m | stats dc(TargetUserName) AS distinct_users by _time, src | where distinct_users>=10 | eval stage="2_spray"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by src
| where stage_count>=2 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=3600
tuning_guidance: Requires correlation-search support; treats the RDP host as the spray's originating point.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed incident.
Isolate the RDP host and investigate for compromise.
response_guidance: Isolate the host and investigate the RDP session's originating credential.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Password Spray Against Privileged Accounts
description: Failed logon attempts specifically targeted accounts on the Tier-0 privileged-group lookup (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, etc.), a materially higher-priority variant of the general spray detection given the blast radius if any one succeeds.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Failed logon events joined against a Tier-0 privileged-account lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4625 events where TargetUserName is on the privileged-account lookup, aggregated per source.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS distinct_privileged_targeted values(TargetUserName) AS targets by _time src
| where distinct_privileged_targeted>=3
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained Tier-0 privileged-account lookup; alert on all occurrences given the severity.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident.
Verify none of the targeted privileged accounts had a successful logon.
response_guidance: Block the source and consider proactive credential rotation for targeted privileged accounts.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Failed Logons Against Disabled Account
description: A logon attempt was made against an account currently disabled in Active Directory, which — beyond routine noise from stale scheduled tasks — can indicate an attacker attempting to use a credential from a disabled (e.g. recently offboarded) account they still possess, or probing whether the disable state can be bypassed.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Failed logon events with the account-disabled substatus.

detection_logic: Filters 4625 events with Sub_Status 0xC0000072 (account currently disabled).
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625 Sub_Status=0xC0000072
| table _time, TargetUserName, src
tuning_guidance: Exclude known stale scheduled-task/service accounts pending cleanup.
investigation_steps: Confirm the account's offboarding status.
Investigate the source's intent.
response_guidance: Low urgency standalone unless the account is Tier-0 or recently disabled for cause.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Successful Logon by Recently-Disabled or Offboarded Account
description: An account authenticated successfully after being disabled, which should be impossible under normal circumstances and indicates either an attacker re-enabled the account just before use (correlate with AD-USER-006) or a directory-replication inconsistency being exploited.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: Account-enable event (4722) immediately followed by a successful logon (4624) for a recently-disabled account
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlates a 4722 (account enabled) event against a subsequent 4624 success for the same account within a short window, restricted to accounts that were disabled shortly before.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4722
| eval stage="1_enabled"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 | eval stage="2_login"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by TargetUserName
| where stage_count>=2 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=1800
tuning_guidance: Confirm against an approved re-enablement ticket (e.g. a legitimate rehire).
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for the re-enablement.
Review the resulting session's activity.
response_guidance: Disable the account and investigate if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Dormant Account Reactivated for Authentication
description: An account with no successful logon for an extended period (90+ days) authenticated successfully, which can indicate use of a forgotten/orphaned credential — a classic persistence target since dormant accounts rarely receive the same monitoring attention as actively-used ones.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Login events compared against each account's last-successful-logon timestamp.

detection_logic: Joins each login against a lookup of last-successful-login-per-account and flags gaps exceeding the dormancy threshold.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| lookup update=true ad_last_login.csv TargetUserName OUTPUT last_login
| eval days_dormant=round((_time-last_login)/86400)
| where days_dormant>=90
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, days_dormant
tuning_guidance: Correlate with HR/offboarding records; some dormancy is legitimate (seasonal, DR-only accounts).
investigation_steps: Verify the account owner is still an active employee/contractor.
Disable if orphaned.
response_guidance: Disable the account and investigate how the credential was obtained if the owner denies the login.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Account Lockout Storm from Single Source
description: A single source caused an unusually large number of distinct accounts to lock out in a short window, consistent with either a misconfigured application hammering AD with a stale credential or a deliberate denial-of-service against user population availability.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Account lockout events aggregated per source per window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct accounts locked out with the same caller computer within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4740
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS locked_count values(TargetUserName) AS accounts by _time, Caller_Computer_Name
| where locked_count>=5
tuning_guidance: Correlate with known password-rotation events or a misconfigured mobile device/service with a stale cached credential.
investigation_steps: Identify the caller computer and its role.
Determine if this is malicious or a misconfiguration.
response_guidance: Remediate the misconfigured source or block if malicious.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Privileged Account Lockout
description: A Tier-0 privileged account was locked out, which — beyond the operational impact of denying the legitimate admin access — may be an intentional side effect of an attacker's spray/brute-force campaign against that specific account.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Account lockout events joined against a Tier-0 privileged-account lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4740 events where TargetUserName is on the privileged-account lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4740
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, Caller_Computer_Name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences given the account's privilege level.
investigation_steps: Determine the cause of the lockout — legitimate mistake vs. attack.
Check for preceding failed-logon activity against the account.
response_guidance: Unlock through verified channels only; investigate the preceding failure pattern.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Repeated Lockout of Same Account
description: The same account was locked out multiple times in succession, which can indicate a persistent brute-force attempt (the attacker keeps retrying after each lockout period expires) or a persistently misconfigured client repeatedly re-triggering the lockout.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Lockout events aggregated per account over an extended window.

detection_logic: Counts lockout events per account within a rolling multi-hour window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4740
| bin _time span=4h
| stats count by _time, TargetUserName
| where count>=3
tuning_guidance: Correlate with a known stale-credential device (phone, mapped drive) before escalating.
investigation_steps: Identify the recurring source of the lockout-triggering attempts.
response_guidance: Fix the misconfigured client or investigate as a persistent attack.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Account Lockout Following Password Spray
description: An account lockout occurred immediately after a spray pattern targeted it, confirming the spray's failure volume actually reached the account's lockout threshold — a useful correlation for prioritizing which specific accounts within a broad spray campaign need closer review.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: AD-AUTH-003 spray pattern followed by a 4740 lockout for one of the targeted accounts
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlates a spray pattern against a subsequent lockout event for one of the targeted accounts.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS distinct_users values(TargetUserName) AS spray_targets by _time src
| where distinct_users>=10
| join type=inner [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4740 | table _time, TargetUserName]
| where mvfind(spray_targets, TargetUserName)>=0
tuning_guidance: Requires correlation-search support.
investigation_steps: Prioritize the locked-out account for password reset review.
Confirm no successful logon preceded the lockout.
response_guidance: Reset the account's credential upon unlock; block the spray source.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Successful Logon by Domain Admin
description: A member of the Domain Admins group authenticated successfully. Not inherently suspicious, but the necessary building block for the higher-confidence correlations elsewhere in this catalogue (first-seen source, non-PAW source, DC interactive logon).

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Login events joined against Domain Admins group membership.

detection_logic: Joins successful login events against a maintained Domain Admins membership lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| lookup domain_admins.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_domain_admin
| where is_domain_admin=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, dest
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained Domain Admins lookup, ideally refreshed from AD-GRP-### membership-change events; high volume by design, primarily a correlation building block.
investigation_steps: Track for use in downstream correlations.
response_guidance: No standalone action; feeds correlation searches.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Successful Logon by Enterprise Admin or Schema Admin
description: A member of Enterprise Admins or Schema Admins authenticated successfully — forest-wide privilege groups whose use should be even rarer than Domain Admins, since Enterprise/Schema Admin activity is normally confined to forest-level operations (trust creation, schema extension) rather than day-to-day administration.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Login events joined against Enterprise/Schema Admins membership.

detection_logic: Joins successful login events against maintained Enterprise Admins/Schema Admins lookups.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| lookup enterprise_schema_admins.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_ea_sa
| where is_ea_sa=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, dest
tuning_guidance: Requires maintained lookups; alert-worthy given how rare legitimate use should be.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for forest-level administrative activity.
response_guidance: Verify immediately if unexpected.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: First-Seen Source for Privileged Domain Logon
description: A Tier-0 privileged account authenticated from a source host never previously seen for that account, a materially higher-confidence variant of the general privileged-logon detection given the source novelty.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Privileged login events compared against a per-account source baseline.

detection_logic: Joins privileged-account logins against a lookup of each account's previously-seen source hosts.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| lookup update=true ad_privileged_src_baseline.csv TargetUserName, src OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, src
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained source baseline; a strong Tier-1 candidate given how rarely legitimate privileged accounts should log on from a genuinely new host.
investigation_steps: Confirm with the admin whether this login is expected.
Review all actions taken during the session.
response_guidance: Verify immediately; reset credentials and terminate the session if unconfirmed.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Privileged Account Authenticating from Non-PAW Source
description: A Tier-0 privileged account authenticated from a host not on the designated Privileged Access Workstation (PAW) inventory, bypassing the hardening and monitoring specifically applied to PAWs and expanding the account's exposure to whatever risks the ordinary endpoint carries.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Privileged login events joined against the PAW inventory lookup.

detection_logic: Filters privileged-account login events where the source host is not on the PAW inventory lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| lookup paw_inventory.csv src OUTPUT is_paw
| where isnull(is_paw)
| table _time, TargetUserName, src
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained PAW inventory; exclude documented break-glass exceptions.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for the PAW-policy exception.
Assess the source host's security posture.
response_guidance: Terminate the session and require re-authentication from an approved PAW.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: RDP or Console Interactive Logon to Domain Controller
description: A user interactively logged onto a Domain Controller via RDP or console (as opposed to a network/service logon), which — regardless of the account's privilege level — puts credential material for that session directly on Tier-0 infrastructure and should be a rare, tightly-controlled administrative action.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.path: index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 Logon_Type IN (2, 10), restricted to Domain Controller hosts
data_sources.description: Interactive/RDP logon events on DC hosts.

detection_logic: Filters 4624 events with Logon_Type 2 (interactive) or 10 (RemoteInteractive) where dest is on the Domain Controller inventory.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 Logon_Type IN (2, 10)
| lookup domain_controllers.csv host AS dest OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, dest, Logon_Type
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets; every interactive DC logon should be traceable to an approved administrative action.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification and jump-host/PAW compliance.
Review actions taken during the session.
response_guidance: Investigate immediately if unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1021.001: Remote Desktop Protocol

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Admin Logon to Domain Controller from Non-Jump-Host Network
description: An administrative logon to a Domain Controller originated from a source network outside the designated jump-host/bastion subnet, bypassing the chokepoint the organization relies on for DC-access monitoring and change control.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.path: index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624, restricted to DC hosts, joined against the jump-host subnet lookup
data_sources.description: DC logon events with source outside the approved jump-host CIDR range.

detection_logic: Filters DC logon events where the source IP falls outside the approved jump-host subnet lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 Logon_Type IN (2, 3, 10)
| lookup domain_controllers.csv host AS dest OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| lookup jump_host_subnets.csv src OUTPUT is_jump_host
| where isnull(is_jump_host)
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, dest
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained jump-host subnet lookup; alert on all occurrences given the bypass of the intended access chokepoint.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for the direct access.
Assess whether the source represents a policy gap or an active bypass attempt.
response_guidance: Terminate the session and enforce jump-host-only access.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1021.001: Remote Desktop Protocol

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Service Account Interactive Logon
description: An account designated as a non-interactive service account authenticated with an interactive or RDP logon type, which — since service-account credentials are typically stored in configuration/automation systems rather than known to a human — can indicate the credential was exfiltrated and is being used manually by an attacker.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Interactive/RDP logon events joined against a service-account lookup.

detection_logic: Filters interactive/RDP logon events for accounts flagged as service accounts in a maintained lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 Logon_Type IN (2, 10)
| lookup service_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_service_account
| where is_service_account=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, Logon_Type
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained service-account lookup; exclude documented legitimate interactive-troubleshooting exceptions.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether an administrator used the service account intentionally for troubleshooting.
If not, treat as a credential-compromise incident.
response_guidance: Rotate the service account's credential and review its automated integrations for tampering.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Service Account Source Change
description: A service account authenticated from a source host it has never previously used, which — since service accounts typically run from a small, stable set of application servers — is a strong behavioral-novelty signal of credential compromise.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service-account logon events compared against a per-account source baseline.

detection_logic: Joins service-account logon events against a lookup of each account's previously-seen source hosts.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| lookup service_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_service_account
| where is_service_account=1
| lookup update=true service_account_src_baseline.csv TargetUserName, src OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, src
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained per-account source baseline; expect noise during legitimate infrastructure migrations.
investigation_steps: Verify the new source is expected application infrastructure.
Rotate the credential if not.
response_guidance: Rotate if compromise is suspected.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Dormant Service Account Reactivated
description: A service account with no authentication activity for an extended period authenticated successfully, which can indicate an attacker discovered and reactivated a forgotten service-account credential left over from a decommissioned application.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service-account logon events compared against a dormancy baseline.

detection_logic: Joins service-account logins against a lookup of last-successful-login-per-account, restricted to accounts on the service-account inventory.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| lookup service_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_service_account
| where is_service_account=1
| lookup update=true ad_last_login.csv TargetUserName OUTPUT last_login
| eval days_dormant=round((_time-last_login)/86400)
| where days_dormant>=90
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, days_dormant
tuning_guidance: Correlate with an application-decommission inventory.
investigation_steps: Confirm the application this account serves is still in production.
Disable if orphaned.
response_guidance: Disable and investigate if the reactivation is unexplained.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Service Account Used Against Unusual Target System
description: A service account authenticated to a destination system it has never previously accessed, which — since service accounts typically operate against a fixed, narrow set of servers — can indicate lateral movement using a compromised service-account credential.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service-account logon events compared against a per-account destination baseline.

detection_logic: Joins service-account logon events against a lookup of each account's previously-accessed destination hosts.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| lookup service_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_service_account
| where is_service_account=1
| lookup update=true service_account_dest_baseline.csv TargetUserName, dest OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, dest
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained per-account destination baseline; expect noise during legitimate infrastructure expansion.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for the new target.
Assess for lateral-movement indicators.
response_guidance: Investigate further if unjustified.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Explicit Credential Logon (4648) by Unusual Process
description: A process used explicit credentials (RunAs, or a process supplying alternate credentials rather than using the current logon session) to authenticate, which — beyond routine administrative RunAs use — is also the pattern seen when a tool like Mimikatz's sekurlsa or a lateral-movement utility passes captured credentials explicitly.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Explicit-credential logon events joined against a known-administrative-tool process baseline.

detection_logic: Filters 4648 events where the originating process is not on a known-administrative-tool allowlist (mmc.exe, runas.exe, and similar).
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4648
| lookup known_runas_processes.csv ProcessName OUTPUT is_known
| where isnull(is_known)
| table _time, SubjectUserName, TargetUserName, ProcessName, dest
tuning_guidance: Maintain a known-process allowlist to keep this actionable; high false-positive rate without one.
investigation_steps: Identify the process and its origin.
Correlate with subsequent authentication/lateral-movement activity.
response_guidance: Investigate the process for credential-theft tooling if unrecognized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Impossible Travel Between Concurrent Domain Sessions
description: The same domain account has active sessions from two source addresses whose geolocation makes legitimate concurrent use implausible within the observed time window, suggesting the credential is in use by more than one party — most likely the legitimate user and an attacker.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Concurrent successful logons for the same account from distinct source IPs, enriched with geolocation.

detection_logic: Groups successful logons by account within a short window and flags cases where two sessions originate from distinct countries with a travel-time-implausible gap.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| iplocation src
| stats values(Country) AS countries dc(Country) AS country_count values(src) AS sources by TargetUserName, _time
| where country_count>1
tuning_guidance: Requires IP geolocation enrichment; exclude known corporate VPN egress points that geolocate incorrectly.
investigation_steps: Confirm with the user which session (if any) is legitimate.
Terminate the illegitimate session and force a credential reset.
response_guidance: Treat as a probable account-compromise incident; reset credentials and terminate all active sessions.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Kerberos TGT Request Volume Anomaly
description: An unusually high volume of Kerberos TGT (AS-REQ) requests occurred against a KDC in a short window, which can indicate automated credential-testing tooling, a misbehaving client, or reconnaissance/enumeration activity generating authentication traffic at scale.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: TGT request events aggregated per window.

detection_logic: Compares 4768 event volume within a rolling window against a historical baseline.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4768
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count by _time
| eventstats avg(count) AS avg_count stdev(count) AS stdev_count
| where count > (avg_count + 3*stdev_count)
tuning_guidance: Correlate with known bulk-authentication events (mass service restart, scheduled batch jobs).
investigation_steps: Identify the top requesting clients/accounts.
Determine if this is legitimate or malicious.
response_guidance: Investigate further if unexplained.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: TGT Request from Rare or First-Seen Client
description: A TGT request originated from a client address never previously seen requesting tickets for this account, which can indicate a new legitimate workstation or credential use from an attacker-controlled host.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: TGT request events compared against a per-account client-address baseline.

detection_logic: Joins TGT request events against a lookup of each account's previously-seen client addresses.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4768
| lookup update=true krb_client_baseline.csv TargetUserName, Client_Address OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, Client_Address
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained baseline; combine with privileged-account status for higher-confidence alerting.
investigation_steps: Confirm the new client is expected.
Escalate if the account is privileged (AD-KRB-006).
response_guidance: Low urgency standalone.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: TGT Request for Disabled Account
description: A TGT request occurred for an account currently disabled in Active Directory, which — since a disabled account should not be able to obtain a valid TGT under normal circumstances — warrants review of whether this represents a KDC-level inconsistency or an attacker probing account state.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: TGT request events joined against account-disabled state.

detection_logic: Filters 4768 events for accounts currently on the disabled-account lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4768
| lookup disabled_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_disabled
| where is_disabled=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, Client_Address, Result_Code
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained disabled-account state lookup, ideally refreshed near-real-time from 4725 events.
investigation_steps: Confirm the account's current state directly in AD.
Investigate the requesting client.
response_guidance: Investigate as a possible KDC-inconsistency exploitation attempt.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: TGT Request with Unusual Encryption Type
description: A TGT request used an encryption type weaker than the domain's configured minimum (e.g. RC4 in an AES-only environment), which can indicate a downgrade attack, legacy/misconfigured client, or a tool deliberately requesting a weaker cipher to ease offline cracking.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: TGT request events with the negotiated encryption type.

detection_logic: Filters 4768 events where Ticket_Encryption_Type indicates RC4 (0x17) or DES (0x1/0x3) in an environment expected to use AES.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4768 Ticket_Encryption_Type IN ("0x17", "0x1", "0x3")
| table _time, TargetUserName, Client_Address, Ticket_Encryption_Type
tuning_guidance: Exclude legacy applications/devices with a documented, approved exception; some environments legitimately still support RC4 broadly, reducing this detection's value there.
investigation_steps: Determine the client's Kerberos capability and whether AES support is expected.
Investigate for downgrade-attack indicators.
response_guidance: Enforce AES-only Kerberos policy where feasible; investigate the client if unexpected.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: TGT Request from Non-Domain System
description: A TGT request originated from a client address that does not resolve to any known domain-joined host, consistent with an attacker requesting tickets from an external or unmanaged system using a compromised credential.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: TGT request events joined against the domain-joined-host inventory.

detection_logic: Filters 4768 events where Client_Address does not match any entry in the domain-joined-computer inventory.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4768
| lookup domain_computer_inventory.csv ip_address AS Client_Address OUTPUT is_domain_joined
| where isnull(is_domain_joined)
| table _time, TargetUserName, Client_Address
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained computer-inventory-to-IP lookup; exclude known non-Windows Kerberos clients (Linux/macOS domain-joined via SSSD/Kerberos).
investigation_steps: Identify the source host.
Treat as a probable credential-compromise incident.
response_guidance: Investigate the source and rotate the account's credential if unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Privileged Account TGT Request from First-Seen Client
description: A Tier-0 privileged account requested a TGT from a client address it has never used before — the privileged-account variant of AD-KRB-002, given far higher priority due to the account's blast radius.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: TGT request events for privileged accounts compared against a source baseline.

detection_logic: Joins TGT request events for accounts on the Tier-0 lookup against a per-account client-address baseline.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4768
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| lookup update=true krb_client_baseline.csv TargetUserName, Client_Address OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, Client_Address
tuning_guidance: A Tier-1 candidate given the combination of privilege and novelty.
investigation_steps: Confirm with the admin whether this is expected.
Reset credentials and terminate the session if unconfirmed.
response_guidance: Verify immediately.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Kerberos Pre-Authentication Failure Burst
description: A burst of Kerberos pre-authentication failures (4771) occurred against one or more accounts, the Kerberos-specific equivalent of a 4625 failure burst and equally indicative of brute-force/spray activity against the KDC directly.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Kerberos pre-authentication failure events.

detection_logic: Counts 4771 events per account within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4771
| bin _time span=10m
| stats count values(IP_Address) AS sources by _time, TargetUserName
| where count>=10
tuning_guidance: Cross-reference with AD-AUTH-001; both events can fire for the same underlying activity depending on which authentication path the client uses.
investigation_steps: Identify the source and determine intent.
response_guidance: Lock the account if externally sourced and unexplained.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Kerberos Service Ticket Request for Unusual SPN
description: A service ticket request (4769) targeted a Service Principal Name the requesting account has never requested before, which — while frequently benign application behavior — is a necessary building block for the Kerberoasting detections that follow.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service ticket request events compared against a per-account SPN baseline.

detection_logic: Joins 4769 events against a lookup of each account's previously-requested SPNs.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769
| lookup update=true krb_spn_baseline.csv TargetUserName, Service_Name OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, Service_Name, Client_Address
tuning_guidance: High noise standalone; primarily a correlation building block for AD-KRB-011/012.
investigation_steps: Track for use in downstream Kerberoasting correlations.
response_guidance: No standalone action.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Single Account Requests Service Tickets for Many Distinct SPNs
description: A single account requested service tickets for an unusually large number of distinct SPNs in a short window — a hallmark of an attacker enumerating and mass-requesting every kerberoastable service ticket in the domain for offline cracking, rather than a normal user/application accessing its usual handful of services.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service ticket request events aggregated per requesting account per window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct Service_Name values requested by the same account within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769 Service_Name!="krbtgt"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats dc(Service_Name) AS spn_count values(Service_Name) AS services by _time, TargetUserName, Client_Address
| where spn_count>=15
tuning_guidance: Exclude known service-discovery/monitoring accounts (e.g. an inventory scanner) that legitimately touch many SPNs.
investigation_steps: Review the specific SPNs requested for high-value services.
Check the encryption type used (RC4 favors offline cracking, AD-KRB-010).
response_guidance: Treat as a probable Kerberoasting attempt; investigate the account and rotate targeted service-account passwords.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Kerberoasting: RC4 Service Ticket Requests at Scale
description: A single account requested many RC4-encrypted service tickets for distinct SPNs — RC4 is favored by Kerberoasting tooling since it is dramatically faster to crack offline than AES, and its request pattern in bulk from a single account is one of the highest-confidence Kerberoasting signals available in standard Windows telemetry.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: RC4-encrypted service ticket request events aggregated per account.

detection_logic: Counts distinct RC4-encrypted service ticket requests per account within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769 Ticket_Encryption_Type=0x17 Service_Name!="krbtgt"
| bin _time span=10m
| stats dc(Service_Name) AS spn_count values(Service_Name) AS services by _time, TargetUserName, Client_Address
| where spn_count>=10
tuning_guidance: Exclude environments where RC4 is still the domain-wide default (reduces this detection's specificity there); AES-only environments should treat any RC4 request as suspicious in its own right.
investigation_steps: Treat as a high-confidence Kerberoasting attempt.
Identify the account and source; rotate passwords for the targeted service accounts.
response_guidance: Investigate the requesting account for compromise; rotate all targeted service-account passwords to long, random values.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Kerberoasting Against High-Value SPN
description: A service ticket request targeted an SPN on a maintained high-value list (SQL Server service accounts, backup service accounts, or any SPN bound to a Tier-0-adjacent service account), warranting immediate review regardless of request volume given the account's privilege.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service ticket request events joined against a high-value SPN lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4769 events where Service_Name is on the high-value SPN lookup, joined against the requesting account's typical access pattern for anomaly scoring.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769
| lookup high_value_spns.csv spn AS Service_Name OUTPUT is_high_value
| where is_high_value=1
| lookup update=true krb_spn_baseline.csv TargetUserName, Service_Name OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, Service_Name, Client_Address
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained high-value SPN lookup; a Tier-1 candidate once tuned.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for the first-time access to this SPN.
Rotate the target service account's password if unexplained.
response_guidance: Investigate immediately given the account's value.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Service Ticket Fan-Out: Many Accounts Requesting the Same SPN
description: An unusually large number of distinct accounts requested service tickets for the same SPN within a short window, which — depending on the service — can be a legitimate scale event (a popular shared service) or coordinated reconnaissance across multiple compromised accounts.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service ticket request events aggregated per SPN per window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct requesting accounts per SPN within a rolling window and flags outliers relative to the SPN's baseline.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769 Service_Name!="krbtgt"
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS requester_count by _time, Service_Name
| eventstats avg(requester_count) AS avg_count stdev(requester_count) AS stdev_count by Service_Name
| where requester_count > (avg_count + 3*stdev_count)
tuning_guidance: Expect high noise for genuinely popular shared services (file servers, print servers); scope to services with a normally-narrow consumer base.
investigation_steps: Determine if the volume increase correlates with a legitimate business event.
response_guidance: Low urgency standalone.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: AS-REP Roastable Account: Pre-Authentication Not Required
description: An account is configured with 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication', which allows an attacker to request an AS-REP for that account without knowing its password and attempt offline cracking against the returned encrypted material — this detection flags the configuration itself, the precondition for AS-REP roasting.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Account-change events where the UserAccountControl flags show pre-auth-not-required newly set.

detection_logic: Filters 4738 events where the new UserAccountControl value includes the DONT_REQ_PREAUTH flag (0x400000) and it was not previously set.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4738
| where UserAccountControl="*0x410000*" OR UserAccountControl="*DONT_REQ_PREAUTH*"
| lookup update=true preauth_baseline.csv TargetUserName OUTPUT was_preauth_required
| where was_preauth_required=1 OR isnull(was_preauth_required)
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets; there is rarely a legitimate reason to disable Kerberos pre-authentication.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for this configuration.
Re-enable pre-authentication if unauthorized.
response_guidance: Re-enable pre-authentication immediately unless a specific, documented legacy requirement exists.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: AS-REP Request Pattern Without Pre-Authentication
description: A 4768 TGT-request event was logged without a corresponding pre-authentication event, matching the observable pattern of an AS-REP roasting tool requesting a ticket for a pre-auth-disabled account and capturing the encrypted response for offline cracking.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: TGT request events with no pre-authentication type recorded.

detection_logic: Filters 4768 events where PreAuthType is 0/absent, restricted to accounts flagged as pre-auth-disabled on the AD-KRB-013 lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4768 PreAuthType=0
| lookup preauth_disabled_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_preauth_disabled
| where is_preauth_disabled=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, Client_Address
tuning_guidance: Requires an up-to-date pre-auth-disabled-account lookup; a Tier-1 candidate given how directly this maps to the technique.
investigation_steps: Identify the requesting client.
Treat as a probable AS-REP roasting attempt.
response_guidance: Rotate the targeted account's password to a long, random value and re-enable pre-authentication.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Privileged Account with Pre-Authentication Disabled
description: A Tier-0 privileged account is configured with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled — combining the AS-REP-roastable configuration with a high-value target, this is one of the most severe standing misconfigurations this catalogue can detect.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.path: index=<windows_index> EventCode=4738, joined against the Tier-0 lookup
data_sources.description: Account-configuration state joined against privilege lookup.

detection_logic: A scheduled search (not purely event-driven) enumerating current UserAccountControl state for Tier-0 accounts via the AD module/LDAP and flagging any with pre-auth disabled.
spl:
| ldapsearch domain=<domain> search="(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304))"
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS sAMAccountName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| table sAMAccountName, userAccountControl
tuning_guidance: Requires an LDAP-search-capable Splunk app/add-on or a scheduled AD-module export feeding Splunk; run daily.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident.
Re-enable pre-authentication immediately.
response_guidance: Re-enable pre-authentication and rotate the account's password.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Golden Ticket Indicator: Ticket Lifetime Exceeds Domain Policy
description: A Kerberos ticket's observed lifetime exceeds the domain's configured maximum ticket lifetime, consistent with a forged TGT (Golden Ticket) built with an attacker-chosen expiration rather than one issued through the normal KDC policy enforcement path. Direct Golden Ticket detection is inherently indirect — this and the following entries each catch a different observable symptom rather than the forgery itself.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service ticket events with a renewal/lifetime field exceeding the domain's configured Kerberos policy maximum.

detection_logic: Compares the ticket's effective lifetime (derived from ticket options/ metadata where exposed) against the domain's configured MaxTicketAge; this is a best-effort indirect signal, not a definitive forgery detection.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769
| eval ticket_lifetime_hours=<computed_from_ticket_options>
| where ticket_lifetime_hours > <domain_max_ticket_age_hours>
| table _time, TargetUserName, ticket_lifetime_hours
tuning_guidance: Standard Windows Security event fields do not directly expose ticket lifetime in a simply-queryable way in all environments; this detection's practical implementation depends on what your Kerberos-event parser actually extracts — validate field availability before relying on it, and treat this as a best-effort indirect indicator rather than a guaranteed Golden Ticket catch.
investigation_steps: Cross-reference with AD-KRB-017 through AD-KRB-020 for corroborating indirect signals.
Treat any match as a potential Tier-0 compromise requiring krbtgt rotation.
response_guidance: If corroborated by other indicators, perform the two-stage krbtgt password reset (AD-KRB-034) and conduct full incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Direct, reliable Golden Ticket detection from standard Windows Security event fields alone is not fully achievable — this and related AD-KRB entries provide corroborating indirect signals rather than a single definitive detection.

title: Golden Ticket Indicator: Service Ticket Activity for Account Not Currently Present
description: Service ticket (4769) activity was observed for a user account that has since been deleted, or a SID that does not currently resolve to any AD object, consistent with a Golden Ticket forged using a captured krbtgt hash and an account identity that no longer exists — since a forged ticket does not require the KDC to validate the account's continued existence at request time the way a normal AS-REQ/TGS-REQ round trip would.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service ticket events joined against the current AD account inventory.

detection_logic: Joins 4769 events against a current AD account/SID inventory export and flags tickets referencing an account/SID no longer present.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769
| lookup update=true current_ad_accounts.csv TargetSid OUTPUT account_exists
| where isnull(account_exists)
| table _time, TargetUserName, TargetSid
tuning_guidance: Requires a near-real-time AD account/SID inventory export; account-deletion timing lag can produce false positives immediately after a legitimate deletion — exclude a short grace window.
investigation_steps: Treat as a high-confidence Golden Ticket indicator.
Immediately begin krbtgt password rotation and full incident response.
response_guidance: Full incident response: two-stage krbtgt reset, forensic investigation of the source, and audit of all activity by the forged identity.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Golden Ticket Indicator: Privileged Access Inconsistent with Current Group Membership
description: An account performed a Tier-0-level administrative action (e.g. DCSync, GPO change at domain root) despite not currently being a member of any group that would grant that capability — consistent with a forged ticket containing PAC group-membership data that no longer matches the account's actual current AD state, since a forged Golden Ticket's PAC is built at forgery time and does not automatically stay in sync with subsequent legitimate group-membership changes.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: A privileged administrative action performed by an account, cross-referenced against that account's current group membership
data_sources.description: Correlation between action performed and current authorization.

detection_logic: Joins Tier-0-level directory-change events against a current group-membership export for the acting account and flags mismatches where the action requires privilege the account does not currently hold.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4662, 5136) action=privileged
| lookup update=true current_group_membership.csv SubjectUserName OUTPUT current_groups
| eval required_group=<action_required_group>
| where NOT match(current_groups, required_group)
| table _time, SubjectUserName, action, current_groups
tuning_guidance: Requires a near-real-time group-membership export and a maintained action-to-required-group mapping; a high-value but implementation-intensive detection.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed forged-ticket or PAC-tampering incident.
Begin krbtgt rotation and full incident response.
response_guidance: Full incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Silver Ticket Indicator: Service Ticket Use Without Corresponding TGT
description: Authentication to a service occurred consistent with Kerberos ticket use, but no corresponding TGT-request (4768) or service-ticket-request (4769) sequence from the KDC was observed for that session — since a Silver Ticket is forged using a service account's own hash rather than the krbtgt hash, it can be presented directly to the target service without ever touching the KDC, leaving this gap in the normal request sequence. Silver Ticket detection is inherently limited by this same absence of telemetry.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: Service-level authentication success without a matching preceding 4769 for the same account/service/source
data_sources.description: Absence-based correlation.

detection_logic: Joins service-level logon-success events against the KDC's 4769 log for a matching prior request within an expected window, flagging service access with no matching KDC record — an inherently noisy signal given normal ticket caching also produces this gap.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 AuthenticationPackageName=Kerberos
| join type=left TargetUserName, dest [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769 | rename Client_Address AS src]
| where isnull(Service_Name)
| table _time, TargetUserName, dest, src
tuning_guidance: High false-positive rate from normal Kerberos ticket caching (a client reuses a cached service ticket without a fresh 4769); this detection's practical value is limited and should be treated as a hunting query, not a reliable standing alert — the specification's own guidance to clearly identify Silver Ticket detection limitations applies directly here.
investigation_steps: Manually verify against endpoint/EDR telemetry for the source before treating as a true positive.
Focus investigation on CIFS/HTTP/MSSQL service access to Tier-0-adjacent systems.
response_guidance: If corroborated, rotate the target service account's password and investigate the source.
author: Threat Detection Library
performance_guidance: This absence-based join is expensive and noisy at scale (legitimate ticket caching produces the same gap); scope to CIFS/HTTP/MSSQL access on Tier-0-adjacent systems only rather than running domain-wide.
attack_mapping_note: Silver Ticket forgery bypasses the KDC entirely, so this detection can only observe an indirect absence-of-telemetry pattern that is easily confused with legitimate Kerberos ticket caching; treat as a low-confidence hunting lead.

title: Silver Ticket Indicator: Suspicious Access to CIFS/HTTP/MSSQL Service Account
description: A high-value service (file share via CIFS, a web application via HTTP, or a database via MSSQL) bound to a service account was accessed from a source that has never accessed it before, consistent with — among several other possible explanations — a Silver Ticket forged for that specific service account being used from attacker-controlled infrastructure.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service-account-bound logon events compared against a per-service source baseline.

detection_logic: Filters logon events for accounts on the CIFS/HTTP/MSSQL service-account lookup where the source is not on the account's established baseline.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| lookup high_value_service_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT service_class
| where isnotnull(service_class)
| lookup update=true service_account_src_baseline.csv TargetUserName, src OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, service_class, src, dest
tuning_guidance: Overlaps significantly with AD-AUTH-026; the distinguishing value here is the explicit CIFS/HTTP/MSSQL service-class framing for Silver Ticket triage specifically.
investigation_steps: Verify the new source through independent means (EDR, network telemetry).
Rotate the service account's password if unexplained.
response_guidance: Rotate the service account credential if compromise is suspected.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Pass-the-Ticket: Same Ticket-Derived Session Used from Multiple Hosts
description: The same account authenticated to multiple distinct hosts within an implausibly short window using cached Kerberos tickets, consistent with Pass-the-Ticket: an attacker extracting a valid ticket from one compromised host's memory and replaying it from another to authenticate without ever knowing the underlying password.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Kerberos-authenticated logon events aggregated per account across distinct hosts within a short window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct destination hosts a single account authenticates to via Kerberos within a short rolling window, flagging counts implausible for a single legitimate user session.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 AuthenticationPackageName=Kerberos
| bin _time span=5m
| stats dc(dest) AS dest_count values(dest) AS destinations by _time, TargetUserName
| where dest_count>=5
tuning_guidance: Exclude known automation/orchestration service accounts that legitimately fan out to many hosts quickly.
investigation_steps: Identify the originating host where the ticket was likely extracted.
Investigate all hosts the ticket was used against.
response_guidance: Treat as a confirmed lateral-movement incident; isolate affected hosts and rotate the account's credential.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.003: Pass the Ticket

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Pass-the-Ticket: Privileged Ticket Used from New Workstation
description: A privileged account's Kerberos ticket was used to authenticate from a workstation it has never previously used, immediately following that same account's activity from a different, established workstation — the specific pattern of a stolen ticket being relayed to a new host while the legitimate session may still be active elsewhere.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Kerberos logon events for privileged accounts compared against a source-host baseline within a short window of established activity.

detection_logic: Joins privileged-account Kerberos logons against a source-host baseline; flags a first-seen source occurring within a short window of the account's activity from an established source.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 AuthenticationPackageName=Kerberos
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| lookup update=true ad_privileged_src_baseline.csv TargetUserName, src OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, dest
tuning_guidance: Overlaps with AD-AUTH-021; scoped here specifically to the Pass-the-Ticket framing for triage.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed incident.
Isolate both the originating and new hosts.
response_guidance: Full incident response.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.003: Pass the Ticket

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Overpass-the-Hash: Credential Access Followed by Kerberos Ticket Issuance
description: A credential-access indicator (e.g. LSASS access, per AD-CRED-###) on a host was followed shortly afterward by that same host requesting a Kerberos TGT for an account different from the one that generated the credential-access event, consistent with Overpass-the-Hash: using an extracted NTLM hash to request a legitimate Kerberos ticket rather than replaying the hash directly via NTLM.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: Credential-access indicator on a host followed by a TGT request from that host for a different account
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlates an LSASS-access event (AD-CRED-013) against a subsequent 4768 TGT request from the same host for an account not matching the host's normal logged-on user.
spl:
| savedsearch "AD-CRED-013 Suspicious LSASS Process Access"
| eval stage="1_credential_access"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4768 | eval stage="2_tgt_request"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by host
| where stage_count>=2 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=1800
tuning_guidance: Requires correlation-search support and Sysmon/EDR for the LSASS-access stage; state this detection's limitations clearly — it flags a plausible sequence, not a confirmed Overpass-the-Hash instance, since legitimate credential-manager and SSO activity can produce a similar pattern.
investigation_steps: Treat as a likely credential-theft-and-reuse incident pending confirmation.
Isolate the host and investigate the LSASS-access tool.
response_guidance: Isolate the host, rotate the affected account's credential, and conduct endpoint forensics.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.002: Pass the Hash

author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Overpass-the-Hash cannot be reliably distinguished from legitimate credential-manager/SSO ticket issuance using this sequence alone; treat as a moderate-confidence lead requiring endpoint corroboration.

title: Kerberos Ticket Request Encryption Downgrade Sequence
description: An account's Kerberos ticket requests shifted from AES to RC4 encryption compared to its established baseline, without a corresponding domain-wide policy change, consistent with an attacker-controlled tool deliberately requesting a weaker cipher for a specific account ahead of an offline-cracking attempt.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Ticket request events compared against a per-account encryption-type baseline.

detection_logic: Compares each account's ticket-request encryption type against its historical baseline and flags a shift to a weaker cipher.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4768, 4769)
| lookup update=true krb_encryption_baseline.csv TargetUserName OUTPUT typical_encryption
| where typical_encryption="AES256" AND Ticket_Encryption_Type="0x17"
| table _time, TargetUserName, Ticket_Encryption_Type, typical_encryption
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained per-account encryption-type baseline.
investigation_steps: Correlate with AD-KRB-010's Kerberoasting detection for the same account.
response_guidance: Investigate for Kerberoasting/downgrade-attack activity.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: krbtgt Account Password Reset
description: The krbtgt account's password was reset. Since the krbtgt hash is what all TGTs in the domain are encrypted with, resetting it is both the standard remediation for a suspected Golden Ticket compromise (via the documented two-reset recovery procedure) and something an attacker with sufficient privilege could abuse to disrupt authentication domain-wide — every occurrence warrants immediate confirmation of intent.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Password-change events for the krbtgt account.

detection_logic: Filters 4738 events where TargetUserName is krbtgt.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4738 TargetUserName=krbtgt
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences; confirm against a documented incident-response krbtgt-reset procedure (see AD-KRB-026 for the two-reset recovery sequence) or planned periodic rotation.
investigation_steps: Confirm the reset was performed by an authorized administrator as part of a documented procedure.
If unconfirmed, treat as a live Tier-0 incident.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, treat as a confirmed compromise requiring full incident response including the two-reset recovery procedure performed correctly.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: krbtgt Reset Outside Documented Recovery Procedure
description: A krbtgt password reset occurred without a matching entry in the documented incident-response krbtgt-recovery runbook, distinguishing the legitimate two-reset Golden-Ticket-remediation procedure (which requires two resets spaced to allow replication, performed by an authorized responder as part of a tracked incident) from an unexpected or unauthorized reset.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: krbtgt reset events joined against a change-ticket/runbook-tracking lookup.

detection_logic: Filters krbtgt reset events not matched against an approved incident/change-ticket lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4738 TargetUserName=krbtgt
| lookup krbtgt_reset_tickets.csv _time OUTPUT is_approved
| where isnull(is_approved)
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Requires maintaining a change-ticket lookup for every legitimate krbtgt reset, including periodic scheduled rotations.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident.
Determine who performed the reset and why.
response_guidance: Full incident response if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: krbtgt Object Modified Outside Password Reset
description: An attribute of the krbtgt object other than its password was modified (e.g. its ACL, SPN, or account-control flags), which — since the krbtgt account should essentially never require configuration changes outside password rotation — is a strong indicator of an attacker establishing persistence directly on the account that underlies the entire domain's Kerberos trust.

data_sources.name: Directory Service Event Log
data_sources.description: Directory object-modification events targeting the krbtgt object.

detection_logic: Filters 5136 events where the target object is the krbtgt account and the modified attribute is not related to password/pwdLastSet.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=5136 Object_DN="*CN=krbtgt*"
| where AttributeLDAPDisplayName!="pwdLastSet" AND AttributeLDAPDisplayName!="unicodePwd"
| table _time, SubjectUserName, AttributeLDAPDisplayName, AttributeValue
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences without exception.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed Tier-0 persistence incident.
Review the change and every other action by the acting account.
response_guidance: Revert the change immediately and begin full incident response, including krbtgt rotation.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Kerberos Domain Policy Weakened
description: The domain's Kerberos policy (maximum ticket lifetime, maximum renewal age, clock-skew tolerance) was weakened, which can extend the usable window for stolen tickets or loosen the time-based constraints that limit certain ticket-forgery attacks.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Domain policy change events for Kerberos policy settings.

detection_logic: Filters 4739 domain-policy-change events where the changed policy category is Kerberos-related.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4739 domain_policy_changed="*Kerberos*"
| table _time, SubjectUserName, domain_policy_changed
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets.
investigation_steps: Diff the policy before and after.
Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1484.001: Group Policy Modification

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Kerberos Delegation Ticket Used for Sensitive Service
description: A service ticket flagged as forwardable/delegated (per the ticket options) was used to authenticate to a Tier-0-adjacent service, warranting review of whether the delegation chain that produced it is authorized — see the dedicated AD-DELEG-### section for the underlying delegation-configuration detections.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service ticket events with delegation-related ticket options, restricted to sensitive destination services.

detection_logic: Filters 4769 events where Ticket_Options indicates forwarded/proxy delegation and the target service is on the Tier-0-adjacent lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769
| where match(Ticket_Options, "(?i)(forwarded|proxy)")
| lookup tier0_adjacent_services.csv spn AS Service_Name OUTPUT is_sensitive
| where is_sensitive=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, Service_Name, Ticket_Options
tuning_guidance: Cross-reference with AD-DELEG-### for the configuration side of this activity.
investigation_steps: Confirm the delegation chain is authorized.
Trace back to the originating delegated computer/service.
response_guidance: Investigate if unexplained.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Ticket Renewal Beyond Expected User Session Duration
description: A Kerberos ticket was renewed (rather than freshly issued) repeatedly over a duration substantially longer than the account's typical session length, which can indicate an attacker maintaining a stolen ticket's validity through repeated renewal rather than the ticket naturally expiring and requiring re-authentication.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Kerberos ticket-renewal events aggregated per account.

detection_logic: Counts ticket-renewal events per account over an extended window and flags counts exceeding a typical session's renewal pattern.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4770
| bin _time span=24h
| stats count by _time, TargetUserName, Client_Address
| where count>=5
tuning_guidance: Exclude known long-running automation/service sessions.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for the extended session.
Cross-reference with other credential-theft indicators for the account.
response_guidance: Investigate further if unexplained.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: SPN Added to User Account Followed by Service Ticket Burst
description: An SPN was added to a user account (as opposed to a computer/service account, an unusual placement in most environments) and shortly afterward a burst of service ticket requests targeted that SPN — the specific setup-and-exploit pattern of an attacker registering an SPN on a compromised or newly-created account specifically to make it Kerberoastable, then immediately harvesting the resulting ticket.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: SPN-attribute-added event for a user object, followed by service ticket requests for that SPN
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlates an SPN-added directory-change event on a user object against a subsequent service-ticket-request burst for that SPN within a short window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=5136 AttributeLDAPDisplayName=servicePrincipalName ObjectClass=user
| eval stage="1_spn_added"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769 | eval stage="2_ticket_burst"]
