| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by AttributeValue
| where stage_count>=2 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=3600
tuning_guidance: Requires correlation-search support; a Tier-1 flagship SPN-abuse chain.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed Kerberoasting setup-and-exploit incident.
Rotate the account's password and remove the SPN.
response_guidance: Full incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: SPN Removed Immediately After Kerberoasting Activity
description: An SPN was removed from an account shortly after that SPN was the target of a service-ticket burst, completing the full setup-exploit-cleanup pattern: an attacker adds an SPN, harvests the resulting Kerberoastable ticket, then removes the SPN to reduce the chance of the artifact being noticed during a later review.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: Service ticket burst followed by an SPN-removed directory-change event for the same SPN
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation, the completion of AD-KRB-031's chain.

detection_logic: Correlates a service-ticket burst against a subsequent SPN-removal event for the same value within a short window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769
| bin _time span=10m
| stats dc(Service_Name) AS spn_count values(Service_Name) AS services by _time, TargetUserName
| where spn_count>=1
| eval stage="1_ticket_burst"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=5136 AttributeLDAPDisplayName=servicePrincipalName info=deleted | eval stage="2_spn_removed"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by services
| where stage_count>=2 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=3600
tuning_guidance: Requires correlation-search support; the completed variant of AD-KRB-031's chain.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed, deliberately-cleaned-up Kerberoasting incident.
Rotate the account's password.
response_guidance: Full incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Rare Client Requesting TGT for Multiple Distinct Accounts
description: A single client address requested TGTs for multiple distinct accounts within a short window, which — since a normal workstation's Kerberos traffic is almost always for a single logged-on user at a time — suggests either a shared jump-host/terminal-server (expected) or an attacker with multiple stolen credentials authenticating in sequence from the same staging host.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: TGT request events aggregated per client address.

detection_logic: Counts distinct accounts requesting TGTs from the same client address within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4768
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS account_count values(TargetUserName) AS accounts by _time, Client_Address
| where account_count>=5
tuning_guidance: Exclude known jump-hosts/terminal servers/RDS session hosts on the shared-infrastructure lookup.
investigation_steps: Confirm the source is a known shared-infrastructure host.
If not, investigate as a possible credential-staging host.
response_guidance: Investigate further if unexplained.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: krbtgt Two-Reset Recovery Sequence Verification
description: Tracks whether a declared krbtgt-compromise incident's remediation followed the documented two-reset recovery procedure (reset, wait for replication convergence, reset again) correctly, distinguishing a properly-executed recovery from an incomplete one that leaves the domain still vulnerable to tickets forged with the pre-first-reset hash.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: krbtgt reset events during a declared incident window, checked for the expected two-reset spacing.

detection_logic: Counts krbtgt reset events during a declared incident window and verifies exactly two resets occurred with adequate replication-convergence spacing between them.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4738 TargetUserName=krbtgt earliest=<incident_start> latest=<incident_end>
| stats count values(_time) AS reset_times
| eval resets_complete=if(count>=2, "yes", "no - remediation incomplete")
tuning_guidance: Run manually as part of incident-response verification, scoped to the declared incident window; not intended as a standing alert.
investigation_steps: If resets_complete is 'no', schedule and execute the second reset immediately.
response_guidance: Complete the second reset if the sequence is incomplete.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Ticket-Granting Service Request with Malformed or Anomalous Ticket Options
description: A service ticket request presented an unusual or rarely-seen combination of Kerberos ticket options (flags controlling forwardability, renewability, and proxy delegation) relative to the domain's normal traffic pattern, which some ticket-forgery and abuse tooling produces as a byproduct of how it constructs requests outside the standard Windows Kerberos client library's normal option combinations.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Service ticket request events with Ticket_Options compared against a domain-wide baseline of common combinations.

detection_logic: Compares each request's Ticket_Options value against a baseline of the most common combinations observed domain-wide and flags rare combinations.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769
| top limit=20 Ticket_Options
| appendcols [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4769 | stats count by Ticket_Options | where count<10]
tuning_guidance: Requires an established domain-wide baseline of normal ticket-option combinations; expect meaningful noise since legitimate client/OS version diversity also produces option variation — treat as a low-confidence hunting lead rather than a standing alert.
investigation_steps: Cross-reference the requesting account/client with other indicators before treating as significant.
response_guidance: Low urgency standalone.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: NTLM Authentication by Privileged Account
description: A Tier-0 privileged account authenticated using NTLM rather than Kerberos, which — beyond the operational goal of migrating to Kerberos-only administration — exposes the account to NTLM-specific attacks (relay, weaker cryptography) that a Kerberos-only posture would avoid.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: NTLM credential-validation events joined against the Tier-0 privileged-account lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4776 events where the account is on the Tier-0 privileged-account lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4776
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, Workstation
tuning_guidance: Confirm against known legacy-application exceptions; work toward eliminating NTLM use for Tier-0 accounts entirely.
investigation_steps: Determine why Kerberos was not used (legacy app, NTLM-only service, misconfiguration).
Assess whether this represents a downgrade/relay risk.
response_guidance: Migrate the authentication path to Kerberos where feasible.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.001: Application Access Token

author: Threat Detection Library

title: NTLM Used Where Kerberos Expected
description: An account/destination pair that has historically authenticated via Kerberos suddenly used NTLM instead, which can indicate a Kerberos-availability issue (SPN misconfiguration, DNS problem) or an attacker deliberately forcing an NTLM downgrade to enable relay or weaker-hash attacks.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Logon events compared against a per-account/destination authentication-package baseline.

detection_logic: Joins logon events against a lookup of each account/destination pair's typical authentication package and flags a shift from Kerberos to NTLM.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624
| lookup update=true auth_package_baseline.csv TargetUserName, dest OUTPUT typical_package
| where typical_package="Kerberos" AND AuthenticationPackageName="NTLM"
| table _time, TargetUserName, dest, AuthenticationPackageName
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained per-pair baseline; correlate with concurrent Kerberos-availability issues before attributing to malicious downgrade.
investigation_steps: Check for a Kerberos-availability issue (SPN/DNS) explaining the fallback.
If not explained, investigate for relay/downgrade activity.
response_guidance: Investigate further if unexplained.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.001: Application Access Token

author: Threat Detection Library

title: NTLMv1 Authentication Observed
description: An authentication used NTLMv1, a cryptographically weak protocol version vulnerable to relatively fast offline cracking and downgrade attacks — its continued presence in an environment is itself a standing risk regardless of whether any specific instance is malicious.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Logon events using the NTLMv1 package.

detection_logic: Filters 4624 events where LmPackageName indicates NTLMv1.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 LmPackageName="NTLM V1"
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, dest
tuning_guidance: Identify and remediate the legacy client/application generating NTLMv1 traffic; enforce NTLMv2-only via GPO where feasible.
investigation_steps: Identify the source and the reason NTLMv1 is in use.
Plan remediation to eliminate NTLMv1 entirely.
response_guidance: Remediate the legacy configuration; treat repeated/unexpected NTLMv1 from a new source as higher-priority.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.001: Application Access Token

author: Threat Detection Library

title: High-Volume NTLM Authentication Against Domain Controller
description: An unusually high volume of NTLM authentication attempts hit a Domain Controller in a short window, which can indicate a relay attack funneling many captured authentications through the DC, or a brute-force/credential-testing tool targeting NTLM specifically since it lacks Kerberos's built-in pre-authentication throttling characteristics in some configurations.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: NTLM credential-validation events aggregated per window.

detection_logic: Compares 4776 event volume within a rolling window against a historical baseline.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4776
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count by _time
| eventstats avg(count) AS avg_count stdev(count) AS stdev_count
| where count > (avg_count + 3*stdev_count)
tuning_guidance: Correlate with known legacy-application batch-authentication windows.
investigation_steps: Identify the top source workstations.
Investigate for relay/brute-force activity.
response_guidance: Investigate further if unexplained.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unusual Workstation/Server Pair for NTLM Authentication
description: An NTLM authentication occurred between a workstation and a server that have never previously communicated, which — since NTLM's Workstation field directly identifies the originating host — is a useful lateral-movement signal not always as clearly visible in Kerberos-based authentication.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: NTLM authentication events compared against a per-pair baseline.

detection_logic: Joins NTLM authentication events against a lookup of previously-observed workstation/destination pairs.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4776
| lookup update=true ntlm_pair_baseline.csv Workstation, dest OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, Workstation, dest
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained pair baseline; expect noise in dynamic environments.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for the new pair.
Cross-reference with other lateral-movement indicators.
response_guidance: Investigate further if unjustified.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.001: Application Access Token

author: Threat Detection Library

title: First-Seen NTLM Source Against Domain Controller
description: A source workstation authenticated via NTLM against a Domain Controller for the first time, which is a routine event for legitimate new endpoints but a necessary correlation input for identifying rogue or unmanaged systems interacting directly with Tier-0 infrastructure.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.path: index=<windows_index> EventCode=4776, restricted to DC hosts
data_sources.description: NTLM events compared against a source-workstation baseline.

detection_logic: Joins NTLM events against DC hosts compared against a lookup of previously-seen source workstations.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4776
| lookup domain_controllers.csv host AS dest OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| lookup update=true ntlm_dc_src_baseline.csv Workstation OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, Workstation, dest
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained source-workstation baseline.
investigation_steps: Confirm the workstation is a known, managed domain-joined host.
response_guidance: Investigate unmanaged/rogue devices interacting with DCs directly.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.001: Application Access Token

author: Threat Detection Library

title: NTLM Relay: Privileged Authentication to LDAP from Unusual Source
description: A privileged machine or user account authenticated via NTLM to LDAP/LDAPS from a source that does not match its normal behavior, consistent with an NTLM-relay attack where a coerced authentication (e.g. via PetitPotam-style techniques) was relayed to the LDAP service to perform privileged directory operations on the attacker's behalf.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: NTLM authentication to LDAP joined against a machine-account behavioral baseline.

detection_logic: Filters NTLM logons to LDAP/LDAPS services where the authenticating account is a computer account and the source does not match its typical behavior.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 AuthenticationPackageName=NTLM
| lookup ldap_service_hosts.csv host AS dest OUTPUT is_ldap
| where is_ldap=1 AND match(TargetUserName, "\$$")
| lookup update=true computer_account_src_baseline.csv TargetUserName, src OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, dest
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained LDAP-service-host lookup and computer-account behavioral baseline; a strong candidate for detecting coercion-and-relay chains once tuned.
investigation_steps: Treat as a probable NTLM-relay incident.
Identify what LDAP operations the relayed session performed.
response_guidance: Enforce LDAP signing/channel binding immediately (see AD-LDAP-###) and investigate the source machine for coercion tooling.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: NTLM Relay: Authentication to SMB Shortly After Coercion-Like Activity
description: An NTLM authentication to an SMB service occurred shortly after network activity consistent with an authentication-coercion technique (e.g. an unexpected outbound connection attempt from a server to an unfamiliar host preceding the authentication), a pattern requiring network/EDR telemetry beyond Windows Security logs alone to observe reliably.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: Network connection anomaly from a server followed by NTLM authentication to an SMB service from a different host
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation requiring network telemetry.

detection_logic: Correlates a server-originated outbound connection to a rare destination against a subsequent NTLM SMB authentication event within a short window; requires network telemetry this library does not assume is universally present.
spl:
index=<network_index> src_category=server
| lookup rare_destination_baseline.csv dest OUTPUT is_rare
| where is_rare=1
| eval stage="1_coercion_candidate"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 AuthenticationPackageName=NTLM dest_port=445 | eval stage="2_smb_auth"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by src
| where stage_count>=2 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=300
tuning_guidance: Requires network telemetry (Zeek/Suricata/NDR) in addition to Windows Security logs; without it, this detection cannot fire — an explicit telemetry dependency, not a gap this library will paper over.
investigation_steps: Treat as a probable coercion-and-relay incident.
Investigate the server for coercion tooling and the destination for relay infrastructure.
response_guidance: Isolate the server and enforce SMB/LDAP signing.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: NTLM Authentication Source/Destination Mismatch
description: An NTLM authentication event's Workstation field (the client that originated the authentication) does not match the network-level source address the request actually arrived from, a classic relay signature since the relayed authentication carries the original victim's identity while traveling over a network connection from the relay host.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: NTLM logon events comparing the claimed Workstation field against the actual network source.

detection_logic: Filters NTLM logon events where the Workstation name does not resolve to the IP address the connection actually originated from.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 AuthenticationPackageName=NTLM
| lookup dns_hostname_to_ip.csv hostname AS Workstation OUTPUT expected_ip
| where isnotnull(expected_ip) AND expected_ip!=src
| table _time, TargetUserName, Workstation, src, expected_ip
tuning_guidance: Requires a DNS-hostname-to-IP lookup and can be noisy in environments with NAT/multi-homed hosts; a high-value relay-specific signal once tuned.
investigation_steps: Treat as a probable NTLM-relay incident.
Identify the relay host and the coerced victim.
response_guidance: Enforce SMB/LDAP signing and investigate the relay infrastructure.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Domain Controller Configured to Restrict NTLM Weakened
description: A domain or DC-level policy restricting NTLM authentication (Restrict NTLM: Incoming/Outgoing traffic, audit-only mode) was weakened or disabled, removing a control specifically intended to reduce the domain's exposure to NTLM-based attacks including relay.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Domain policy change events for NTLM-restriction settings.

detection_logic: Filters 4739 events where the changed policy category is NTLM-related.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4739 domain_policy_changed="*NTLM*"
| table _time, SubjectUserName, domain_policy_changed
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets.
investigation_steps: Diff the policy before and after.
Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1484.001: Group Policy Modification

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Machine Account NTLM Authentication to Unexpected Host
description: A computer account authenticated via NTLM to a destination it does not normally communicate with, which — since a DC or server's own machine-account credential authenticating outbound is a common byproduct of a successful coercion attack (the coerced machine authenticates to the attacker-controlled relay target) — is a valuable, if imperfect, indicator when the destination is unexpected.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Machine-account NTLM logon events compared against a per-account destination baseline.

detection_logic: Filters NTLM logon events where TargetUserName is a computer account ($) and the destination is not on the account's established baseline.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 AuthenticationPackageName=NTLM
| where match(TargetUserName, "\$$")
| lookup update=true computer_account_dest_baseline.csv TargetUserName, dest OUTPUT first_seen
| where isnull(first_seen)
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, dest
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained per-machine-account destination baseline; particularly valuable for Domain Controller machine accounts given the DCSync-via-relay attack path.
investigation_steps: Treat DC machine accounts with elevated urgency.
Identify the destination and investigate for relay infrastructure.
response_guidance: Enforce signing/channel binding and investigate the coercion source.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Domain Controller Machine Account Coerced to Authenticate Outbound
description: A Domain Controller's own machine account authenticated outbound via NTLM to a non-DC destination, the single highest-value NTLM-relay target in the domain since a successfully relayed DC machine-account authentication (e.g. relayed to LDAP to grant DCSync rights) can lead directly to full domain compromise.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: DC machine-account outbound NTLM authentication events.

detection_logic: Filters NTLM logon events where TargetUserName is a DC's machine account (per the domain_controllers lookup) and the destination is not another DC.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 AuthenticationPackageName=NTLM
| lookup domain_controllers.csv machine_account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_dc_account
| where is_dc_account=1
| lookup domain_controllers.csv host AS dest OUTPUT is_dc_dest
| where isnull(is_dc_dest)
| table _time, TargetUserName, src, dest
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences given the severity; there is essentially no legitimate reason for a DC's machine account to authenticate outbound via NTLM to a non-DC host.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live, high-priority incident.
Identify what the relayed session was used for (check for DCSync rights grants, AD-REPL-###).
response_guidance: Enforce LDAP signing/channel binding domain-wide immediately; investigate for successful privilege-escalation via the relay.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: NTLM Authentication from Internet-Routable Source
description: An NTLM authentication attempt against internal Active Directory infrastructure originated from a public, Internet-routable IP address, which should never occur under a correctly-segmented network architecture and indicates either a severe network exposure or a successful external breach already inside the perimeter relaying traffic.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: NTLM events where the source address is public/Internet-routable.

detection_logic: Filters 4776 events where the source IP falls outside the organization's internal RFC 1918/documented address space.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4776
| eval is_internal=if(cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", Workstation) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12", Workstation) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16", Workstation), 1, 0)
| where is_internal=0
| table _time, TargetUserName, Workstation
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences; validate the internal-CIDR list matches your actual address plan.
investigation_steps: Treat as a critical incident.
Determine how external traffic is reaching AD infrastructure.
response_guidance: Block the exposure immediately and conduct full incident response.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.001: Application Access Token

author: Threat Detection Library

title: NTLM Pass-the-Hash: Same Hash-Derived Session Fan-Out
description: A single account authenticated via NTLM to an unusually large number of distinct destination hosts within a short window, the NTLM-specific equivalent of the Pass-the-Ticket fan-out pattern (AD-KRB-021) — consistent with Pass-the-Hash tooling replaying a captured NTLM hash across many hosts to identify where it grants access.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: NTLM logon events aggregated per account across distinct destinations within a short window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct destination hosts a single account authenticates to via NTLM within a short rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 AuthenticationPackageName=NTLM
| bin _time span=5m
| stats dc(dest) AS dest_count values(dest) AS destinations by _time, TargetUserName
| where dest_count>=5
tuning_guidance: Exclude known automation/orchestration accounts that legitimately fan out via NTLM.
investigation_steps: Identify the originating host where the hash was likely captured.
Investigate all destination hosts.
response_guidance: Treat as a confirmed lateral-movement incident; isolate affected hosts and rotate the account's credential.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.002: Pass the Hash

author: Threat Detection Library

title: NTLM Audit Logging Disabled or Weakened
description: The audit policy governing NTLM authentication event logging was weakened, which removes visibility into every other AD-NTLM-### detection in this catalogue without necessarily affecting Kerberos-focused audit categories at all.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Audit policy change events for the NTLM/Credential Validation subcategory.

detection_logic: Filters 4719 events where the changed subcategory is Credential Validation or NTLM-related.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4719 Subcategory="Credential Validation"
| table _time, SubjectUserName, Category, Subcategory, AuditPolicyChanges
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences; confirm against a documented audit-policy change ticket.
investigation_steps: Restore the audit policy immediately.
Investigate what activity occurred during the visibility gap.
response_guidance: Restore auditing and treat the gap window with elevated scrutiny.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New User Account Created
description: A new user account was created in Active Directory. Routine during legitimate onboarding, but the necessary building block for detecting unauthorized account creation, especially when the new account is soon added to a privileged group.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: User-creation events.

detection_logic: Filters 4720 user-creation audit events.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4720
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against provisioning-workflow tickets.
investigation_steps: Confirm the account was created through the approved provisioning process.
response_guidance: No standalone action.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: User Created by Unusual Administrator
description: A user account was created by an administrator account not on the maintained list of accounts authorized to provision users, which — since account creation is normally centralized through a small set of HR-integrated automation accounts or designated identity administrators — is a strong signal of out-of-process account creation.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: User-creation events joined against an authorized-provisioner lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4720 events where SubjectUserName is not on the authorized-provisioner lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4720
| lookup authorized_provisioners.csv account AS SubjectUserName OUTPUT is_authorized
| where isnull(is_authorized)
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained authorized-provisioner lookup.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Investigate the creating account's other recent activity.
response_guidance: Disable the created account pending review if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: User Created Outside Business Hours
description: A user account was created well outside normal business hours, which can be legitimate for global-team provisioning but also matches the timing pattern an attacker would choose to reduce the chance of real-time review.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: User-creation events compared against a business-hours baseline.

detection_logic: Filters 4720 events falling outside the organization's defined business-hours window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4720
| eval hour=strftime(_time, "%H"), dow=strftime(_time, "%w")
| where hour<6 OR hour>20 OR dow=0 OR dow=6
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Exclude known global-team provisioning windows.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Low urgency standalone; escalate if paired with other indicators.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Many Users Created Quickly by Same Actor
description: A single actor created an unusually large number of user accounts in a short window, consistent with a scripted, attacker-driven mass-provisioning operation rather than routine, incremental identity administration.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: User-creation events aggregated per actor per window.

detection_logic: Counts 4720 events per actor within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4720
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count values(TargetUserName) AS created_users by _time, SubjectUserName
| where count>=10
tuning_guidance: Raise the threshold for known bulk-onboarding automation accounts.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented bulk-provisioning project.
Treat as a live incident absent one.
response_guidance: Suspend the actor and audit every account created.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: New User Added to Privileged Group Shortly After Creation
description: A newly-created user account was added to a Tier-0 privileged group within a short window of its creation, skipping the normal pattern of a new account starting with limited access and escalating (if ever) only after a documented approval process — a common attacker persistence technique when they already hold sufficient privilege to create and immediately elevate an account.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: User-creation event followed by a privileged-group-membership-add event for the same account
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlates a 4720 creation event against a subsequent 4728/4732/4756 privileged-group-add event for the same account within a short window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4720
| eval stage="1_created"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4728, 4732, 4756) | lookup tier0_privileged_groups.csv group AS Group_Name OUTPUT is_tier0 | where is_tier0=1 | eval stage="2_privileged_add"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by TargetUserName
| where stage_count>=2 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=3600
tuning_guidance: Requires correlation-search support and a Tier-0 group lookup; alert on all occurrences given the severity.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed privilege-escalation incident.
Suspend the account and investigate the creating/adding actor.
response_guidance: Remove the account from the privileged group immediately and investigate.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Disabled Account Re-Enabled
description: A previously-disabled account was re-enabled, which can indicate an attacker reactivating an offboarded/orphaned credential they still possess, or a legitimate rehire/leave-of-absence return.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Account-enable events.

detection_logic: Filters 4722 events.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4722
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against HR/rehire records.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Check for a subsequent logon (AD-AUTH-013).
response_guidance: Disable if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: High-Value Account Disabled
description: An account on the Tier-0 privileged or high-value lookup was disabled, which — beyond a routine offboarding action — can be used to deny a legitimate administrator's access ahead of or during an attack, or to disable a break-glass/monitoring account specifically.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Account-disable events joined against the Tier-0/high-value lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4725 events where TargetUserName is on the Tier-0/high-value lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4725
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against offboarding tickets; alert on all occurrences for break-glass accounts specifically.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Re-enable if unauthorized.
response_guidance: Re-enable immediately if unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1531: Account Access Removal

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Multiple Accounts Disabled in Short Window
description: An unusually large number of accounts were disabled by a single actor in a short window, which can indicate a destructive attack aimed at locking out legitimate users/SOC staff, or a mass-offboarding event that should be confirmed against a corresponding business process.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Account-disable events aggregated per actor per window.

detection_logic: Counts 4725 events per actor within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4725
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count values(TargetUserName) AS disabled_users by _time, SubjectUserName
| where count>=10
tuning_guidance: Correlate with legitimate offboarding-batch processes.
investigation_steps: Confirm against an offboarding project.
Treat as a live incident absent one.
response_guidance: Re-enable affected accounts immediately if unauthorized; lock the acting account.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1531: Account Access Removal

author: Threat Detection Library

title: User Account Deleted
description: A user account was deleted, permanently removing the object (recoverable only via AD Recycle Bin/tombstone restoration where enabled) and destroying its historical group-membership and attribute record along with it.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: User-deletion events.

detection_logic: Filters 4726 events, prioritized by the Tier-0/high-value lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4726
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, is_privileged
tuning_guidance: Confirm against offboarding/decommission tickets; alert on all occurrences for Tier-0 accounts.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Restore from AD Recycle Bin if unauthorized (AD-PERSIST-###).
response_guidance: Restore if unauthorized.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1531: Account Access Removal

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Bulk User Deletion
description: An unusually large number of user accounts were deleted by a single actor in a short window, a severe destructive-activity indicator consistent with an identity-focused ransomware/sabotage attack rather than routine offboarding, which almost always disables rather than immediately deletes.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: User-deletion events aggregated per actor per window.

detection_logic: Counts 4726 events per actor within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4726
| bin _time span=15m
| stats count values(TargetUserName) AS deleted_users by _time, SubjectUserName
| where count>=10
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences; legitimate identity administration almost never deletes accounts in bulk (disable is the norm).
investigation_steps: Treat as a live destructive-attack incident.
Halt further deletions and assess AD Recycle Bin recovery options immediately.
response_guidance: Engage incident response immediately; restore from AD Recycle Bin or backup.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1531: Account Access Removal

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Enabled Account Immediately Used for Privileged Action
description: An account was enabled and, within a short window, performed a privileged administrative action — a materially higher-confidence variant of AD-AUTH-013 that flags the specific downstream action taken rather than just the logon itself.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: Account-enable event followed by a privileged directory-modification event for the same account
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlates a 4722 event against a subsequent privileged 4662 event for the same account within a short window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4722
| eval stage="1_enabled"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4662 action=privileged | rename SubjectUserName AS TargetUserName | eval stage="2_privileged_action"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by TargetUserName
| where stage_count>=2 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=1800
tuning_guidance: Requires correlation-search support; a strong Tier-1 candidate.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed incident.
Disable the account and investigate the enabling actor.
response_guidance: Full incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Administrator Resets Another User's Password
description: An administrator reset another user's password, which — while a routine help-desk action — can also be used by an attacker with sufficient privilege to take over another user's (especially another admin's) account.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Password-reset-attempt events where the acting user differs from the target.

detection_logic: Filters 4724 events where SubjectUserName differs from TargetUserName.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4724
| where SubjectUserName!=TargetUserName
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against help-desk tickets; scope closer scrutiny to resets targeting privileged accounts (AD-USER-013).
investigation_steps: Confirm the reset was requested by the account owner through the proper channel.
Check for a subsequent login from an unfamiliar source.
response_guidance: Notify the account owner and verify the reset was legitimate.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Privileged User Password Reset
description: A Tier-0 privileged account's password was reset by another user, warranting elevated scrutiny given the target's blast radius compared to the general password-reset detection.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Password-reset events joined against the Tier-0 lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4724 events where TargetUserName is on the Tier-0 lookup and SubjectUserName differs.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4724
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1 AND SubjectUserName!=TargetUserName
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets; alert on all occurrences.
investigation_steps: Confirm the reset was authorized.
Verify with the account owner directly through an out-of-band channel.
response_guidance: Reset again through the proper channel if unauthorized and investigate the acting account.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Single Actor Resets Many Users' Passwords
description: A single actor reset an unusually large number of distinct users' passwords in a short window, a pattern consistent with a mass account-lockout/ransomware-style attack against the user population's ability to authenticate, or credential-harvesting preparation ahead of a broader compromise.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Password-reset events aggregated per actor per window.

detection_logic: Counts distinct target accounts reset by the same actor within a rolling window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4724
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(TargetUserName) AS reset_count values(TargetUserName) AS accounts by _time, SubjectUserName
| where reset_count>=10
tuning_guidance: Correlate with a documented mass-password-reset security response (e.g. post-breach precautionary reset) before treating as malicious.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented security response.
Treat as a live incident absent one.
response_guidance: Engage incident response immediately absent a documented justification.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Service Account Password Reset
description: A service account's password was reset, which — beyond a legitimate scheduled rotation — can disrupt the applications depending on it (if not coordinated) or indicate an attacker seizing control of the account by locking out its legitimate automated consumers.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Password-reset events joined against the service-account lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4724 events where TargetUserName is on the service-account lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4724
| lookup service_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_service_account
| where is_service_account=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against a scheduled rotation calendar.
investigation_steps: Confirm the reset was coordinated with the account's application owner.
Verify the application continues functioning correctly.
response_guidance: Investigate if unexpected.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Password Reset Followed by Immediate Authentication
description: A password reset was immediately followed by a successful authentication using the new password, which — while consistent with a legitimate help-desk-assisted reset-and-login flow — is also exactly the sequence expected when an attacker with reset privilege takes over an account: reset the password, then log in with the new value before the legitimate owner notices.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: Password-reset event followed by a successful logon for the same account within a short window
data_sources.description: Two-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlates a 4724 reset event against a subsequent 4624 success for the same account within a short window, where the resetting actor differs from the account owner.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4724
| where SubjectUserName!=TargetUserName
| eval stage="1_reset"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 | eval stage="2_login"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count values(src) AS sources by TargetUserName
| where stage_count>=2 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=600
tuning_guidance: Exclude documented help-desk-assisted reset workflows where the analyst confirms the reset with the user before hanging up, and the user then logs in.
investigation_steps: Confirm with the account owner that they performed the login.
If not, treat as a confirmed account-takeover incident.
response_guidance: Reset again and investigate if the login is not confirmed as legitimate.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Password Never Expires Flag Set on Privileged Account
description: A Tier-0 privileged account had its 'Password never expires' flag newly enabled, removing the standard rotation cadence that limits how long a compromised credential remains valid — a weakening of the account's security posture that is particularly consequential given its privilege level.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Account-change events where UserAccountControl shows the password-never-expires flag newly set, joined against the Tier-0 lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4738 events where the new UserAccountControl includes the DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD flag (0x10000) for accounts on the Tier-0 lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4738
| where match(UserAccountControl, "(?i)(DONT_EXPIRE_PASSWORD|0x10000)")
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against a documented exception for break-glass accounts specifically designed with this flag.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Revert if unauthorized.
response_guidance: Revert and enforce normal rotation if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Smart Card Requirement Removed from Privileged Account
description: A Tier-0 privileged account's 'Smart card is required for interactive logon' flag was removed, downgrading the account's authentication requirement from possession-based multi-factor to password-only — a significant weakening of a high-value account's security posture that would allow an attacker with only the account's password (e.g. from a hash-derived attack) to authenticate interactively.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Account-change events where the smart-card-required flag transitions from set to unset, joined against the Tier-0 lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4738 events for Tier-0 accounts where the SMARTCARD_REQUIRED flag (0x40000) is removed.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4738
| lookup update=true smartcard_required_baseline.csv TargetUserName OUTPUT was_smartcard_required
| where was_smartcard_required=1 AND NOT match(UserAccountControl, "(?i)(SMARTCARD_REQUIRED|0x40000)")
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS TargetUserName OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained smart-card-requirement baseline; alert on all occurrences for Tier-0 accounts.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident.
Restore the requirement immediately.
response_guidance: Restore the smart-card requirement and rotate the account's password given the downgrade window.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Trusted-for-Delegation Flag Set on User Account
description: A user account had the 'Trusted for Delegation' (unconstrained delegation) or 'Trusted to Authenticate for Delegation' flag set, an unusual configuration for a user object (this flag is far more commonly applied to service/computer accounts) and a significant delegation-abuse enabler — see the dedicated AD-DELEG-### section for the full unconstrained-delegation detection coverage.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Account-change events where a delegation-related UserAccountControl flag is newly set on a user object.

detection_logic: Filters 4738 events on user (non-computer) objects where a delegation flag (TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION 0x80000, TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION 0x1000000) is newly set.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4738
| where NOT match(TargetUserName, "\$$") AND match(UserAccountControl, "(?i)(TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION|TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION|0x80000|0x1000000)")
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, UserAccountControl
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences; cross-reference with AD-DELEG-001.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification — this is rarely legitimate on a user account.
Revert if unauthorized.
response_guidance: Revert immediately.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK T1558: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Primary Group ID Changed to Privileged RID
description: An account's primaryGroupID attribute was changed to a privileged well-known RID (e.g. 512 for Domain Admins), a rarely-used but effective privilege-escalation and persistence technique since primary-group membership does not always appear in the same member-list views administrators typically audit for group membership.

data_sources.name: Directory Service Event Log
data_sources.description: primaryGroupID attribute-change events.

detection_logic: Filters 5136 events where the modified attribute is primaryGroupID and the new value matches a privileged well-known RID.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=5136 AttributeLDAPDisplayName=primaryGroupID
| lookup privileged_rids.csv rid AS AttributeValue OUTPUT is_privileged_rid
| where is_privileged_rid=1
| table _time, Object_DN, AttributeValue, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences; primaryGroupID changes are exceptionally rare in normal administration.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed privilege-escalation incident.
Revert the primaryGroupID and audit the account's actual group memberships.
response_guidance: Revert immediately and investigate the acting account.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: User Added to Domain Admins
description: An account was added to the Domain Admins group, the single most consequential privilege grant in a typical Active Directory domain — every occurrence should be traceable to an approved, documented change.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Global-group membership-add events for Domain Admins.

detection_logic: Filters 4728 events where Group_Name is Domain Admins.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4728 Group_Name="Domain Admins"
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, Group_Name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences; confirm against an approved privileged-access-request ticket.
investigation_steps: Confirm the grant against an approved request.
Review the new member's subsequent activity.
response_guidance: Remove if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: User Removed from Domain Admins
description: An account was removed from Domain Admins. Routine offboarding/role-change activity, but the necessary building block for detecting the add-use-remove pattern (AD-GRP-006) an attacker uses to minimize their standing footprint in the group's membership list.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Global-group membership-remove events for Domain Admins.

detection_logic: Filters 4729 events where Group_Name is Domain Admins.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4729 Group_Name="Domain Admins"
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, Group_Name
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Cross-reference with AD-GRP-006 for a short-lived-membership pattern.
response_guidance: No standalone action.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: User Added to Enterprise Admins or Schema Admins
description: An account was added to Enterprise Admins or Schema Admins, forest-wide privilege groups whose membership should normally be empty or near-empty outside of specific, time-boxed forest-level operations (schema extension, trust creation).

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.path: index=<windows_index> EventCode=4728 Group_Name IN ("Enterprise Admins", "Schema Admins")
data_sources.description: Global-group membership-add events for forest-level privilege groups.

detection_logic: Filters 4728 events for Enterprise Admins/Schema Admins.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4728 Group_Name IN ("Enterprise Admins", "Schema Admins")
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, Group_Name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences; confirm against an approved forest-level-operation change ticket.
investigation_steps: Confirm the grant against an approved, time-boxed request.
Verify removal after the forest-level operation completes.
response_guidance: Remove immediately if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: User Added to Local Administrators on Domain Controller
description: An account was added to the local Administrators group on a Domain Controller specifically — functionally equivalent to Domain Admins on that DC (and, transitively, on the whole domain given the DC's role), but potentially overlooked by reviews scoped only to domain-level group membership.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.path: index=<windows_index> EventCode=4732 Group_Name="Administrators", restricted to DC hosts
data_sources.description: Local-group membership-add events for Administrators on DC hosts.

detection_logic: Filters 4732 events where Group_Name is Administrators and dest is on the Domain Controller inventory.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4732 Group_Name="Administrators"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv host AS dest OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, dest
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences.
investigation_steps: Confirm the grant against an approved request.
Review the new member's subsequent activity.
response_guidance: Remove if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: User Added to Account Operators, Backup Operators, or Server Operators
description: An account was added to one of the built-in Tier-0-adjacent operator groups (Account Operators, Backup Operators, Server Operators), each of which grants a specific, powerful capability on Domain Controllers — Account Operators can modify most user/group objects, Backup Operators can bypass file permissions to back up (and therefore access) NTDS.dit, and Server Operators can manage DC services.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.path: index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4728, 4732) Group_Name IN ("Account Operators", "Backup Operators", "Server Operators")
data_sources.description: Group membership-add events for the built-in operator groups.

detection_logic: Filters 4728/4732 events for the three operator groups.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4728, 4732) Group_Name IN ("Account Operators", "Backup Operators", "Server Operators")
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, Group_Name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences given each group's Tier-0-adjacent capability.
investigation_steps: Confirm the grant against an approved request.
See AD-CRED-018 through AD-CRED-020 for the corresponding abuse-detection coverage.
response_guidance: Remove if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Rapid Privileged Group Add-Use-Remove Pattern
description: An account was added to a Tier-0 privileged group, performed at least one privileged action, and was then removed from the group — all within a short window — the specific pattern of an attacker minimizing the standing footprint of their privilege escalation by only holding the elevated membership for as long as strictly necessary to act.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: Privileged-group-add event, a privileged action by the same account, and a subsequent privileged-group-remove event
data_sources.description: Three-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlation search requiring: (1) 4728/4732 add to a Tier-0 group, (2) a privileged action by the account, (3) 4729/4733 removal from the same group — all within a 2-hour window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4728, 4732)
| lookup tier0_privileged_groups.csv group AS Group_Name OUTPUT is_tier0
| where is_tier0=1
| eval stage="1_added"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4662 action=privileged | rename SubjectUserName AS TargetUserName | eval stage="2_action"]
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4729, 4733) | lookup tier0_privileged_groups.csv group AS Group_Name OUTPUT is_tier0 | where is_tier0=1 | eval stage="3_removed"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by TargetUserName
| where stage_count>=3 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=7200
tuning_guidance: Requires correlation-search support; the flagship privileged-group-abuse chain — alert on all matches.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed privilege-escalation incident.
Investigate the acting account and every privileged action taken during the window.
response_guidance: Full incident response: suspend the account, audit every action taken while privileged, and review who performed the add/remove operations.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Universal Group Membership Change for Privileged Group
description: An account was added to or removed from a universal group on the Tier-0 lookup (universal groups can carry membership across the entire forest, making them a particularly high-leverage privilege-grant mechanism in multi-domain environments).

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Universal-group membership-change events joined against the Tier-0 lookup.

detection_logic: Filters 4756/4757 events where Group_Name is on the Tier-0 lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4756, 4757)
| lookup tier0_privileged_groups.csv group AS Group_Name OUTPUT is_tier0
| where is_tier0=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, Group_Name, EventCode
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences.
investigation_steps: Confirm the change against an approved request.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Privileged Group Membership Changed by Unusual Actor
description: A Tier-0 group's membership was changed by an account outside the small, established set of identity administrators who normally manage privileged group membership — a materially higher-priority variant of the general group-change detections given the actor's novelty.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Privileged group membership-change events joined against an authorized-identity-admin lookup.

detection_logic: Filters privileged group-change events where SubjectUserName is not on the authorized-identity-admin lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4728,4729,4732,4733,4756,4757)
| lookup tier0_privileged_groups.csv group AS Group_Name OUTPUT is_tier0
| where is_tier0=1
| lookup authorized_identity_admins.csv account AS SubjectUserName OUTPUT is_authorized
| where isnull(is_authorized)
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, Group_Name
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained authorized-identity-admin lookup; a Tier-1 candidate.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident.
Investigate how the acting account obtained the capability to change Tier-0 group membership.
response_guidance: Revert immediately and suspend the acting account pending investigation.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Group Policy Creator Owners Membership Changed
description: An account was added to Group Policy Creator Owners, granting the ability to create new GPOs — combined with the ability to link a newly-created GPO to a sensitive OU (if the account or a colluding account also holds link rights there), this can be a path to fleet-wide compromise via GPO-based persistence (see AD-GPO-###).

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.path: index=<windows_index> EventCode=4728 Group_Name="Group Policy Creator Owners"
data_sources.description: Global-group membership-add events for Group Policy Creator Owners.

detection_logic: Filters 4728 events where Group_Name is Group Policy Creator Owners.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=4728 Group_Name="Group Policy Creator Owners"
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets.
investigation_steps: Confirm the grant against an approved request.
Monitor the account for subsequent GPO creation/linking activity.
response_guidance: Remove if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DNSAdmins Membership Changed
description: An account was added to DNSAdmins, a group historically abused via a known privilege-escalation technique where a malicious DLL is configured as a DNS server plugin and loaded with SYSTEM privileges when the DNS service restarts — see the dedicated DNS-server-configuration detection (AD-DC-###) for the corresponding abuse indicator.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Group membership-add events for DNSAdmins.

detection_logic: Filters 4728/4732 events where Group_Name is DNSAdmins.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4728, 4732) Group_Name="DNSAdmins"
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against change tickets; alert on all occurrences given the known privilege-escalation path this group enables.
investigation_steps: Confirm the grant against an approved request.
Monitor for a subsequent DNS server configuration change (custom plugin DLL) and DNS service restart.
response_guidance: Remove if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Nested Low-Privilege Group Added to Privileged Group
description: A group (rather than a user) was added as a member of a Tier-0 privileged group, which — since group nesting means every current and future member of the nested group inherits the privilege — is a broader and less immediately visible escalation than adding a single user, and warrants tracing the nested group's own membership to understand the true resulting population with privileged access.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Group-membership-add events where the added member is itself a group, joined against the Tier-0 lookup.

detection_logic: Filters group-membership-add events where the target Group_Name is Tier-0 and the added member (TargetUserName) resolves to a group object rather than a user.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4728, 4732)
| lookup tier0_privileged_groups.csv group AS Group_Name OUTPUT is_tier0
| where is_tier0=1
| lookup ad_object_class.csv object AS TargetUserName OUTPUT object_class
| where object_class="group"
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, Group_Name
tuning_guidance: Requires an object-class lookup distinguishing users from groups; alert on all occurrences given the scope of nested privilege expansion.
investigation_steps: Enumerate the full current and historical membership of the nested group.
Treat every member as now effectively Tier-0 privileged.
response_guidance: Remove the nesting immediately if unauthorized and audit every member of the nested group.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Multi-Level Nested Group Chain to Tier-0 Discovered
description: A periodic recursive membership-resolution scan discovered a user account that is indirectly a member of a Tier-0 group through two or more levels of group nesting, which — since standard membership reviews often check only direct membership — can represent a long-standing, undetected privilege-escalation path an attacker (or a well-intentioned but risky nesting decision) has created.

data_sources.name: Recursive Membership Scan
data_sources.path: Scheduled recursive group-membership resolution against Tier-0 groups via the AD module/LDAP
data_sources.description: Periodic full membership-chain resolution.

detection_logic: A scheduled search (not event-driven) that recursively resolves every Tier-0 group's full transitive membership and flags accounts reachable only through 2+ levels of nesting.
spl:
| ldapsearch domain=<domain> search="(&(objectCategory=group)(cn=Domain Admins))" attrs="member"
| <recursive_membership_expansion>
| where nesting_depth>=2
| table account, nesting_depth, chain
tuning_guidance: Requires an LDAP-search-capable Splunk app/add-on or an external recursive-resolution script feeding results into Splunk.
investigation_steps: Review each discovered indirect-privilege path for legitimacy.
Flatten unnecessary nesting to improve membership auditability.
response_guidance: Remove unauthorized nesting chains.
author: Threat Detection Library
performance_guidance: Recursive membership resolution is expensive; run as a daily/weekly scheduled search using an LDAP-search-capable app rather than ad-hoc, and cache results between runs.

title: AdminSDHolder ACL Modified
description: The AdminSDHolder object's ACL was modified — since the SDProp process periodically copies AdminSDHolder's ACL onto every object in a protected (Tier-0) group, a malicious ACE added here silently propagates to every current and future protected account/group, making this one of the highest-leverage single persistence points in the entire domain.

data_sources.name: Directory Service Event Log
data_sources.description: Directory object-modification events targeting the AdminSDHolder object's ACL.

detection_logic: Filters 5136 events where the target object is AdminSDHolder and the modified attribute is nTSecurityDescriptor.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=5136 Object_DN="*CN=AdminSDHolder*" AttributeLDAPDisplayName=nTSecurityDescriptor
| table _time, SubjectUserName, Object_DN
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences without exception; this object's ACL should change only through a rare, carefully-reviewed administrative process.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed Tier-0 persistence incident.
Determine what ACE was added and to whom it grants access.
response_guidance: Revert immediately and audit every protected object for the propagated ACE; force an immediate SDProp cycle after reverting.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unusual ACE Added to AdminSDHolder
description: A new access control entry was added to AdminSDHolder's DACL granting a trustee outside the small set of built-in, expected principals (Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, SYSTEM, Administrators) a right such as GenericAll, WriteDACL, or WriteOwner — the specific, most dangerous form of AdminSDHolder tampering, since this grants the attacker's chosen trustee standing control over every current and future protected account.

data_sources.name: Directory Service Event Log
data_sources.description: AdminSDHolder ACL-change events with the new trustee/right, compared against an expected-trustee lookup.

detection_logic: Filters AdminSDHolder ACL-change events where the added trustee is not on a maintained expected-trustee lookup.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=5136 Object_DN="*CN=AdminSDHolder*" AttributeLDAPDisplayName=nTSecurityDescriptor
| rex field=AttributeValue "trustee=(?<new_trustee>[^;]+)"
| lookup expected_adminsdholder_trustees.csv trustee AS new_trustee OUTPUT is_expected
| where isnull(is_expected)
| table _time, SubjectUserName, new_trustee
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained expected-trustee lookup; alert on all occurrences.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed Tier-0 persistence incident.
Determine every protected object the new trustee can now control.
response_guidance: Remove the ACE immediately and audit for its use.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: AdminSDHolder Inheritance Setting Changed
description: AdminSDHolder's ACL-inheritance-blocking configuration was changed, which controls a core part of how the SDProp process protects Tier-0 objects from inheriting unintended permissions from their parent OU — tampering here can weaken the entire protection mechanism the domain depends on for its most sensitive accounts.

data_sources.name: Directory Service Event Log
data_sources.description: AdminSDHolder inheritance-flag configuration-change events.

detection_logic: Filters AdminSDHolder modification events touching the inheritance-blocking flag specifically.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=5136 Object_DN="*CN=AdminSDHolder*" AttributeLDAPDisplayName=nTSecurityDescriptor
| where match(AttributeValue, "(?i)inheritance")
| table _time, SubjectUserName, Object_DN
tuning_guidance: Alert on all occurrences.
investigation_steps: Treat as a live incident.
Restore the correct inheritance configuration.
response_guidance: Restore immediately.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: SDProp-Protected Object ACL Diverges from AdminSDHolder Template
description: A protected (Tier-0) object's ACL was found to differ from the current AdminSDHolder template outside of the normal SDProp propagation cycle, which can indicate either a protected object was modified directly and SDProp has not yet run to correct it, or (less commonly) a modification specifically timed to survive briefly before the next SDProp cycle overwrites it — worth investigating in either case.

data_sources.name: Directory Service Event Log
data_sources.description: ACL-change events on protected (AdminSDHolder-governed) objects compared against the current AdminSDHolder template.

detection_logic: Filters ACL-change events on objects flagged as SDProp-protected (adminCount=1) where the resulting ACL does not match the current AdminSDHolder template.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=5136 AttributeLDAPDisplayName=nTSecurityDescriptor
| lookup sdprop_protected_objects.csv Object_DN OUTPUT is_protected
| where is_protected=1
| lookup update=true adminsdholder_template.csv OUTPUT current_template
| where AttributeValue!=current_template
| table _time, Object_DN, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained current-AdminSDHolder-template snapshot; expect the divergence to self-correct at the next SDProp cycle (roughly every 60 minutes by default) for legitimate transient states.
investigation_steps: Determine if this is a transient pre-SDProp state or a persistent divergence.
Investigate the modifying account if persistent.
response_guidance: Force an SDProp cycle if the divergence persists beyond the expected interval.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: AdminCount Attribute Set on Ordinary Account
description: An account's adminCount attribute was manually set to 1 without the account currently being a member of any Tier-0 protected group, which can be used to opt an ordinary account into SDProp protection (and its associated ACL) for reasons unrelated to legitimate group membership, or as a marker/side-effect of other persistence tooling.

data_sources.name: Directory Service Event Log
data_sources.description: adminCount attribute-change events joined against current Tier-0 group membership.

detection_logic: Filters adminCount-set-to-1 events where the target account is not currently a member of any Tier-0 group.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode=5136 AttributeLDAPDisplayName=adminCount AttributeValue=1
| lookup tier0_group_members.csv account AS Object_DN OUTPUT is_currently_privileged
| where isnull(is_currently_privileged)
| table _time, Object_DN, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained current-membership lookup; some legitimate lingering adminCount=1 values exist from historical membership and are lower priority than a fresh manual set on a never-privileged account.
investigation_steps: Determine why this account was manually flagged as protected.
Investigate the acting account.
response_guidance: Investigate further if unexplained.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Custom Tier-0 Group Membership Changed
description: An organization-specific custom Tier-0 group (defined on the configurable asset/group lookup rather than one of AD's built-in privilege groups) had its membership changed, extending this catalogue's privileged-group coverage to whatever groups the organization has designated as sensitive beyond the Microsoft defaults.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Group membership-change events joined against the custom Tier-0 group lookup.

detection_logic: Filters group-membership-change events where Group_Name is on the custom Tier-0 group lookup (separate from the built-in-group lookup used elsewhere).
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4728,4729,4732,4733,4756,4757)
| lookup custom_tier0_groups.csv group AS Group_Name OUTPUT is_custom_tier0
| where is_custom_tier0=1
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, Group_Name, EventCode
tuning_guidance: Requires and depends entirely on the organization maintaining its own custom Tier-0 group inventory.
investigation_steps: Confirm the change against an approved request.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Group Membership Change Immediately Followed by Privileged Logon
description: An account was added to a Tier-0 group and, within minutes, logged on and immediately began performing privileged actions — confirming the escalation was actually exploited rather than a routine, unused administrative grant.

data_sources.name: Correlated Multi-Source Log
data_sources.path: Privileged-group-add event followed by a logon and privileged action for the same account
data_sources.description: Multi-stage correlation.

detection_logic: Correlates a Tier-0 group-add event against a subsequent logon and privileged action for the same account within a short window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4728, 4732)
| lookup tier0_privileged_groups.csv group AS Group_Name OUTPUT is_tier0
| where is_tier0=1
| eval stage="1_added"
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4624 | eval stage="2_login"]
| append [search index=<windows_index> EventCode=4662 action=privileged | rename SubjectUserName AS TargetUserName | eval stage="3_action"]
| stats earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen values(stage) AS stages dc(stage) AS stage_count by TargetUserName
| where stage_count>=3 AND (last_seen-first_seen)<=1800
tuning_guidance: Requires correlation-search support; a Tier-1 candidate.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed incident.
Investigate the entire chain: who added the account, and what it did.
response_guidance: Full incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Protected Users Group Membership Removed
description: A privileged account was removed from the Protected Users group, which — since Protected Users disables several credential-caching and legacy-authentication behaviors specifically to reduce Pass-the-Hash/ticket-abuse risk for its members — reduces that account's protection against exactly the credential-theft techniques covered throughout this catalogue's AD-KRB and AD-CRED sections.

data_sources.name: Windows Security Event Log
data_sources.description: Group membership-remove events for Protected Users.

detection_logic: Filters 4729/4733 events where Group_Name is Protected Users.
spl:
index=<windows_index> EventCode IN (4729, 4733) Group_Name="Protected Users"
| table _time, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName
tuning_guidance: Confirm against a documented, justified exception (Protected Users membership can occasionally break legacy application compatibility, requiring a deliberate opt-out).
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Re-add if unauthorized.
response_guidance: Re-add the account if the removal was unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Computer Account Created by Standard User via MachineAccountQuota
description: Detects a computer object created in AD by a security principal that is not a member of a delegated computer-join group or IT staff. By default every authenticated user can join up to ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota (default 10) computers to the domain, creating a self-controlled computer account. Attackers abuse this to mint an account they control the password for, which is then used as the impersonation account in Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) attacks. Legitimate joins are usually performed by IT staff, SCCM/Intune service accounts, or the join happens via a delegated OU with a dedicated group.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4741 (computer account created).

detection_logic: Event ID 4741 (computer account created) where Subject_Account_Name is not present in an authorized-joiners lookup.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4741
| lookup authorized_computer_joiners.csv account OUTPUT is_authorized
| where isnull(is_authorized)
| table _time, dvc, Sam_Account_Name, Subject_Account_Name
tuning_guidance: Populate authorized_computer_joiners.csv with IT staff, SCCM/Intune/MDT service accounts, and any delegated OU-join service accounts. This is the essential precondition check for RBCD via MachineAccountQuota (see AD-X chain).
investigation_steps: Identify the creating account and its group memberships.
Check ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota effective value for the domain.
Review the new computer object's msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute for RBCD configuration.
Correlate with subsequent authentication from the new computer account.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, disable and investigate the new computer object; consider lowering ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0 domain-wide and delegating join rights explicitly instead.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Single Source Creates Multiple Computer Accounts Rapidly
description: Detects one security principal creating multiple computer accounts within a short window — consistent with an attacker probing MachineAccountQuota limits, staging several attacker-controlled computer objects for RBCD, or automated tooling (e.g. Impacket addcomputer.py, PowerMad) sweeping the quota.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4741.

detection_logic: Event ID 4741 grouped by Subject_Account_Name; alert when distinct_count(Sam_Account_Name) >= 4 within 30 minutes.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4741
| bucket _time span=30m
| stats dc(Sam_Account_Name) as computers_created values(Sam_Account_Name) as computer_names by _time, Subject_Account_Name
| where computers_created >= 4
tuning_guidance: Exclude bulk-provisioning windows for known imaging/SCCM service accounts via a lookup allowlist.
investigation_steps: Identify the source workstation/session of the creating account.
Check whether Impacket/PowerMad/PowerShell AD module tooling artifacts are present on the source host.
Review each created computer object for RBCD attributes.
response_guidance: Disable all newly created computer accounts pending validation; reset credentials of the creating account if compromise is suspected.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Computer Account Deleted
description: Detects deletion of a computer object from AD. While normal during decommission cycles, deletion of computer accounts for domain controllers, servers, or Tier-0 infrastructure is highly abnormal and may indicate destructive activity or an attempt to hide a compromised computer account's history.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4743 (computer account deleted).

detection_logic: Event ID 4743 (computer account deleted).
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4743
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS Target_Account_Name OUTPUT is_dc
| lookup tier0_computers.csv computer_name AS Target_Account_Name OUTPUT is_tier0
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Target_Account_Name, is_dc, is_tier0
tuning_guidance: Alert immediately if is_dc or is_tier0 is populated; otherwise route to a lower-priority change-review queue.
investigation_steps: Confirm change-ticket/decommission approval exists.
Verify the deleted computer's last activity and role.
Check for concurrent deletion of related objects (DNS records, GPO links).
