detection_logic: Scheduled comparison of versionNumber (AD) against GPT.INI Version (SYSVOL) for every GPO; alert on any mismatch.
spl:
| ldapsearch domain=<domain> search="(objectClass=groupPolicyContainer)" attrs="cn,versionNumber,gPCFileSysPath"
| join gpo_guid [ | inputlookup sysvol_gptini_scan.csv ]
| where ad_version!=sysvol_version
| table gpo_guid, cn, ad_version, sysvol_version
tuning_guidance: This detection requires an LDAP-search-capable Splunk app/add-on plus a scripted SYSVOL scan input — it cannot run purely from Windows Security event data. Explicitly flagged as a telemetry dependency to validate before deployment.
investigation_steps: Identify the specific GPO and which side (AD vs SYSVOL) is out of sync.
Review the actual applied SYSVOL content for unexpected changes.
Check file-system access logs for the account that modified SYSVOL directly.
response_guidance: Investigate as probable direct SYSVOL tampering; restore SYSVOL content from a known-good backup and reconcile the version numbers.

references.title: Domain Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification

author: Threat Detection Library
performance_guidance: Run as a scheduled (e.g. hourly) report rather than a real-time search; requires a companion SYSVOL GPT.INI scan process feeding sysvol_gptini_scan.csv.
attack_mapping_note: Requires an LDAP-search-capable Splunk add-on and a scripted SYSVOL GPT.INI scan feeding a lookup; this is not achievable from Windows Security event data alone.

title: GPO Owner Changed
description: Detects the owner attribute of a GPO's security descriptor changing. As with any AD object, the owner implicitly holds WriteDACL rights, so an attacker who becomes owner of a broadly linked GPO gains a durable path to modify its permissions and content regardless of the current explicit ACL.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on nTSecurityDescriptor Owner field for a groupPolicyContainer object.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 on a groupPolicyContainer object where the security-descriptor Owner SID changes to an unexpected principal.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="nTSecurityDescriptor" Object_Class=groupPolicyContainer
| rex field=Attribute_Value "Owner=(?<new_owner>\S+)"
| lookup gpo_management_principals.csv trustee AS new_owner OUTPUT is_expected
| where isnotnull(new_owner) AND isnull(is_expected)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, new_owner
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches for GPOs linked to broad or Tier-0 scope.
investigation_steps: Resolve the new owner and determine how ownership was obtained.
Review the GPO's ACL and content for subsequent tampering.
response_guidance: Revert ownership to the expected principal and audit for further ACL abuse.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: GPO Modifies Logon/Startup Script Path
description: Detects a GPO's logon or startup script assignment being changed. A malicious logon/startup script pushed via GPO executes automatically for every affected user or computer, making this a reliable fleet-wide execution and persistence mechanism.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: File-system auditing Event ID 4663 on scripts.ini or the GPO Scripts folder under SYSVOL.

detection_logic: Event ID 4663 write access under a GPO's '*\Scripts\' SYSVOL path or scripts.ini file.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4663 (Object_Name="*\\Scripts\\*" OR Object_Name="*\\scripts.ini")
| search Accesses="*WriteData*" OR Accesses="*AppendData*"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_Name
tuning_guidance: Requires SYSVOL SACL auditing; correlate with GPO link scope for prioritization.
investigation_steps: Retrieve and review the script content for malicious commands.
Identify the GPO's link scope and affected user/computer population.
response_guidance: Remove/revert the malicious script and hunt across affected endpoints for evidence of execution.

references.title: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts: Logon Script (Windows)

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Deleted GPO Remains Linked (Orphaned Link / SYSVOL-AD Desync)
description: Detects a gPLink reference pointing to a GPO GUID that no longer has a corresponding groupPolicyContainer object in AD. While often benign cleanup debris, this state can also result from an attacker directly manipulating SYSVOL or AD out of sync with each other to obscure a GPO's true history.

data_sources.name: ldapsearch
data_sources.description: Periodic comparison of gPLink references across all OUs against the current set of groupPolicyContainer GUIDs.

detection_logic: Scheduled comparison finding a gPLink-referenced GPO GUID with no matching groupPolicyContainer object.
spl:
| ldapsearch domain=<domain> search="(gPLink=*)" attrs="distinguishedName,gPLink"
| rex field=gPLink "LDAP://cn=\{(?<linked_gpo_guid>[^\}]+)\}" max_match=0
| mvexpand linked_gpo_guid
| lookup all_gpo_guids.csv gpo_guid AS linked_gpo_guid OUTPUT exists
| where isnull(exists)
| table distinguishedName, linked_gpo_guid
tuning_guidance: Requires an LDAP-search-capable Splunk app/add-on run on a periodic schedule; not a real-time streaming detection.
investigation_steps: Determine whether this is routine cleanup debris or evidence of AD/SYSVOL desynchronization.
Check SYSVOL for a lingering folder matching the orphaned GUID.
response_guidance: Clean up the orphaned link; investigate further only if paired with other suspicious GPO activity.

references.title: Domain Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification

author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires an LDAP-search-capable Splunk add-on run on a schedule; this is a hygiene/integrity check, not a real-time attack detection.

title: GPO Central Store Policy Definition Files Modified
description: Detects a write to the Central Store (PolicyDefinitions) folder under SYSVOL, which holds the ADMX/ADML template files used to render available GPO settings in GPMC. Tampering with these templates can be used to hide certain settings from administrators reviewing a GPO in the console, or to mislead reviewers about a setting's actual effect.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: File-system auditing Event ID 4663 on the SYSVOL PolicyDefinitions folder.

detection_logic: Event ID 4663 write access under '*\SYSVOL\*\Policies\PolicyDefinitions\*'.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4663 Object_Name="*\\Policies\\PolicyDefinitions\\*"
| search Accesses="*WriteData*" OR Accesses="*AppendData*"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_Name
tuning_guidance: Requires SYSVOL SACL auditing; expect low but non-zero legitimate frequency during ADMX central-store maintenance.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented ADMX update.
Review the specific template file changed for content that could mask malicious settings.
response_guidance: Restore from a known-good ADMX source if unauthorized.

references.title: Domain Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Many GPOs Modified by a Single Actor in a Short Window
description: Detects a single actor modifying an unusually large number of distinct GPOs within a short window — a pattern consistent with an automated or scripted mass-GPO-tampering tool rather than routine administrative editing, which typically touches one or a handful of GPOs per session.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on groupPolicyContainer objects grouped by actor.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 where Object_Class=groupPolicyContainer, grouped by Subject_Account_Name over 1 hour; alert when distinct_count(Object_DN) >= 5.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Object_Class=groupPolicyContainer
| bucket _time span=1h
| stats dc(Object_DN) as gpos_modified values(Object_DN) as gpos by _time, Subject_Account_Name
| where gpos_modified >= 5
tuning_guidance: Exclude known GPO-management automation/scripted-deployment accounts via gpo_management_principals.csv.
investigation_steps: Review the specific changes made to each GPO.
Determine whether this reflects a legitimate mass-update project or an attack.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, treat as an active mass-tampering event and review every modified GPO's current content against its last known-good state.

references.title: Domain Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification

author: Threat Detection Library

title: GPO Modifies User Rights Assignment (Logon as a Service / Debug Programs)
description: Detects a GPO change to User Rights Assignment settings such as SeDebugPrivilege, SeServiceLogonRight, SeTcbPrivilege, or SeLoadDriverPrivilege. Granting these rights fleet-wide (or to a specific attacker-controlled account) via GPO can enable credential-dumping tooling or kernel-level persistence that would otherwise require local administrative configuration on each host.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: File-system auditing Event ID 4663 on a GPO's GptTmpl.inf [Privilege Rights] section.

detection_logic: Event ID 4663 write access on GptTmpl.inf, flagged for content review of the [Privilege Rights] section for sensitive right grants.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4663 Object_Name="*\\SecEdit\\GptTmpl.inf"
| search Accesses="*WriteData*" OR Accesses="*AppendData*"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_Name
| note "Correlate with a periodic GptTmpl.inf content scan for SeDebugPrivilege, SeServiceLogonRight, SeTcbPrivilege, SeLoadDriverPrivilege grants to non-standard principals."
tuning_guidance: Requires SYSVOL SACL auditing plus a companion content-scan process to confirm the specific right granted.
investigation_steps: Retrieve and review the [Privilege Rights] section for the specific right and grantee.
Identify the GPO's link scope.
response_guidance: Revert unauthorized rights grants; audit affected endpoints for exploitation of the granted privilege.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires SYSVOL SACL auditing plus content inspection; the file-write event alone does not identify which specific right was changed.

title: GPO Applied to OU Containing Tier-0 Assets Without Change-Ticket Correlation
description: Detects a gPLink change targeting an OU flagged as containing Tier-0 assets (e.g. a jump-host OU, PAM-server OU, or PKI-server OU) where no corresponding entry exists in the organization's change-management lookup for that time window. Complements AD-GPO-003/004 (DC/domain-root-specific) by covering the broader set of Tier-0-adjacent OUs that also warrant change-correlated review.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on gPLink correlated against a change-ticket lookup.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 on gPLink where Object_DN is in tier0_ous.csv and no matching entry exists in approved_change_windows.csv for the timestamp.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="gPLink"
| lookup tier0_ous.csv target_ou AS Object_DN OUTPUT is_tier0_ou
| where is_tier0_ou=1
| lookup approved_change_windows.csv object_dn AS Object_DN OUTPUT change_ticket, window_start, window_end
| where isnull(change_ticket) OR _time < window_start OR _time > window_end
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, change_ticket
tuning_guidance: Requires maintaining approved_change_windows.csv fed from the change-management system; without it this falls back to alerting on all Tier-0 OU link changes.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether a change ticket exists but was not recorded in the lookup versus a genuinely unauthorized change.
Review the linked GPO's content.
response_guidance: Escalate to change-management verification; unlink if no legitimate justification is found.

references.title: Domain Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification

author: Threat Detection Library

title: GPO Content Change Immediately Followed by Fleet-Wide Authentication Spike
description: Detects a GPO content or link-scope change followed within a short window by an abnormal spike in authentication or service-ticket volume across many distinct computers — consistent with a malicious GPO applying at the next policy refresh cycle and triggering fleet-wide execution (e.g. a scheduled task or logon script phoning home, or credentials being harvested at scale).

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log correlating SYSVOL/GPO change events with a subsequent fleet-wide authentication-volume anomaly.

detection_logic: A GPO content-change event (AD-GPO-007/008/009/014/015/016/019/023) followed within 4 hours (the default gpupdate background-refresh interval) by a domain-wide spike in Event ID 4768/4769/4624 distinct-computer volume exceeding a 14-day baseline.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4663 Object_Name="*\\SYSVOL\\*"
| eval etype="gpo_change"
| append [
    search index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4768 OR EventCode=4769 OR EventCode=4624)
    | bucket _time span=15m
    | stats dc(Computer) as computer_count by _time
    | eventstats avg(computer_count) as avg_count, stdev(computer_count) as std_count
    | where computer_count > (avg_count + 3*std_count)
    | eval etype="auth_spike"
  ]
| transaction etype maxspan=4h startswith=eval(etype="gpo_change") endswith=eval(etype="auth_spike")
| where eventcount=2
tuning_guidance: This Level 5 chain is intentionally broad-scoped as a fleet-wide safety net; expect to tune the auth-spike threshold per environment size before relying on it in production.
investigation_steps: Identify the specific GPO change that preceded the spike.
Sample several of the newly authenticating computers to confirm the GPO's effect.
Determine whether the authentication pattern is consistent with credential harvesting versus normal policy application.
response_guidance: Treat as an active fleet-wide compromise event pending validation; unlink/revert the GPO and isolate affected endpoint segments if credential harvesting is confirmed.

references.title: Domain Policy Modification: Group Policy Modification

author: Threat Detection Library
performance_guidance: Run as a scheduled correlation search rather than real-time given the two-stage aggregation; requires 14 days of authentication-volume history for a meaningful baseline.

title: New Domain or Forest Trust Created
description: Detects creation of a new trust relationship (trustedDomain object) with another domain or forest. A new trust extends the domain's authentication boundary and, unless SID filtering is properly configured, can allow privilege escalation from the trusted side into the trusting domain. Attackers have used rogue trust creation as a durable, high-value persistence and cross-domain pivot mechanism.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4706 (new trust created).

detection_logic: Event ID 4706 (a new trust was created to a domain).
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4706
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Domain_Name, Trust_Type, Trust_Direction, Trust_Attributes
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; new trust creation should be an extremely rare, deliberate, well-documented change.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented business justification for the new trust.
Review Trust_Direction (inbound/outbound/bidirectional) and Trust_Attributes for SID filtering (quarantine) status.
Identify the actor and their authorization to create domain trusts.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, remove the trust immediately; if authorized but SID filtering is disabled, enable quarantine mode pending a documented exception.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Existing Trust Relationship Modified
description: Detects modification of an existing trust's attributes — most critically, SID filtering (quarantine) being disabled, or the trust direction being widened. Disabling SID filtering on an existing trust is a well-documented technique to enable SIDHistory-based privilege escalation (e.g. forging Domain Admin SIDHistory in a compromised trusted/child domain and using it to gain equivalent rights in the trusting/forest-root domain).

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4716 (trust attributes modified).

detection_logic: Event ID 4716 where New_Trust_Attributes reflects SID filtering being disabled (removal of the quarantine bit) relative to Old_Trust_Attributes.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4716
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Domain_Name, Old_Trust_Attributes, New_Trust_Attributes
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; treat any weakening of SID filtering as Critical regardless of stated justification pending review.
investigation_steps: Compare old vs. new trust attributes to identify exactly what weakened.
Check for SIDHistory-bearing authentication from the trusted domain immediately following (correlate AD-TRUST-005).
response_guidance: Revert to the prior, more restrictive trust configuration unless a documented, risk-accepted exception exists.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Trust Relationship Removed
description: Detects removal of a trust relationship. While often a legitimate decommissioning action, unexpected trust removal can disrupt authentication for the trusting/trusted side and, in some ransomware/destructive playbooks, is used deliberately to isolate a domain during an attack.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4707 (trust removed).

detection_logic: Event ID 4707 (a trust to a domain was removed).
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4707
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Domain_Name
tuning_guidance: Escalate priority if paired with other destructive-activity indicators (bulk deletion, backup tampering).
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented decommissioning plan.
Check for concurrent destructive activity elsewhere in the domain.
response_guidance: Recreate the trust if unauthorized, following the same review process as new-trust creation.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Authentication Event Carries a SIDHistory Value
description: Detects a Kerberos TGT or service-ticket issuance event where the resulting token includes a non-empty SIDHistory value. SIDHistory is legitimately populated during domain/forest migrations to preserve access during a transition period, but any SIDHistory value pointing to a privileged SID (e.g. Domain Admins RID 512, Enterprise Admins RID 519) outside a known, time-boxed migration window is a strong indicator of SID History injection used for privilege escalation across a trust.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4768/4769 with populated SIDHistory-related token fields, or 4624 with a non-empty SIDHistory certificate/claims data.

detection_logic: Correlate Event ID 4768/4769 with the account's known SIDHistory attribute (via a periodic LDAP export lookup) to flag any principal actively authenticating with a non-empty SIDHistory outside an approved migration window.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4768 OR EventCode=4769)
| lookup sidhistory_inventory.csv account AS Account_Name OUTPUT sid_history_values
| where isnotnull(sid_history_values) AND sid_history_values!=""
| lookup approved_migration_accounts.csv Account_Name OUTPUT is_approved_migration
| where isnull(is_approved_migration)
| table _time, dvc, Account_Name, sid_history_values
tuning_guidance: Maintain approved_migration_accounts.csv for the duration of any legitimate migration project and remove entries once complete — lingering SIDHistory values after a migration should have been cleaned up and are themselves worth periodic review.
investigation_steps: Resolve which privileged SID(s) are present in the SIDHistory value.
Confirm whether an active, approved migration justifies this.
If not, treat as likely SIDHistory injection and review the account's effective privileged access.
response_guidance: Clear the unauthorized SIDHistory value using ADSI Edit/PowerShell and review all access the account gained via the injected SID.
author: Threat Detection Library
performance_guidance: Requires a periodically refreshed sidhistory_inventory.csv lookup built from an LDAP export of the sIDHistory attribute domain-wide; Windows Security events do not directly surface the SIDHistory value inline.
attack_mapping_note: Windows Security events do not directly expose the SIDHistory value inline; this detection depends on a periodic LDAP-sourced sIDHistory inventory lookup rather than being derivable from streaming event data alone.

title: Cross-Trust Authentication from a Privileged SIDHistory Value
description: A higher-confidence variant of AD-TRUST-004: detects an authentication event originating from across a trust boundary (the authenticating account's domain differs from the resource domain) where the account carries a SIDHistory value matching a privileged group RID in the resource domain. This is the specific attack pattern for cross-forest/cross-domain privilege escalation via a compromised trusted domain.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4768/4769 correlated with sidhistory_inventory.csv and privileged_rids.csv.

detection_logic: Event ID 4768/4769 where Account_Domain differs from the local domain, and the account's SIDHistory (via lookup) matches an entry in privileged_rids.csv for the local domain.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4768 OR EventCode=4769)
| lookup local_domain_sid.csv domain_sid_prefix AS Account_Domain OUTPUT is_local
| where isnull(is_local)
| lookup sidhistory_inventory.csv account AS Account_Name OUTPUT sid_history_values
| lookup privileged_rids.csv rid AS sid_history_values OUTPUT rid_group_name
| where isnotnull(rid_group_name)
| table _time, dvc, Account_Name, Account_Domain, sid_history_values, rid_group_name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; this is one of the highest-confidence cross-trust privilege-escalation indicators available. Requires the same sidhistory_inventory.csv dependency as AD-TRUST-004.
investigation_steps: Determine whether this is a legitimate, time-boxed migration in progress.
Review what access the account exercised using the escalated privilege.
Assess whether the trusted domain itself is compromised.
response_guidance: Treat as an active cross-domain compromise; clear the SIDHistory value, review SID filtering on the trust, and consider disabling the trust pending investigation of the trusted domain's security posture.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Depends on the same periodic LDAP-sourced SIDHistory inventory lookup as AD-TRUST-004; not derivable from streaming Windows Security events alone.

title: Trust Direction Changed from One-Way to Bidirectional
description: Detects a trust's direction changing from a restricted one-way configuration to bidirectional. A one-way trust intentionally limits which domain can authenticate into the other; widening it to bidirectional expands the attack surface by allowing authentication to flow in the previously blocked direction as well.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4716 with Trust_Direction field change.

detection_logic: Event ID 4716 where the trust direction attribute changes to a broader value (one-way to bidirectional).
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4716
| where New_Trust_Attributes!=Old_Trust_Attributes
| search Domain_Name=*
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Domain_Name, Old_Trust_Attributes, New_Trust_Attributes
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; this is functionally the same review priority as AD-TRUST-002.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for the widened direction.
Review SID filtering status on the newly bidirectional path.
response_guidance: Revert to the original restricted direction unless a documented exception exists.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Authentication from an Unexpected/Undocumented Trusted Domain
description: Detects a successful cross-domain authentication event from a trusted domain not present in a maintained inventory of expected/documented trust relationships. This can indicate an undocumented trust was created (missed by AD-TRUST-001 due to a logging gap), or a forest-transitive trust is being exercised further than intended.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4768/4624 with a foreign Account_Domain compared to documented_trusts.csv.

detection_logic: Event ID 4768/4624 where Account_Domain is not present in documented_trusts.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4768 OR EventCode=4624)
| lookup local_domain_sid.csv domain_sid_prefix AS Account_Domain OUTPUT is_local
| where isnull(is_local)
| lookup documented_trusts.csv domain_name AS Account_Domain OUTPUT is_documented
| where isnull(is_documented)
| table _time, dvc, Account_Name, Account_Domain
tuning_guidance: Maintain documented_trusts.csv accurately; this is a coverage/hygiene check that complements AD-TRUST-001's event-based detection.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether the trust is real but undocumented, versus a transitive-trust path being exploited.
Review recent 4706 events for the missing domain.
response_guidance: Document the trust if legitimate; investigate as unauthorized if not.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Selective Authentication Setting Disabled on a Trust
description: Detects Selective Authentication being disabled on a forest trust. When enabled, Selective Authentication requires explicit Allowed-to-Authenticate permission on each resource before a principal from the trusted forest can access it; disabling it lets any authenticated user from the trusted forest attempt to authenticate to any resource, significantly widening the attack surface exposed across the trust.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4716 with Trust_Attributes reflecting the Selective Authentication bit (0x10) being cleared.

detection_logic: Event ID 4716 where the New_Trust_Attributes value no longer includes the Selective Authentication flag present in Old_Trust_Attributes.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4716
| where NOT (New_Trust_Attributes="*0x10*") AND Old_Trust_Attributes="*0x10*"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Domain_Name, Old_Trust_Attributes, New_Trust_Attributes
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; treat as equivalent priority to SID filtering being disabled.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Review which resources are now reachable without explicit per-resource permission.
response_guidance: Re-enable Selective Authentication unless a documented, risk-accepted exception exists.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Trust Password Reset or Changed
description: Detects the inter-domain trust account password being reset outside the normal automatic 30-day rotation. As with computer-account password resets, an out-of-cycle manual reset can indicate an attacker regaining control of the trust account's credential material, or preparing to forge inter-realm referral tickets.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4742 on the trust account object (named for the trusted domain, ending in $).

detection_logic: Event ID 4742 where Target_Account_Name corresponds to a known inter-domain trust account and Subject_Account_Name is not a machine-initiated automatic rotation.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4742
| lookup trust_accounts.csv account AS Target_Account_Name OUTPUT is_trust_account
| where is_trust_account=1
| where Subject_Account_Name!=Target_Account_Name
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Target_Account_Name
tuning_guidance: Maintain trust_accounts.csv with the trust-account names for each configured trust.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented trust-maintenance action.
Review for concurrent inter-realm ticket activity.
response_guidance: Investigate if unexplained; coordinate with the trusted domain's administrators.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Inter-Realm TGT Issued for an Unusual Destination Domain
description: Detects a Kerberos referral (inter-realm) TGT being issued for a trusted-domain destination that a given account or source system has not previously accessed — a possible sign of lateral movement across a trust boundary using compromised credentials, or of an inter-realm ticket being reused/forged (Golden Ticket variants targeting the trust).

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4768 with a Service_Name matching an inter-realm krbtgt (krbtgt/<TRUSTED-DOMAIN>) service ticket.

detection_logic: Event ID 4768/4769 where Service_Name matches 'krbtgt/<trusted-domain>' and the account/source pair is not present in ad_privileged_src_baseline.csv for that destination.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4768 OR EventCode=4769) Service_Name="krbtgt/*"
| lookup interrealm_baseline.csv Account_Name, Service_Name OUTPUT is_baseline
| where isnull(is_baseline)
| table _time, dvc, Account_Name, Service_Name
tuning_guidance: Requires at least 14-30 days of baseline history in interrealm_baseline.csv; expect meaningful noise during onboarding of the baseline itself.
investigation_steps: Confirm the account has a legitimate reason to access resources in the trusted domain.
Review what the inter-realm ticket was subsequently used for.
response_guidance: Investigate unexplained cross-trust access as potential lateral movement.

references.title: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Ticket

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Trust Modification Immediately Followed by Privileged SIDHistory Authentication (Chain)
description: The flagship trust-abuse chain: an existing trust's SID filtering is disabled (AD-TRUST-002) and shortly afterward an authentication event carrying a privileged SIDHistory value crosses that same trust (AD-TRUST-005). This sequence is a near-complete cross-domain privilege-escalation attack in progress and should be treated with the highest available priority.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4716 (trust attribute weakened) followed by 4768/4769 with a privileged SIDHistory value from the same trusted domain.

detection_logic: AD-TRUST-002 match followed within 24 hours by an AD-TRUST-005 match from the same Domain_Name.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4716
| eval etype="trust_weakened"
| append [
    search index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4768 OR EventCode=4769)
    | lookup sidhistory_inventory.csv account AS Account_Name OUTPUT sid_history_values
    | lookup privileged_rids.csv rid AS sid_history_values OUTPUT rid_group_name
    | where isnotnull(rid_group_name)
    | eval etype="privileged_sidhistory_auth"
  ]
| transaction Domain_Name maxspan=24h startswith=eval(etype="trust_weakened") endswith=eval(etype="privileged_sidhistory_auth")
| where eventcount=2
| table _time, dvc, Domain_Name, Account_Name, rid_group_name, duration
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches without exception; this chain has essentially no legitimate business explanation outside an active, tightly time-boxed migration with prior change-management approval.
investigation_steps: Treat as an active domain-compromise incident immediately.
Determine the full scope of access exercised via the escalated privilege.
Review the trusted domain's own security posture for the initial compromise.
response_guidance: Disable the trust, clear the SIDHistory value, force a krbtgt double-reset in the affected domain, and engage full incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Forest Trust Transitivity or Domain Filtering Modified
description: Detects a change to a forest trust's domain-name-suffix routing or exclusion list. These settings control which specific child/UPN domains within a trusted forest are permitted to authenticate; removing an exclusion widens the set of external domains that can reach resources across the trust.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4716 or a directory-service-change on msDS-TrustForestTrustInfo.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 where Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name=msDS-TrustForestTrustInfo.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-TrustForestTrustInfo"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, Attribute_Value
tuning_guidance: Low-frequency; review each occurrence manually against documented forest-trust routing policy.
investigation_steps: Determine which domain suffix routing entries changed.
Confirm business justification.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Directory Replication Request from a Non-Domain-Controller Source (DCSync Use)
description: Detects an actual DRSGetNCChanges replication request (the DCSync operation) originating from a source that is not a recognized domain controller. This detection covers the replication-use half of DCSync and is deliberately kept separate from the rights-grant detection (AD-ACL-010) per the requirement to treat DCSync rights and DCSync use as distinct signals — a principal can hold replication rights for months without exercising them, and the moment of actual use is the higher-urgency event.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4662 with Properties containing the DS-Replication-Get-Changes/-All GUIDs against the domain NC object, from a non-DC source.

detection_logic: Event ID 4662 where Properties includes the replication-GUIDs (1131f6aa-.../1131f6ad-...) against the domain naming-context object, and Subject_Account_Name/source is not in domain_controllers.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4662
| search Properties="*1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*" OR Properties="*1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*"
| where match(Object_Name, "^DC=")
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS Subject_Account_Name OUTPUT is_dc
| where isnull(is_dc)
| lookup dcsync_authorized_principals.csv trustee AS Subject_Account_Name OUTPUT is_authorized
| where isnull(is_authorized)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, IpAddress, Object_Name
tuning_guidance: Requires DS Access auditing (Directory Service Access) enabled on all DCs. Alert on all matches — this is the single highest-priority credential-access detection in the AD catalogue.
investigation_steps: Identify the exact source account/system and its recent activity.
Determine how the account obtained replication rights (correlate AD-ACL-010).
Assume the entire domain's password hashes and krbtgt key have been exfiltrated.
response_guidance: Treat as a full domain compromise. Follow the krbtgt double-reset procedure, force a domain-wide password reset for all privileged accounts, and initiate full incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DCSync Rights Granted and Exercised Within a Short Window (Chain)
description: The flagship DCSync chain: a principal is granted DS-Replication-Get-Changes rights at the domain root (AD-ACL-010) and then actually performs a replication pull (AD-REPL-001) shortly afterward. While each half is tracked independently per the master requirement to separate rights-grant from rights-use, their combination within a short window is treated as a near-certain, complete DCSync attack rather than two unrelated events.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 (rights grant) and 4662 (replication use) correlated by trustee within a short window.

detection_logic: AD-ACL-010 match followed within 4 hours by an AD-REPL-001 match for the same trustee.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=5136 OR EventCode=4662)
| eval etype=case(EventCode=5136 AND (Attribute_Value="*1131f6aa*" OR Attribute_Value="*1131f6ad*"), "rights_grant", EventCode=4662 AND (Properties="*1131f6aa*" OR Properties="*1131f6ad*"), "rights_use", true(), null())
| where isnotnull(etype)
| rex field=Attribute_Value "Trustee=(?<trustee>\S+)"
| eval actor=coalesce(trustee, Subject_Account_Name)
| transaction actor maxspan=4h startswith=eval(etype="rights_grant") endswith=eval(etype="rights_use")
| where eventcount=2
| table _time, dvc, actor, duration
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches without exception.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed, complete DCSync attack — skip straight to full domain-compromise incident response.
response_guidance: Execute the krbtgt double-reset procedure immediately, reset all privileged account passwords, and begin full incident response under the assumption of complete credential-material compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Full Domain Naming Context Replication Pull (High-Volume DCSync)
description: Detects an abnormally high volume of object-level replication access events against the domain naming context within a short window from a single source — consistent with a full-domain DCSync pull (e.g. mimikatz lsadump::dcsync with no /user filter, or Impacket secretsdump.py) rather than a narrow, targeted single-object query.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4662 volume against domain-NC objects grouped by source.

detection_logic: Event ID 4662 replication-property access count grouped by Subject_Account_Name over 10 minutes; alert when count exceeds 50 (indicating a bulk multi-object pull).
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4662
| search Properties="*1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*" OR Properties="*1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*"
| bucket _time span=10m
| stats count as replication_events by _time, Subject_Account_Name
| where replication_events > 50
tuning_guidance: Legitimate DC-to-DC replication traffic will also match this pattern — exclude known domain_controllers.csv sources; this detection is intended for the non-DC-source case in combination with AD-REPL-001.
investigation_steps: Confirm the source is genuinely non-DC.
Assume the entire domain database (NTDS.dit-equivalent) has been exfiltrated.
response_guidance: Same as AD-REPL-001 — treat as full domain compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Targeted Replication Request for a Single High-Value Account (Narrow DCSync)
description: Detects a narrowly scoped DCSync-style replication request targeting a single specific privileged account (e.g. mimikatz lsadump::dcsync /user:krbtgt), rather than a full-domain pull. Attackers increasingly favor this narrower form specifically to evade volume-based detections like AD-REPL-003 while still obtaining the single credential (often krbtgt) they need for a Golden Ticket.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4662 replication-property access against a single privileged user object DN, from a non-DC source.

detection_logic: Event ID 4662 where Properties includes the replication GUIDs, Object_Name is a specific user object (not the domain-root NC), the object is in tier0_privileged_accounts.csv, and the source is not a DC.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4662
| search Properties="*1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*" OR Properties="*1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*"
| where match(Object_Name, "^CN=")
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv object_dn AS Object_Name OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS Subject_Account_Name OUTPUT is_dc
| where isnull(is_dc)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_Name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches, with special urgency if Object_Name corresponds to the krbtgt account.
investigation_steps: If the target was krbtgt, assume Golden Ticket forging capability has been obtained — execute krbtgt double-reset immediately.
For other privileged accounts, reset that account's password immediately.
response_guidance: Treat with equal urgency to a full-domain DCSync pull, since a single krbtgt or Domain Admin credential is often sufficient for complete domain compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Rogue Domain Controller Object Registered Without Promotion Workflow (Possible DCShadow)
description: DCShadow abuses replication to temporarily register a non-DC computer as a domain controller in the configuration partition, push a malicious change (such as adding SIDHistory or DCSync rights to an attacker-controlled account), and then deregister — all while bypassing standard security-event logging on the target DC because the change arrives via replication rather than a normal LDAP write. This detection looks for the best available indirect signal: a new nTDSDSA/server object appearing in the Configuration partition without a corresponding, complete DCPROMO event sequence (4742/dcpromo-related events) on the same computer. Per the master detection requirements, this cannot be claimed as a direct, reliable DCShadow detection — it is a best-effort gap-based indicator.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5137 for a new nTDSDSA or server object under CN=Sites,CN=Configuration.

detection_logic: Event ID 5137 where Object_Class is nTDSDSA or server, under the Configuration partition, for a computer name not already present in domain_controllers.csv, without a corresponding DCPROMO Directory Service event sequence in the surrounding time window.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5137 (Object_Class=nTDSDSA OR Object_Class=server)
| where match(Object_DN, "CN=Configuration,DC=")
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name OUTPUT is_known_dc
| where isnull(is_known_dc)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN
tuning_guidance: This is explicitly a best-effort, low-confidence indicator — DCShadow is specifically engineered to minimize its own footprint in standard security logs. Network-level replication traffic monitoring (RPC/DRSUAPI on port 135/49152+) and Microsoft Defender for Identity are significantly more reliable detection surfaces for DCShadow and should be treated as the primary control where available.
investigation_steps: Immediately check whether the source computer completed a full, legitimate promotion (ntdsutil/dcpromo logs, matching change ticket).
Review the configuration-partition object for signs of rapid creation and removal (the DCShadow deregistration step).
Cross-check with Defender for Identity or network DRSUAPI telemetry if available.
response_guidance: If no legitimate promotion is found, treat as a probable DCShadow attack and review all AD objects for unexpected changes in the surrounding time window (SIDHistory, ACL grants, DCSync rights).
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: DCShadow is specifically designed to evade standard DC security-event logging by injecting changes via replication rather than LDAP writes; this detection is an indirect, best-effort indicator only, not a reliable direct signature. Network-level RPC/DRSUAPI monitoring or Defender for Identity is the more reliable control for this technique.

title: Replication Connection Object Manually Created Outside KCC
description: Detects a replication connection object (nTDSConnection) being manually created rather than generated by the automatic Knowledge Consistency Checker (KCC). Manual connection objects are occasionally used for legitimate site-topology tuning, but they are also part of the DCShadow technique's replication-partner setup and warrant review whenever they appear outside a known site-topology change window.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5137 where Object_Class=nTDSConnection.

detection_logic: Event ID 5137 where Object_Class=nTDSConnection and Subject_Account_Name is not the KCC's SYSTEM context.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5137 Object_Class=nTDSConnection
| where Subject_Account_Name!="SYSTEM" AND NOT match(Subject_Account_Name, "\$$")
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN
tuning_guidance: Exclude known site-topology administrators performing legitimate manual connection tuning via a lookup allowlist.
investigation_steps: Identify the source and destination DCs of the new connection object.
Confirm against a documented site-topology change.
response_guidance: Remove if unauthorized and let the KCC regenerate the topology automatically.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Replication Traffic from an Unauthorized Source IP Address
description: Detects replication-related authentication or access events where the source IP address does not match any known domain controller's registered IP range. Legitimate replication always originates from a DC's own network identity; a mismatch is a strong signal that replication protocols are being invoked from an attacker-controlled host rather than genuine infrastructure.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4662/4624 with replication-related access where IpAddress/Source_Network_Address is outside dc_ip_ranges.csv.

detection_logic: Event ID 4662 with replication-GUID properties where IpAddress is not within any range in dc_ip_ranges.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4662
| search Properties="*1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*" OR Properties="*1131f6ad-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*"
| lookup dc_ip_ranges.csv ip_cidr AS IpAddress OUTPUT is_dc_range
| where isnull(is_dc_range)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, IpAddress
tuning_guidance: Maintain dc_ip_ranges.csv with every DC's IP addresses across all sites; overlaps heavily with AD-REPL-001 and serves as a network-layer corroborating signal for the same underlying activity.
investigation_steps: Same as AD-REPL-001 investigation steps.
response_guidance: Same as AD-REPL-001 response guidance.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: FSMO Role Transferred
description: Detects a Flexible Single Master Operations (FSMO) role — Schema Master, Domain Naming Master, RID Master, PDC Emulator, or Infrastructure Master — being transferred to a different domain controller through the normal, graceful transfer process. FSMO role holders have unique authority (e.g. the RID Master issues RID pools used to create new security principals; the Schema Master is the only DC that can modify the schema), so an unplanned transfer changes which DC an attacker would need to compromise for certain high-value actions.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 1458 (Active Directory Domain Services Operational log, role transfer) or equivalent directory-service-change event.

detection_logic: Directory Service Operational log role-transfer event, or Event ID 5136 on the fSMORoleOwner attribute of the relevant role-owner object.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="fSMORoleOwner"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, Attribute_Value
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; FSMO transfers should be rare, deliberate, and well-documented events.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented change ticket (e.g. DC decommission/replacement).
Verify the new role holder is a trusted, expected DC.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, transfer the role back to the expected DC and investigate the actor's authorization.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: FSMO Role Seized (Forced Transfer)
description: Detects indicators consistent with a forced FSMO role seizure (ntdsutil 'seize' operation) rather than a graceful transfer. Seizure is intended only for disaster-recovery scenarios where the original role holder is permanently unavailable; using it while the original holder is still healthy can create role conflicts (e.g. two DCs believing they hold the RID Master role, leading to duplicate/overlapping RID pools) and is a known technique to disrupt or manipulate the domain's object-creation integrity.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on fSMORoleOwner without a preceding graceful-transfer log entry on the original role holder, or role owner conflict events in the Directory Service log.

detection_logic: fSMORoleOwner attribute change (5136) where the previously recorded role holder shows no corresponding outbound transfer acknowledgment, or a Directory Service Operational-log role-conflict warning appears.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="fSMORoleOwner"
| lookup fsmo_role_baseline.csv role_name OUTPUT expected_holder_dvc
| where dvc!=expected_holder_dvc
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, Attribute_Value, expected_holder_dvc
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained fsmo_role_baseline.csv reflecting the last known-good role assignment. Alert on all matches — this should be an emergency-only operation.
investigation_steps: Confirm this was a documented disaster-recovery seizure with the original holder confirmed permanently lost.
Check for role-owner conflicts across the domain.
If unexplained, treat as active tampering with domain-object-creation integrity.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, investigate immediately; if the original role holder later comes back online, follow Microsoft's documented FSMO-conflict-resolution procedure to avoid duplicate RID pools or schema conflicts.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Replication Schedule Modified to Enable Off-Hours Replication
description: Detects a change to a site-link or connection-object replication schedule. While mostly a routine capacity-planning change, unusual schedule modifications (e.g. enabling replication only during a narrow off-hours window) can be used to time a DCShadow-style change to occur when defenders are least likely to be monitoring.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on schedule attribute of a siteLink or nTDSConnection object.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 where Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name=schedule on a siteLink or nTDSConnection object.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="schedule"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN
tuning_guidance: Low priority on its own; use primarily as supporting context for other AD-REPL findings occurring in the newly scheduled window.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification (e.g. WAN link capacity planning).
response_guidance: Not independently actionable.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Repeated Urgent Replication Triggers (repadmin /replicate Abuse Pattern)
description: Detects an unusually high frequency of manually triggered, out-of-schedule replication requests (e.g. via repadmin /replicate or /syncall) from a single source. While administrators use these commands for legitimate troubleshooting, repeated forced replication can also be used to rapidly propagate a malicious change across the domain before it would otherwise reach all DCs on the normal schedule.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4662 replication-property access grouped by source over a short window with high frequency but low per-request volume (distinguishing it from AD-REPL-003's bulk-pull pattern).

detection_logic: Event ID 4662 replication-property access count grouped by Subject_Account_Name over 15 minutes where request_count >= 10 but each request touches few objects (excludes AD-REPL-003 bulk-pull cases).
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4662
| search Properties="*1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS Subject_Account_Name OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| bucket _time span=15m
| stats count as request_count by _time, Subject_Account_Name
| where request_count >= 10
tuning_guidance: Scoped to DC-sourced requests specifically (unlike AD-REPL-001/003 which focus on non-DC sources) — this detection is about anomalous frequency from legitimate DC identities, potentially reflecting an attacker who has already compromised a DC and is using it to rapidly propagate changes.
investigation_steps: Correlate with recent object changes on the source DC to identify what is being rapidly propagated.
Confirm against known troubleshooting activity.
response_guidance: If unexplained, treat the source DC as potentially compromised and review recent changes for propagation of malicious content.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Lingering/Deleted Object Reanimated via Replication
description: Detects a previously tombstoned/deleted AD object being restored (reanimated) from the AD Recycle Bin or via a lingering-object reintroduction. While the Recycle Bin is a legitimate recovery feature, reanimating a privileged object that was deleted as part of incident-response cleanup can be an attacker attempting to restore a persistence mechanism that was previously removed.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5137 where the created object's isDeleted attribute transitions from TRUE to absent (a Recycle Bin restore).

detection_logic: Event ID 5136/5137 reflecting an isDeleted attribute clear (object restore) on a previously tombstoned object.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="isDeleted"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, Attribute_Value
tuning_guidance: Correlate the restored object's identity against recent incident-response deletion actions if any occurred; otherwise treat as a routine, low-priority recovery action.
investigation_steps: Determine why the object was originally deleted.
If deletion was part of a security remediation, treat the restore as re-establishment of the same risk and remediate again.
response_guidance: Re-delete if the object was removed for security reasons and its restoration was unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Replication Between Sites Outside Documented Site Topology
description: Detects replication traffic between two DCs whose site pairing is not present in the documented site-link topology. This can indicate a manually created connection object bypassing normal topology management (see AD-REPL-006), or a rogue replication partner attempting to pull changes from an unexpected path.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4662 replication access correlated with dc_site_topology.csv.

detection_logic: Event ID 4662 replication-property access where the source DC's site and destination DC's site pairing is not present in dc_site_topology.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4662
| search Properties="*1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2*"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS Subject_Account_Name OUTPUT site AS source_site
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT site AS dest_site
| lookup dc_site_topology.csv source_site, dest_site OUTPUT is_documented
| where isnull(is_documented)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, source_site, dest_site
tuning_guidance: Requires maintained dc_site_topology.csv and domain_controllers.csv with site assignments; treat as a supporting/corroborating signal alongside AD-REPL-006.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether this reflects a legitimate topology change not yet documented.
Cross-reference with AD-REPL-006 for a manually created connection object.
response_guidance: Document if legitimate; investigate as potential unauthorized replication path if not.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Read-Only Domain Controller (RODC) Password Replication Policy Widened
description: Detects a Read-Only Domain Controller's Password Replication Policy (PRP) being widened to allow caching of credentials for a privileged account or group. RODCs are intended to cache only a limited, non-privileged set of credentials appropriate for their (often physically less-secure, branch-office) deployment location; adding Domain Admins or other Tier-0 principals to an RODC's allowed-list creates a high-value credential cache on a lower-assurance system.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4741/4742 changes to msDS-RevealOnDemandGroup or msDS-NeverRevealGroup on an RODC computer object.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 where Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name=msDS-RevealOnDemandGroup on an RODC computer object, where the added value matches a Tier-0 group.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-RevealOnDemandGroup"
| lookup rodc_computers.csv computer_name AS Object_DN OUTPUT is_rodc
| where is_rodc=1
| lookup tier0_privileged_groups.csv group_dn AS Attribute_Value OUTPUT is_tier0_group
| where is_tier0_group=1
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, Attribute_Value
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; there is essentially no legitimate reason for an RODC to be allowed to cache Tier-0 credentials.
investigation_steps: Determine why the PRP was widened and by whom.
Assess the RODC's physical/network security posture.
response_guidance: Revert the PRP change immediately; if the RODC has already cached the credential, treat it as exposed and reset it.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Replication Metadata Version Number Anomaly on a Privileged Object
description: Detects an unusual jump in an attribute's replication metadata version number (uSNChanged/version) on a Tier-0 object without a corresponding, matching count of standard directory-service-change security events. Because DCShadow and other replication-layer manipulation techniques modify objects via replication rather than a locally logged LDAP write, comparing an object's replication metadata (via repadmin /showobjmeta or an equivalent periodic export) against the security-event count for that object is one of the few indirect ways to spot changes that occurred outside normal logging.

data_sources.name: repadmin_showobjmeta
data_sources.description: Periodic export of replication metadata (attribute version numbers, originating DC, originating time) for Tier-0 objects.

detection_logic: Scheduled comparison: an attribute's replication-metadata version number increments without a corresponding 5136 event for that object/attribute in the Windows Security event log within the same window.
spl:
| inputlookup repadmin_showobjmeta_scan.csv
| lookup tier0_objects.csv object_dn OUTPUT is_tier0
| where is_tier0=1
| join object_dn, attribute [
    search index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136
    | rename Object_DN as object_dn, Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name as attribute
    | stats count by object_dn, attribute
  ]
| where isnull(count)
| table object_dn, attribute, version_number, originating_dc
tuning_guidance: This is the most direct available indirect indicator for replication-layer manipulation (DCShadow-class attacks) that this library can offer without network-level RPC/DRSUAPI visibility or Defender for Identity — flag clearly to the user as a supplementary, not primary, DCShadow control.
investigation_steps: Identify the originating DC recorded in the metadata and confirm it is legitimate.
Review the actual current value of the attribute for unexpected content.
response_guidance: Treat a confirmed mismatch as a likely replication-layer manipulation event and follow the same response as AD-REPL-005.
author: Threat Detection Library
performance_guidance: Requires a scripted periodic repadmin /showobjmeta (or equivalent replication-metadata) export feeding a lookup; run as a scheduled report, not real-time.
attack_mapping_note: Requires a scripted periodic repadmin/showobjmeta export; standard Windows Security event logging alone cannot surface this gap, which is precisely the property DCShadow-class attacks exploit.

title: New Domain Controller Promoted
description: Detects a server being promoted to a domain controller (DCPROMO). A new DC receives a full read-write copy of the AD database and can originate changes that replicate domain-wide, making unauthorized promotion one of the most significant persistence and access mechanisms an attacker could establish.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4742 on the new DC's computer object combined with Directory Service Operational log promotion events.

detection_logic: Event ID 5137 for a new nTDSDSA object under Configuration, or a Directory Service Operational-log promotion-completed event, for a computer not previously in domain_controllers.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5137 Object_Class=nTDSDSA
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name OUTPUT was_known_dc
| where isnull(was_known_dc)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; update domain_controllers.csv immediately after any legitimate promotion to avoid repeat alerts and to keep every other DC-scoped lookup in this catalogue accurate.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented, approved DC-build change ticket.
Verify the promoting account's authorization (Enterprise Admins/Domain Admins with delegated promotion rights).
Review the new DC's build provenance (image source, patch level).
response_guidance: If unauthorized, demote the rogue DC immediately and treat as an active domain-compromise incident; assume the rogue DC may have already received a full replica of the domain database.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Domain Controller Demoted
description: Detects a domain controller being demoted back to a member server. Demotion is a normal part of DC lifecycle management, but an unplanned or unauthorized demotion reduces the domain's replica count and, if it targets the last healthy DC in a site or the last holder of a needed FSMO role, can constitute a destructive/availability attack.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5141 for the nTDSDSA object removal under Configuration.

detection_logic: Event ID 5141 where Object_Class=nTDSDSA.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5141 Object_Class=nTDSDSA
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; escalate immediately if this reduces the domain to a single remaining DC or removes an FSMO role holder without a prior graceful transfer.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented change ticket.
Verify remaining DC count and FSMO role distribution post-demotion.
response_guidance: Investigate immediately if unauthorized; re-promote if needed to restore replica redundancy.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) Password Reset
description: Detects the DSRM administrator password being reset on a domain controller. DSRM is a local, SAM-based (not AD-based) administrative account on every DC used for offline maintenance; it is frequently overlooked in credential-rotation programs and, since Windows Server 2008, can be configured (DsrmAdminLogonBehavior) to allow network logon, making it an attractive, rarely rotated backdoor credential if compromised.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4794 (an attempt was made to set the Directory Services Restore Mode administrator password).

detection_logic: Event ID 4794.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4794
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; DSRM password resets should be rare, deliberate, and tied to a documented maintenance window.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented DC-maintenance activity.
Check the DsrmAdminLogonBehavior registry value to determine whether DSRM network logon is enabled.
Review for any subsequent DSRM-account authentication.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, reset the DSRM password again via a trusted process and confirm DsrmAdminLogonBehavior is set to its intended (default-disabled) value.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: DSRM Administrator Account Authentication
description: Detects a successful network logon using the DSRM administrator account while the DC is running normally (not in restore mode). This is only possible when DsrmAdminLogonBehavior has been configured to allow it, and is a known persistence technique because the DSRM account is a local SAM account, invisible to normal AD-based account monitoring, and its password does not expire or rotate through standard AD password policy.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4624 where Account_Name=Administrator and Logon_Process/Authentication_Package indicates a local SAM logon on a DC.

detection_logic: Event ID 4624 on a DC where the logon is authenticated against the local SAM (not the domain) using the built-in Administrator/DSRM account name.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4624
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| where Account_Name="Administrator" AND Authentication_Package="NTLM"
| table _time, dvc, Account_Name, Source_Network_Address, Logon_Type
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; this is a rarely-if-ever legitimate authentication path outside an active DSRM maintenance session.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether a legitimate DSRM maintenance session is underway.
If not, treat as an active persistence-backdoor use and investigate the source.
response_guidance: Reset the DSRM password immediately, verify/disable DsrmAdminLogonBehavior, and investigate the source of the authentication as a likely compromise indicator.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: NTDS Service Stopped on a Domain Controller
description: Detects the Active Directory Domain Services (NTDS) service being stopped on a live domain controller. Stopping NTDS takes the DC out of AD service entirely (authentication, replication) and, outside a planned maintenance restart into DSRM, is a strong indicator of either an availability attack or preparation for offline access to the NTDS.dit database file while the database is unlocked from the running service.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:System
data_sources.description: System event log, Event ID 7036 (service state change) for the NTDS service.

detection_logic: System log Event ID 7036 where service_name="Active Directory Domain Services" and service_state="stopped".
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=7036 service_name="Active Directory Domain Services" service_state="stopped"
| table _time, dvc, service_name, service_state
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; correlate with a documented maintenance window before escalating, but do not suppress by default.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented maintenance restart into DSRM.
Check whether NTDS.dit was subsequently accessed or copied while the service was stopped (correlate AD-CRED namespace).
Verify the service restarts as expected.
response_guidance: If unexplained, treat as a potential availability attack or precursor to offline NTDS.dit access; investigate the stopping account and restore service immediately.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Volume Shadow Copy Created on a Domain Controller
description: Detects a Volume Shadow Copy being created on a domain controller's system volume. VSS is the mechanism most credential-dumping tools (ntdsutil 'ifm', vssadmin + copy, or automated tools like secretsdump's local-VSS path) use to access a locked, live copy of NTDS.dit and the SYSTEM registry hive for offline hash extraction without needing to stop the NTDS service.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log/Sysmon, process creation for vssadmin.exe, diskshadow.exe, or wbadmin.exe with shadow-copy-creation arguments.

detection_logic: Sysmon Event ID 1 (process creation) on a DC where Image matches vssadmin.exe/diskshadow.exe/wbadmin.exe and CommandLine includes shadow-copy-creation syntax (e.g. 'create shadow').
spl:
index=sysmon sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=1
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| where match(Image, "(?i)(vssadmin|diskshadow|wbadmin)\.exe$") AND match(CommandLine, "(?i)(create shadow|shadow.*create)")
| lookup service_accounts.csv Account_Name AS User OUTPUT is_expected_backup_account
| where isnull(is_expected_backup_account)
| table _time, dvc, User, Image, CommandLine
tuning_guidance: Requires Sysmon (or equivalent process-creation EDR telemetry) on domain controllers — this is an explicit telemetry dependency beyond native Windows Security auditing. Exclude known backup-solution service accounts (Veeam, Windows Server Backup, etc.).
investigation_steps: Identify the process and account that created the shadow copy.
Check for subsequent access/copy of ntds.dit or the SYSTEM hive from the shadow-copy device path.
Confirm against a documented backup schedule.
response_guidance: If unexplained, treat as an active NTDS.dit credential-dumping attempt; delete the unauthorized shadow copy and reset all domain credentials if extraction is confirmed.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires Sysmon or equivalent process-creation/EDR telemetry on domain controllers; native Windows Security auditing alone does not reliably capture vssadmin/diskshadow command-line arguments.

title: NTDS.dit File Copied or Accessed Outside the NTDS Service
description: Detects file-access activity against the NTDS.dit database file (or a copy of it, e.g. under a shadow-copy device path or a staged output directory) by a process other than the NTDS/lsass service itself. Direct file access to NTDS.dit is the core objective of ntdsutil-based extraction and most offline credential-dumping toolchains.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC file-system auditing Event ID 4663 on ntds.dit, or Sysmon Event ID 11 (file create) for a file named ntds.dit outside the expected NTDS service directory.

detection_logic: Event ID 4663 on a file path ending in 'ntds.dit' where Process_Name is not lsass.exe/ntds service context, or Sysmon Event ID 11 for TargetFilename ending in ntds.dit outside %windir%\NTDS\.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4663 Object_Name="*ntds.dit"
| where NOT match(Process_Name, "(?i)lsass\.exe$")
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Process_Name, Object_Name
tuning_guidance: Requires SACL-based file auditing on the NTDS.dit file path (not enabled by default) or Sysmon file-create monitoring. Alert on all matches without exception.
investigation_steps: Identify the accessing process and account.
Determine the destination of any copy operation.
Assume full domain credential-database compromise if confirmed.
response_guidance: Treat as a full domain compromise equivalent to a successful DCSync; follow krbtgt double-reset and domain-wide credential-rotation incident response.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires SACL-based file-system auditing on the NTDS.dit path or Sysmon file-monitoring — not captured by default Windows Security auditing.

title: LSASS Process Access on a Domain Controller by an Unexpected Process
description: Detects a process opening a handle to lsass.exe with memory-read access rights on a domain controller — the signature behavior of credential-dumping tools (Mimikatz sekurlsa, comsvcs.dll MiniDump abuse, Task Manager 'Create dump file', ProcDump) attempting to extract cached credential material directly from process memory rather than via replication (DCSync) or the database file (NTDS.dit).

data_sources.name: Sysmon Event ID 10
data_sources.description: ProcessAccess events targeting lsass.exe with GrantedAccess indicating memory-read rights (e.g. 0x1010, 0x1410, 0x1438, 0x143a, 0x1fffff).

detection_logic: Sysmon Event ID 10 where TargetImage ends in lsass.exe, GrantedAccess matches a known credential-dumping access mask, and SourceImage is not a recognized security/EDR agent process.
spl:
index=sysmon sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=10
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| where match(TargetImage, "(?i)lsass\.exe$")
| where GrantedAccess IN ("0x1010","0x1410","0x1438","0x143a","0x1fffff")
| lookup edr_agent_processes.csv SourceImage OUTPUT is_edr_agent
| where isnull(is_edr_agent)
| table _time, dvc, SourceImage, TargetImage, GrantedAccess, SourceProcessId
tuning_guidance: Requires Sysmon (or equivalent EDR process-access telemetry) on domain controllers — an explicit telemetry dependency. Maintain edr_agent_processes.csv to exclude legitimate security-tooling access.
investigation_steps: Identify the source process and its full execution chain.
Assume domain-wide credential compromise if confirmed as a dumping tool.
Check for the resulting dump file being written to disk or exfiltrated.
response_guidance: Treat as an active, high-confidence credential-dumping event on Tier-0 infrastructure; isolate the DC network segment for investigation and follow the krbtgt double-reset procedure.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires Sysmon or equivalent EDR process-access telemetry on domain controllers; not observable via default Windows Security event logging.

title: New Service Installed on a Domain Controller
description: Detects a new Windows service being installed on a domain controller. Installing a service on a DC provides SYSTEM-level code execution and persistence on one of the highest-value assets in the environment; while legitimate management/backup/monitoring agents install services during normal operations, this is a low-frequency enough event on DCs specifically to warrant per-occurrence review.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4697 (a service was installed in the system).

detection_logic: Event ID 4697 on a domain controller.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4697
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| lookup dc_approved_services.csv Service_Name OUTPUT is_approved
| where isnull(is_approved)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Service_Name, Service_File_Name
tuning_guidance: Maintain dc_approved_services.csv listing expected agents (backup, EDR, monitoring). Alert on all unrecognized matches.
investigation_steps: Review the service binary path and signature.
Confirm against a documented change (patch/agent deployment).
Check for the service's subsequent execution behavior.
response_guidance: Remove unauthorized services immediately and investigate the installing account and process for the initial access vector.

references.title: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service

author: Threat Detection Library

title: Scheduled Task Created on a Domain Controller
description: Detects a new scheduled task being registered directly on a domain controller (as opposed to pushed via GPO, see AD-GPO-007). A locally created scheduled task on a DC provides a straightforward, SYSTEM-capable persistence and execution mechanism on Tier-0 infrastructure.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log/Task Scheduler Operational log, Event ID 4698 (a scheduled task was created).

detection_logic: Event ID 4698 on a domain controller.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4698
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| lookup dc_approved_scheduled_tasks.csv Task_Name OUTPUT is_approved
| where isnull(is_approved)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Task_Name
tuning_guidance: Maintain dc_approved_scheduled_tasks.csv for known maintenance/backup tasks; alert on all unrecognized matches.
investigation_steps: Review the task's action, trigger, and running account.
Confirm against a documented change.
response_guidance: Remove unauthorized tasks immediately and investigate the creating account.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Local Account Created on a Domain Controller
description: Detects creation of a local (SAM, not AD-domain) account on a domain controller. Because domain controllers do not have a meaningful independent local SAM database for regular user accounts (they only host the built-in Administrator/DSRM account after promotion), any new local account creation event here is unusual and can indicate an attacker attempting to establish a persistence mechanism outside normal AD-based account monitoring.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4720 where the target is a local SAM account rather than an AD domain account.

detection_logic: Event ID 4720 on a domain controller where Target_Domain_Name matches the local computer name rather than the AD domain name.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4720
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| where Target_Domain_Name=dvc
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Target_Account_Name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; this event should be exceptionally rare on a healthy DC.
investigation_steps: Identify the creating account and its process of execution.
Assess whether this reflects direct SAM manipulation via offline tooling.
response_guidance: Remove the unauthorized local account immediately and treat as an active compromise indicator.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Windows Defender Disabled or Tampered on a Domain Controller
description: Detects Windows Defender real-time protection being disabled or its configuration weakened directly on a domain controller (as opposed to via GPO push, see AD-GPO-014). Disabling AV on Tier-0 infrastructure directly is a high-value, high-urgency defense-evasion action typically preceding malware or credential-dumping tool deployment.
