data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational
data_sources.description: Defender Operational log, Event ID 5001 (real-time protection disabled) or similar configuration-change events.

detection_logic: Windows Defender Operational log Event ID 5001/5010/5012 on a domain controller.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational" (EventCode=5001 OR EventCode=5010 OR EventCode=5012)
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| table _time, dvc, EventCode, Message
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; this event should be exceptionally rare on a DC outside a documented AV-exception/replacement-tooling change window.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented change (e.g. approved third-party EDR replacing Defender).
Check for subsequent suspicious process execution while unprotected.
response_guidance: Re-enable Defender immediately if unauthorized and investigate for malware/tooling deployed during the exposure window.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Windows Firewall Disabled on a Domain Controller
description: Detects the Windows Firewall being disabled for any profile on a domain controller. Disabling host-based firewall protection on Tier-0 infrastructure widens the DC's exposed attack surface and can facilitate lateral movement or remote exploitation attempts.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4950 (Windows Firewall setting changed) or 4954 (Group Policy settings for Windows Firewall changed).

detection_logic: Event ID 4950/4954 reflecting a firewall-disable setting change on a domain controller.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4950 OR EventCode=4954)
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; this should be a rare, deliberate change tied to specific documented troubleshooting.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Re-enable immediately if unauthorized.
Review for exploitation attempts during the exposure window.
response_guidance: Re-enable the firewall and investigate the disabling account.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Local Audit Policy Modified on a Domain Controller (auditpol)
description: Detects the local security audit policy being modified on a domain controller, whether via auditpol.exe or direct registry manipulation. Since DC-level audit policy governs whether events like 4662 (replication access), 5136 (directory-service changes), and 4768/4769 (Kerberos) are logged at all, weakening it can silently blind every other detection in this catalogue that depends on DC security-event telemetry.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4719 (system audit policy was changed).

detection_logic: Event ID 4719 on a domain controller.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4719
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Category, Subcategory, Changes
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches without exception. This is one of the highest-priority detections in the entire library, since its failure silently degrades every other DC-scoped detection.
investigation_steps: Identify exactly which audit subcategory changed and in which direction (enabled vs disabled).
Confirm against a documented, approved audit-policy change.
Immediately review activity that occurred while any subcategory was disabled for gaps.
response_guidance: Revert to the intended audit-policy baseline immediately and treat any period with disabled auditing as an investigative blind spot requiring compensating review (process/network telemetry, other DCs' logs for the same replicated activity).
author: Threat Detection Library

title: PowerShell Script Block Logging Disabled on a Domain Controller
description: Detects PowerShell Script Block Logging (or Module/Transcription logging) being disabled on a domain controller, whether via local policy or a targeted registry change. Since many AD-attack toolchains (AD module cmdlets, custom recon/exploitation scripts) run through PowerShell, disabling this logging specifically on a DC removes a key detection and forensic-recovery source for exactly the systems most likely to be targeted.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4657/5136 on the registry path governing PowerShell Script Block Logging (HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging).

detection_logic: Event ID 4657 (registry value modified) on the ScriptBlockLogging registry key with a value change to 0/disabled, on a domain controller.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4657 Object_Name="*PowerShell\\ScriptBlockLogging*"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| where New_Value="0"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_Name, New_Value
tuning_guidance: Requires registry SACL auditing enabled on the relevant key. Alert on all matches.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Review PowerShell activity from surrounding hosts/EDR telemetry to compensate for the logging gap.
response_guidance: Re-enable immediately and treat the exposure window as an investigative blind spot.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: RDP Enabled on a Domain Controller That Normally Disallows It
description: Detects Remote Desktop being enabled on a domain controller whose baseline configuration disallows it (many hardened environments restrict DC access to PAW/jump-host-only console or WinRM). Enabling RDP widens the DC's remote access surface and interactive-logon exposure.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4657 on the fDenyTSConnections registry value.

detection_logic: Event ID 4657 on HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\fDenyTSConnections transitioning from 1 to 0 on a DC flagged as RDP-disallowed in dc_rdp_baseline.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4657 Object_Name="*Terminal Server\\fDenyTSConnections"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| where New_Value="0"
| lookup dc_rdp_baseline.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT rdp_allowed
| where rdp_allowed=0 OR isnull(rdp_allowed)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, New_Value
tuning_guidance: Requires registry SACL auditing and a maintained dc_rdp_baseline.csv reflecting each DC's intended RDP posture.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Review subsequent RDP logon activity to the DC.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized and investigate the changing account.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: WinRM/PowerShell Remoting Enabled on a Domain Controller
description: Detects Windows Remote Management (WinRM) being enabled on a domain controller where it was not previously configured. WinRM is a common, legitimate remote-administration channel, but enabling it unexpectedly on a DC widens the set of remote-execution paths available to anyone who subsequently compromises an account with access.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, service-start event for the WinRM service, or 4697 service-install if not previously present.

detection_logic: System log Event ID 7036 for the WinRM service transitioning to 'running' on a DC previously baselined as WinRM-disabled.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=7036 service_name="Windows Remote Management (WS-Management)" service_state="running"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| lookup dc_winrm_baseline.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT winrm_expected
| where winrm_expected=0 OR isnull(winrm_expected)
| table _time, dvc
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained dc_winrm_baseline.csv; in most modern environments WinRM is expected to be enabled for legitimate remote administration (PAW-sourced), so tune this primarily for environments with a documented console/RDP-only DC access policy.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Review subsequent WinRM session activity to the DC.
response_guidance: Disable if unauthorized per the environment's DC-access policy.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Domain Controller Rebooted Outside Maintenance Window
description: Detects a domain controller restarting outside a documented maintenance window. While reboots are routine for patching, an unexpected reboot can indicate an availability attack, a crash induced by exploitation attempts, or a side effect of unauthorized changes (e.g. a forced role/service change requiring a restart).

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:System
data_sources.description: System event log, Event ID 6005 (Event Log service started, indicating a boot) or 1074 (system shutdown/restart initiated).

detection_logic: Event ID 6005/1074 on a domain controller where the timestamp falls outside approved_maintenance_windows.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" (EventCode=6005 OR EventCode=1074)
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| lookup approved_maintenance_windows.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT window_start, window_end
| where isnull(window_start) OR _time < window_start OR _time > window_end
| table _time, dvc, EventCode
tuning_guidance: Requires maintained approved_maintenance_windows.csv; without it every reboot will alert. Correlate with any preceding suspicious activity (AD-DC-005/012/013/014) before escalating.
investigation_steps: Confirm cause of restart (patch, crash, forced change).
Check DC health/error logs for crash indicators consistent with exploitation attempts.
response_guidance: Investigate if unexplained; not independently high-severity absent other correlating indicators.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Domain Controller Time Service (W32Time) Source Changed
description: Detects a change to the Windows Time service configuration on a domain controller, particularly its time source. Since Kerberos relies on tightly synchronized clocks (typically a 5-minute default skew tolerance) and many forensic timelines depend on consistent DC time, manipulating a DC's time source can be used to disrupt Kerberos authentication for targeted accounts or to muddy forensic timeline reconstruction.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4657 on the W32Time NtpServer/Type registry values.

detection_logic: Event ID 4657 on HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\Parameters registry values on a domain controller.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4657 Object_Name="*W32Time\\Parameters*"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_Name, New_Value
tuning_guidance: Requires registry SACL auditing; expect this to be a rare, infrastructure-level change reviewed manually rather than tuned by threshold.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification (e.g. NTP source hardening project).
Check for Kerberos authentication failures due to clock skew immediately following.
response_guidance: Revert if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Suspicious Process Spawned from lsass.exe or services.exe on a Domain Controller
description: Detects a child process being spawned from lsass.exe or services.exe on a domain controller. Neither process normally spawns interactive child processes under legitimate conditions; this pattern is strongly associated with process-injection or in-memory credential-dumping tooling that hooks into these SYSTEM-level processes.

data_sources.name: Sysmon Event ID 1
data_sources.description: Process creation where ParentImage is lsass.exe or services.exe.

detection_logic: Sysmon Event ID 1 where ParentImage ends in lsass.exe or services.exe (excluding known legitimate child processes of services.exe, which does legitimately spawn service binaries).
spl:
index=sysmon sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=1
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| where match(ParentImage, "(?i)lsass\.exe$") OR (match(ParentImage, "(?i)services\.exe$") AND NOT match(Image, "(?i)\\(svchost|dllhost|" . "known_service_binaries" . ")\.exe$"))
| table _time, dvc, ParentImage, Image, CommandLine
tuning_guidance: Requires Sysmon (or equivalent EDR process-tree telemetry) on domain controllers. lsass.exe should have effectively zero legitimate child processes; tune the services.exe branch against a maintained list of known legitimate service binaries.
investigation_steps: Review the spawned process's full command line and any subsequent activity.
Treat as a probable process-injection or credential-dumping indicator.
response_guidance: Isolate the DC for forensic investigation; treat as an active Tier-0 compromise.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires Sysmon or equivalent EDR process-tree telemetry on domain controllers; not observable from default Windows Security auditing.

title: Unsigned or Unusual Binary Loaded into LSASS on a Domain Controller
description: Detects an unsigned or otherwise unexpected DLL being loaded into the lsass.exe process on a domain controller. This is the load-time signature of an LSASS Security Support Provider (SSP) or Authentication Package persistence mechanism (e.g. a Skeleton-Key-like DLL patch) that hooks the authentication path to accept an attacker-chosen master password for any account.

data_sources.name: Sysmon Event ID 7
data_sources.description: Image/DLL load events where the target process is lsass.exe and the loaded module is unsigned or from an unexpected path.

detection_logic: Sysmon Event ID 7 where Image ends in lsass.exe, Signed=false, and ImageLoaded is outside the expected system32 SSP/AP module set.
spl:
index=sysmon sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=7
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| where match(Image, "(?i)lsass\.exe$") AND Signed="false"
| lookup expected_lsass_modules.csv ImageLoaded OUTPUT is_expected
| where isnull(is_expected)
| table _time, dvc, Image, ImageLoaded, Signed
tuning_guidance: Requires Sysmon Event ID 7 (image load) enabled on domain controllers, which can be verbose — scope collection or filtering to lsass.exe specifically to manage volume. Alert on all matches.
investigation_steps: Identify the unsigned module and its file-system origin and creation time.
Assume the technique is active and check for authentication-bypass behavior (successful logons that don't match the account's real password) domain-wide.
Treat as equivalent severity to a Skeleton Key compromise.
response_guidance: Reboot the DC to clear the in-memory patch (this technique typically does not survive a reboot without a corresponding boot-persistence mechanism), remove the malicious module from disk, and force a domain-wide credential reset; investigate for a boot-persistence companion mechanism.

references.title: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: LSASS Driver

author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires Sysmon Event ID 7 (DLL/image load) telemetry scoped to lsass.exe on domain controllers; this volume of telemetry is not available from default Windows Security auditing and Sysmon's image-load event can itself be very high-volume if not carefully scoped.

title: Domain Controller Computer Object's Delegation Attributes Reset to Unconstrained
description: Domain controllers are trusted for unconstrained delegation by default as a structural requirement of AD. This detection instead flags a change to a non-DC computer object's userAccountControl delegation flags that newly sets TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION (unconstrained) — since a rogue unconstrained-delegation host functions similarly to a DC for ticket-capture purposes if an attacker can coerce a privileged account to authenticate to it.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4742 with userAccountControl reflecting the TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION flag (0x80000) newly set on a non-DC computer object.

detection_logic: Event ID 4742 where User_Account_Control includes TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION and Target_Account_Name is not in domain_controllers.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4742
| search User_Account_Control="*TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION*"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS Target_Account_Name OUTPUT is_dc
| where isnull(is_dc)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Target_Account_Name, User_Account_Control
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; unconstrained delegation on a non-DC computer is a legacy, high-risk configuration that modern deployments should avoid entirely (see AD-DELEG namespace for the fuller unconstrained-delegation detection set).
investigation_steps: Determine why unconstrained delegation was enabled on this computer.
Assess whether it can be replaced with constrained or resource-based constrained delegation instead.
response_guidance: Remove the unconstrained-delegation flag unless there is a documented, unavoidable legacy requirement, and monitor the host closely for ticket-capture-based abuse in the meantime.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Domain Controller Outbound Connection to a Non-Standard External Destination
description: Detects a domain controller initiating an outbound network connection to a destination outside its expected baseline (replication partners, time servers, patch-management infrastructure, monitoring/backup targets). DCs are not typically expected to initiate general internet-bound traffic, so an unexpected outbound connection can indicate command-and-control communication or data exfiltration from a compromised DC.

data_sources.name: Sysmon Event ID 3
data_sources.description: Network connection events initiated from a domain controller to a destination outside dc_expected_destinations.csv.

detection_logic: Sysmon Event ID 3 on a DC where DestinationIp is not within any range in dc_expected_destinations.csv (replication partners, DNS, time, patch, backup, monitoring infrastructure).
spl:
index=sysmon sourcetype="XmlWinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" EventCode=3
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| lookup dc_expected_destinations.csv ip_cidr AS DestinationIp OUTPUT is_expected
| where isnull(is_expected)
| table _time, dvc, Image, DestinationIp, DestinationPort
tuning_guidance: Requires Sysmon network-connection logging (or equivalent firewall/NDR telemetry) plus a well-maintained destination baseline — an explicit telemetry and tuning-effort dependency to flag before deployment.
investigation_steps: Identify the initiating process and destination reputation.
Check for data-staging or exfiltration indicators preceding the connection.
response_guidance: Isolate the DC's network access pending investigation if the destination is confirmed malicious or unexplained.
author: Threat Detection Library
performance_guidance: Network-connection telemetry at DC scale can be high-volume; ensure dc_expected_destinations.csv is comprehensive before enabling as a real-time alert, and consider running as a periodic outlier report initially.
attack_mapping_note: Requires Sysmon network-connection telemetry (or equivalent NDR/firewall visibility) plus a comprehensive expected-destination baseline; this is a high-effort-to-tune detection called out explicitly rather than assumed turnkey.

title: Backup Operators Group Membership Changed
description: Detects a membership change to the built-in Backup Operators group. Backup Operators can back up and restore any file on a domain controller regardless of its ACL — including NTDS.dit and the registry SYSTEM hive — making membership in this group functionally equivalent to an offline credential-dumping capability even without Domain Admin rights.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4728/4729/4732/4733 where Group_Name=Backup Operators.

detection_logic: Event ID 4728/4732 (member added) where Group_Name=Backup Operators.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4728 OR EventCode=4732) Group_Name="Backup Operators"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Member_Name, Group_Name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; this duplicates the general privileged-operators coverage in AD-GRP-005 but is retained here specifically for DC-integrity analysts monitoring backup-capability-granting changes as a distinct concern from general group-membership analysts.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification for backup-operator rights.
Review the added account's subsequent backup/restore activity.
response_guidance: Remove if unauthorized and treat as equivalent priority to an NTDS.dit access finding.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: System State / NTDS Backup Restored on an Unexpected Domain Controller
description: Detects a system-state or NTDS-inclusive backup restore operation on a domain controller. Restoring an old backup can be used to revert recent security changes (e.g. restoring a version of AD from before a compromised account was disabled, or before an ACL fix was applied) or to reintroduce a previously removed persistence mechanism.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Windows Server Backup / wbadmin Operational log restore-start events, or Event ID 1917/1918-class NTDS restore indicators.

detection_logic: Backup-application Operational log events indicating a system-state/NTDS restore operation began on a domain controller.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Backup" EventCode=4 OR (index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Application" EventCode=1917)
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| table _time, dvc, EventCode, Message
tuning_guidance: Backup product and event-source specifics vary significantly by vendor (Windows Server Backup vs. Veeam vs. Commvault, etc.); validate the exact event source/ID against the environment's actual backup tooling before relying on this detection.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented disaster-recovery exercise or genuine restore need.
Compare object state before/after the restore for reintroduced risk (re-enabled accounts, restored group memberships, restored ACLs).
response_guidance: If unauthorized, treat as an active attempt to revert security remediation; re-apply any security fixes the restore may have undone.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Backup-restore event sources and IDs vary significantly by backup product; the SPL shown assumes Windows Server Backup and must be adapted to the environment's actual tooling.

title: Server Operators Group Membership Changed
description: Detects a membership change to the built-in Server Operators group on a domain controller. Server Operators can log on locally to DCs, start/stop most services, and manage shares — a combination that provides a practical path to further privilege escalation on Tier-0 infrastructure.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4728/4732 where Group_Name=Server Operators.

detection_logic: Event ID 4728/4732 where Group_Name=Server Operators.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4728 OR EventCode=4732) Group_Name="Server Operators"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Member_Name, Group_Name
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; retained alongside AD-GRP-005 for DC-integrity-focused analysts.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Review the added account's subsequent activity on DCs.
response_guidance: Remove if unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Print Spooler Service Running on a Domain Controller
description: Detects the Print Spooler service running on a domain controller. Following the PrintNightmare and PrinterBug (SpoolSample) disclosures, running the Print Spooler on a DC is a well-documented, high-risk configuration that enables remote coercion of the DC's computer account to authenticate to an attacker-controlled listener for NTLM relay attacks. Microsoft's post-disclosure guidance is to disable this service on domain controllers entirely.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:System
data_sources.description: System event log, Event ID 7036 for the Spooler service transitioning to 'running' on a DC.

detection_logic: System log Event ID 7036 where service_name="Print Spooler" and service_state="running" on a domain controller.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=7036 service_name="Print Spooler" service_state="running"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| table _time, dvc, service_name, service_state
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; this is a known-bad configuration that should be remediated by policy (disable Spooler on all DCs) rather than merely monitored, per current Microsoft guidance.
investigation_steps: Confirm no legitimate print-server role is co-located on this DC (itself a discouraged configuration).
Disable the service if not explicitly required.
response_guidance: Disable the Print Spooler service on the DC and audit for any PrinterBug/coercion activity that may have already occurred (correlate AD-COMP-006).
author: Threat Detection Library

title: EFS-RPC or WebClient Service Enabled on a Domain Controller (Coercion Surface)
description: Detects the WebClient (WebDAV) service, or conditions consistent with the EFS-RPC (MS-EFSR) interface being reachable, on a domain controller. Both are known coercion surfaces (PetitPotam abuses EFS-RPC; the WebClient service extends coercion techniques to HTTP-based relay) that allow a remote, unauthenticated or low-privileged attacker to force the DC to authenticate to an attacker-controlled destination.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:System
data_sources.description: System event log, Event ID 7036 for the WebClient service transitioning to 'running' on a DC.

detection_logic: System log Event ID 7036 where service_name="WebClient" and service_state="running" on a domain controller.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:System" EventCode=7036 service_name="WebClient" service_state="running"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS dvc OUTPUT is_dc
| where is_dc=1
| table _time, dvc, service_name, service_state
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; combine with confirmation that LDAP signing/channel binding and the EFS-RPC hardening patch/registry mitigation are in place as compensating controls, since the EFS-RPC interface itself cannot be fully disabled via a stoppable service.
investigation_steps: Disable the WebClient service if not explicitly required.
Verify EFS-RPC coercion mitigations (MS-EFSR hardening, RPC filters) are applied.
Correlate with AD-COMP-006 for evidence of active coercion.
response_guidance: Disable the service and apply current Microsoft coercion-mitigation guidance; treat as a standing risk-reduction gap until remediated.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: The EFS-RPC (MS-EFSR/PetitPotam) coercion surface is not fully represented by a single stoppable Windows service; this detection covers the WebClient/WebDAV-based coercion surface specifically and should be paired with EFS-RPC-specific hardening validation outside Splunk's visibility.

title: Domain Controller Object Class or Schema-Relevant Attribute Modified
description: Detects a modification to the AD schema itself (an attribute or class definition under the Schema naming context). Schema changes are extremely rare in a mature environment (typically only during a new Exchange/product installation or a deliberate schema-extension project) and, because the Schema Master is the only DC that can originate them, any unexpected schema change warrants immediate review — schema poisoning has been documented as a long-term, difficult-to-remove persistence technique.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136/5137 where Object_DN is under the Schema naming context (CN=Schema,CN=Configuration).

detection_logic: Event ID 5136/5137 where Object_DN contains 'CN=Schema,CN=Configuration'.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=5136 OR EventCode=5137)
| where match(Object_DN, "CN=Schema,CN=Configuration,DC=")
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name, Attribute_Value
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches without exception; maintain a documented allowlist window for legitimate product-installation schema extensions (e.g. Exchange setup) rather than suppressing broadly.
investigation_steps: Identify the specific schema object changed and by whom.
Confirm against a documented, approved schema-extension project.
Assess whether the change introduces a new attribute/right that could be abused (e.g. a new attribute added to a sensitive class's default security descriptor).
response_guidance: If unauthorized, engage Microsoft/AD-schema expertise before attempting to reverse the change — schema modifications can be difficult or impossible to fully undo; in the interim, treat the domain as having a persistent, hard-to-remove compromise indicator.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Domain or Forest Functional Level Changed
description: Detects the domain or forest functional level being raised. Functional-level changes are one-way (cannot be reverted) and enable new AD features that change available security defaults (e.g. raising to a level that changes default Kerberos encryption support or authentication-policy-silo availability); while a routine modernization step, it is significant enough to track and confirm as deliberate rather than as an unexpected side effect of another change.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on msDS-Behavior-Version attribute.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 where Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name=msDS-Behavior-Version.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-Behavior-Version"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, Attribute_Value
tuning_guidance: Low-frequency, deliberate infrastructure change; review each occurrence manually rather than tuning thresholds.
investigation_steps: Confirm against a documented modernization project.
Review any new security features/defaults the new functional level enables and whether they should be actively adopted (e.g. authentication policy silos).
response_guidance: Not independently actionable if confirmed legitimate; investigate if unexplained.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unconstrained Delegation Flag Set on a User Account
description: Detects the TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION userAccountControl flag being set on a user account. Unconstrained delegation is intended only for domain controllers as a structural requirement; on a user account it means any service that account authenticates to receives a copy of the user's TGT, which an attacker who compromises that service can then reuse to impersonate the user anywhere in the domain — this is an even higher-risk configuration on a user object than on a computer object, since user accounts are more often directly compromised via phishing/password attacks.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4738 (user account changed) with User_Account_Control reflecting TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION.

detection_logic: Event ID 4738 where User_Account_Control includes TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION (0x80000) newly set.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4738
| search User_Account_Control="*TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION*"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Target_Account_Name, User_Account_Control
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches without exception; there is essentially no legitimate reason for unconstrained delegation on a user account in a modern AD deployment.
investigation_steps: Determine why this flag was set and by whom.
Identify what the account subsequently authenticates to.
Assess the account's overall exposure (is it used interactively, from what sources).
response_guidance: Remove the flag immediately and reset the account's password (any cached TGT delegated to a service remains valid until expiry regardless of the flag being cleared).
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Unconstrained Delegation Flag Set on a Non-Tier-0 Computer Account
description: Detects the TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION flag being set on a computer account that is not a domain controller. A workstation or member server configured for unconstrained delegation becomes a high-value target: any privileged account that authenticates to it (even for an unrelated service) leaves a copy of its TGT in the host's memory, retrievable by an attacker with local admin/SYSTEM access there.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4742 (computer account changed) with User_Account_Control reflecting TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION.

detection_logic: Event ID 4742 where User_Account_Control includes TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION and Target_Account_Name is not in domain_controllers.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4742
| search User_Account_Control="*TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION*"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS Target_Account_Name OUTPUT is_dc
| where isnull(is_dc)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Target_Account_Name, User_Account_Control
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; a small number of legacy environments still legitimately require this for specific application servers (e.g. older print or terminal-services scenarios) — maintain an explicit, reviewed exception list rather than broad suppression.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification and whether constrained/RBCD delegation could replace this legacy configuration.
Identify what privileged accounts have recently authenticated to this host (correlate AD-AUTH namespace for privileged logons to this destination).
response_guidance: Migrate to constrained or resource-based constrained delegation where possible; if unconstrained delegation must remain, treat the host as Tier-0-equivalent and apply matching hardening/monitoring.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Constrained Delegation Target List Modified to Add a High-Value SPN
description: Detects the msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo attribute being modified to add an SPN belonging to a Tier-0 service (e.g. an SPN on a domain controller, such as LDAP/<DC-hostname>, HOST/<DC-hostname>, or krbtgt-equivalent services). Constrained delegation lets the configured account impersonate any user (subject to protocol-transition settings) to only the listed target services, so adding a Tier-0 SPN to the list is functionally close to granting the delegating account impersonation rights over the domain controller itself.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 where Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name=msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo and Attribute_Value matches an SPN on a DC or other Tier-0 host.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS Attribute_Value OUTPUT is_dc_spn
| lookup tier0_computers.csv computer_name AS Attribute_Value OUTPUT is_tier0_spn
| where is_dc_spn=1 OR is_tier0_spn=1
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, Attribute_Value
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches without exception; there is no ordinary legitimate reason for a service to be granted constrained delegation to a domain controller's own services.
investigation_steps: Identify the delegating account and how it obtained write access to this attribute (correlate with the AD-ACL namespace).
Check for immediate S4U2Proxy ticket requests using the new delegation path (AD-DELEG-008).
response_guidance: Remove the unauthorized delegation target immediately and treat as an active privilege-escalation attempt.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Constrained Delegation Target List Modified (General)
description: A broader, lower-severity complement to AD-DELEG-003: detects any modification to msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, including additions to non-Tier-0 targets. Even mid-tier delegation grants can be chained toward privilege escalation depending on what the target service itself has access to, so all changes are tracked for baseline/attack-path review even when not immediately Critical.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 where Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name=msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, excluding matches already covered by AD-DELEG-003.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo"
| lookup domain_controllers.csv computer_name AS Attribute_Value OUTPUT is_dc_spn
| lookup tier0_computers.csv computer_name AS Attribute_Value OUTPUT is_tier0_spn
| where isnull(is_dc_spn) AND isnull(is_tier0_spn)
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN, Attribute_Value
tuning_guidance: Route to a lower-priority delegation-inventory review queue; feed into periodic BloodHound-style attack-path analysis.
investigation_steps: Confirm business justification.
Feed into periodic attack-path graph review for chained escalation potential.
response_guidance: Not independently high-urgency; use for delegation inventory hygiene and attack-path analysis.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Protocol Transition (Trust This User/Computer for Delegation to Any Service) Enabled
description: Detects the TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION userAccountControl flag being set, which enables protocol transition for constrained delegation. This allows the account to use S4U2Self to obtain a service ticket on behalf of any user without that user having authenticated first — combined with a broad msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo list, this removes the requirement that the impersonated user have actually authenticated to the delegating service at all, meaningfully widening the abuse surface versus constrained delegation without protocol transition.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4738/4742 with User_Account_Control reflecting TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION (0x1000000).

detection_logic: Event ID 4738/4742 where User_Account_Control includes TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION newly set.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4738 OR EventCode=4742)
| search User_Account_Control="*TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION*"
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Target_Account_Name, User_Account_Control
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; review in conjunction with the account's current msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo list to assess actual abuse potential.
investigation_steps: Review the account's delegation target list.
Confirm business justification for protocol transition specifically.
response_guidance: Remove if unauthorized or unnecessary; prefer resource-based constrained delegation for new deployments where possible.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Resource-Based Constrained Delegation Configured on a User Object
description: Detects msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity being set on a user object. This is a companion detection to AD-COMP-015 (which covers computer objects, the far more common RBCD target); RBCD on a user object is rarer and, since user objects are typically higher-value impersonation targets themselves, any occurrence warrants review with equal or greater priority.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity where Object_Class=user.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 where Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name=msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity and Object_Class=user.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity" Object_Class=user
| table _time, dvc, Subject_Account_Name, Object_DN
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; RBCD on a user object has essentially no common legitimate use case.
investigation_steps: Resolve the trustee(s) written into the attribute.
Check for subsequent S4U2Proxy ticket requests targeting this user.
response_guidance: Remove the unauthorized attribute immediately.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: High Volume of S4U2Self Ticket Requests from a Single Account
description: Detects a single service account requesting an unusually high number of S4U2Self tickets (service tickets obtained on behalf of other users without their credentials) within a short window. A legitimate delegation-enabled service typically issues S4U2Self requests in proportion to real user traffic; a sudden spike, especially covering many distinct impersonated users, is consistent with an attacker abusing protocol transition to enumerate or impersonate a broad set of accounts.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4769 with S4U flags set, or 4768 S4U2Self indicator, grouped by the requesting service account.

detection_logic: Event ID 4769 where the ticket request reflects S4U semantics (Transited_Services populated), grouped by Service_Name over 30 minutes; alert when distinct_count(Account_Name) exceeds a per-service baseline.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4769
| where isnotnull(Transited_Services) AND Transited_Services!=""
| bucket _time span=30m
| stats dc(Account_Name) as impersonated_count by _time, Service_Name
| lookup s4u_baseline.csv Service_Name OUTPUT baseline_max
| where impersonated_count > baseline_max
tuning_guidance: Requires a maintained per-service S4U baseline (s4u_baseline.csv) since normal volume varies enormously by service popularity; start with a generous threshold and tighten after a baselining period.
investigation_steps: Identify the delegating service account and its normal function.
Review the specific set of impersonated accounts for privileged-account overlap.
Check whether the account's msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo/RBCD configuration recently changed.
response_guidance: If unexplained, treat as active delegation abuse and review/restrict the account's delegation configuration.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Delegation Configuration Change Followed by S4U2Proxy Ticket Request (Chain)
description: The flagship delegation-abuse chain: a delegation attribute (msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity, or the TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION flag) is modified, and shortly afterward the same account performs an S4U2Proxy request to obtain a service ticket impersonating another user against the newly configured target. This sequence represents a delegation grant being actively exercised, and — like the DCSync rights-grant/use chain — treats the grant and the use as related but distinct signals whose combination is the highest-confidence indicator available.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 (delegation attribute change) followed by 4769 (S4U2Proxy ticket request) from the same account.

detection_logic: AD-DELEG-003/004/005/006 match followed within 4 hours by an Event ID 4769 S4U2Proxy request (Transited_Services populated) from the same account.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=5136 OR EventCode=4769)
| eval etype=case(EventCode=5136 AND (Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo" OR Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity"), "deleg_change", EventCode=4769 AND isnotnull(Transited_Services) AND Transited_Services!="", "s4u2proxy_use", true(), null())
| where isnotnull(etype)
| eval actor=coalesce(Subject_Account_Name, Account_Name)
| transaction actor maxspan=4h startswith=eval(etype="deleg_change") endswith=eval(etype="s4u2proxy_use")
| where eventcount=2
| table _time, dvc, actor, duration
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; this is one of the highest-confidence RBCD/constrained-delegation-abuse chains available from Windows Security event data.
investigation_steps: Identify the impersonated user and target service in the S4U2Proxy request.
Assume the impersonated user's access has been exercised by the attacker.
Review the full attack chain leading to the delegation-attribute write (correlate AD-ACL/AD-COMP for how the delegation right was obtained).
response_guidance: Remove the delegation configuration immediately, reset the impersonated user's credentials/sessions, and treat as an active, likely successful privilege-escalation attack.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: S4U2Proxy Ticket Requested for a Privileged Impersonated User
description: Detects an S4U2Proxy service-ticket request where the impersonated user (reflected in the ticket's transited-services/target-user field) is a Tier-0/privileged account. Even without a preceding delegation-configuration change visible in the current search window (e.g. the delegation was configured before logging began, or configured via replication as in a DCShadow-assisted attack), any S4U2Proxy request impersonating a privileged user is independently worth immediate review.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4769 S4U2Proxy request where the impersonated account is in tier0_privileged_accounts.csv.

detection_logic: Event ID 4769 with Transited_Services populated where Account_Name (the impersonated user) is in tier0_privileged_accounts.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4769
| where isnotnull(Transited_Services) AND Transited_Services!=""
| lookup tier0_privileged_accounts.csv account AS Account_Name OUTPUT is_privileged
| where is_privileged=1
| table _time, dvc, Account_Name, Service_Name, Transited_Services
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches; legitimate delegation-based impersonation of Domain Admin-tier accounts is exceptionally rare and worth an explicit exception list if it occurs at all (e.g. certain break-glass automation).
investigation_steps: Identify the delegating service and confirm its delegation configuration.
Assume the privileged user's access has been exercised via delegation.
response_guidance: Treat as a likely privilege-escalation event; review and restrict the delegating service's configuration and the privileged account's exposure.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Multiple Delegation Configuration Changes by a Single Actor
description: Detects a single actor modifying delegation attributes on multiple distinct objects within a short window — a pattern consistent with an automated tool (e.g. a scripted RBCD-staging utility) sweeping multiple objects to plant several redundant delegation-abuse paths rather than a single deliberate, documented administrative change.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on delegation-related attributes grouped by actor.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 where Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name is msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo or msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity, grouped by Subject_Account_Name over 1 hour; alert when distinct_count(Object_DN) >= 3.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 (Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo" OR Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity")
| bucket _time span=1h
| stats dc(Object_DN) as objects_modified values(Object_DN) as objects by _time, Subject_Account_Name
| where objects_modified >= 3
tuning_guidance: Exclude known identity-governance/delegation-management tooling accounts via a lookup allowlist.
investigation_steps: Review every modified object's new delegation configuration.
Determine whether this reflects a legitimate bulk-delegation project or attack staging.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, treat as active multi-object delegation-abuse staging and remove all newly added delegation configurations pending review.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Delegation Attribute Removed Then Immediately Reconfigured (Evasion Pattern)
description: Detects a delegation attribute being cleared and then re-set within a short window, potentially with a different target. This oscillation pattern can reflect an attacker testing a delegation configuration, or deliberately toggling it to reduce the window of exposure visible to periodic point-in-time configuration scans while still exercising it in between.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on delegation attributes, two changes to the same object within a short window.

detection_logic: Two or more Event ID 5136 changes to the same object's msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo or msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity attribute within 2 hours.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 (Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo" OR Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity")
| bucket _time span=2h
| stats count as change_count values(Attribute_Value) as values by _time, Object_DN, Subject_Account_Name
| where change_count >= 2
tuning_guidance: Exclude known configuration-management/automation tooling that may legitimately reconcile delegation state repeatedly.
investigation_steps: Review the sequence of values set to understand the intent.
Check for ticket activity (S4U2Proxy) occurring in the gap between changes.
response_guidance: Treat as suspicious testing/evasion behavior and review the actor's broader recent activity.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Service Account with Delegation Rights Authenticates from an Unusual Source
description: Detects a service account known to hold constrained-delegation or RBCD-trustee rights authenticating from a source outside its established baseline. Since delegation-capable accounts are high-value (their compromise enables impersonation of other users), a source-location anomaly for one of these specific accounts warrants tighter scrutiny than the general service-account source-anomaly detection in AD-AUTH.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4624/4768 for an account present in delegation_capable_accounts.csv from a source outside service_account_src_baseline.csv.

detection_logic: Event ID 4624/4768 where Account_Name is in delegation_capable_accounts.csv and Source_Network_Address is not in service_account_src_baseline.csv for that account.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" (EventCode=4624 OR EventCode=4768)
| lookup delegation_capable_accounts.csv account AS Account_Name OUTPUT is_delegation_capable
| where is_delegation_capable=1
| lookup service_account_src_baseline.csv Account_Name, Source_Network_Address OUTPUT is_baseline
| where isnull(is_baseline)
| table _time, dvc, Account_Name, Source_Network_Address
tuning_guidance: Requires maintaining delegation_capable_accounts.csv from a periodic scan of msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo/msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity/TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION across the domain.
investigation_steps: Confirm whether the new source is a legitimate new deployment location.
Review the account's subsequent S4U activity from the new source.
response_guidance: Investigate as potential compromise of a high-value delegation-capable account; reset credentials if unexplained.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Delegation Rights Granted to a Recently Created Computer Account
description: Detects a computer account created within the past 24 hours being granted constrained-delegation or RBCD-trustee rights. This combination — a very recently self-created computer account (per AD-COMP-001/002, easily created by any user via MachineAccountQuota) immediately receiving delegation rights — is the specific pattern behind the classic MachineAccountQuota-to-RBCD attack chain and is one of the highest-confidence indicators in this namespace even before any ticket activity is observed.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 4741 (computer created) correlated with a later 5136 delegation-attribute grant for the same object within 24 hours.

detection_logic: Event ID 4741 for a computer object followed within 24 hours by an Event ID 5136 setting msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity, or TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION on the same object, OR the new computer account appearing as a trustee in another object's RBCD attribute.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4741
| eval etype="computer_created"
| append [
    search index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 (Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo" OR Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity" OR Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="userAccountControl")
    | eval etype="delegation_grant"
  ]
| transaction Object_DN, Sam_Account_Name maxspan=24h startswith=eval(etype="computer_created") endswith=eval(etype="delegation_grant")
| where eventcount=2
| table _time, dvc, Sam_Account_Name, Object_DN, duration
tuning_guidance: Alert on all matches without exception; this chain closely mirrors AD-COMP-015 but is anchored on the computer-creation event rather than the delegation-grant event, providing an earlier-warning variant of the same underlying attack.
investigation_steps: Treat as a confirmed MachineAccountQuota-to-RBCD staging attempt.
Identify the creating/granting actor (often the same identity).
Check for immediate S4U2Proxy use (correlate AD-DELEG-008).
response_guidance: Delete the computer account and remove the delegation grant immediately; treat as an active privilege-escalation attempt in progress.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Delegation-Capable Account's SPN Modified Immediately Before Delegation Grant
description: Detects an SPN being added to an account shortly before that same account is granted constrained-delegation rights. Since constrained delegation targets are specified by SPN, an attacker preparing an abuse path sometimes first adds a plausible-looking SPN to a controlled account before configuring delegation, particularly when targeting a service SPN that does not already exist on the attacker's account.

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Security
data_sources.description: DC security event log, Event ID 5136 on servicePrincipalName followed by 5136 on msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo for the same object.

detection_logic: Event ID 5136 on servicePrincipalName followed within 2 hours by Event ID 5136 on msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo for the same Object_DN.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=5136 (Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="servicePrincipalName" OR Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo")
| eval etype=if(Attribute_LDAP_Display_Name="servicePrincipalName", "spn_added", "delegation_granted")
| transaction Object_DN maxspan=2h startswith=eval(etype="spn_added") endswith=eval(etype="delegation_granted")
| where eventcount=2
| table _time, dvc, Object_DN, duration
tuning_guidance: Correlate with the creating/modifying actor's broader activity; legitimate service-onboarding workflows can also match this pattern, so treat as a moderate-confidence supporting signal rather than a standalone Critical alert.
investigation_steps: Review both the new SPN and the new delegation target for consistency with a legitimate service deployment.
Check for subsequent S4U activity.
response_guidance: Investigate as a potential delegation-abuse staging sequence; not independently conclusive.
author: Threat Detection Library

title: Delegation Rights Held by an Account Outside the Expected Delegation Inventory
description: A periodic reconciliation check: compares the live set of accounts currently holding any delegation capability (unconstrained, constrained, or RBCD trustee) against a maintained inventory of approved delegation configurations. This catches delegation grants that predate current logging, were configured via a method that bypassed the streaming detections above (e.g. during a period of disabled auditing), or have drifted from their originally approved scope over time.

data_sources.name: ldapsearch
data_sources.description: Periodic LDAP query for all objects with a non-empty msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity, or TRUSTED_FOR_DELEGATION/TRUSTED_TO_AUTH_FOR_DELEGATION flag.

detection_logic: Scheduled LDAP query for all delegation-capable objects, compared against approved_delegation_inventory.csv; alert on any object present in the live scan but absent from the approved inventory.
spl:
| ldapsearch domain=<domain> search="(|(msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo=*)(msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity=*)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=524288)(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=16777216))" attrs="distinguishedName,msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo,userAccountControl"
| lookup approved_delegation_inventory.csv object_dn AS distinguishedName OUTPUT is_approved
| where isnull(is_approved)
| table distinguishedName, msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, userAccountControl
tuning_guidance: Requires an LDAP-search-capable Splunk add-on and a maintained approved_delegation_inventory.csv reflecting every deliberately approved delegation configuration in the domain — the essential reconciliation control that catches anything the streaming detections in this namespace might have missed.
investigation_steps: Review each unapproved delegation configuration found.
Determine whether it is legacy debris, a missed approval, or an active compromise indicator.
response_guidance: Remove unapproved delegation configurations found during reconciliation; update the approved inventory for anything found to be legitimate but undocumented.
author: Threat Detection Library
performance_guidance: Run as a scheduled (e.g. daily) report using an LDAP-search-capable Splunk app/add-on; not a real-time streaming search.
attack_mapping_note: Requires an LDAP-search-capable Splunk add-on run on a schedule; this reconciliation control is intended as a safety net for delegation grants that predate logging or occurred during an audit-policy gap, not a real-time detection.

title: Unsigned LDAP Bind Accepted by a Domain Controller
description: Detects a domain controller accepting an LDAP simple bind without signing (LDAP Signing not enforced). Unsigned LDAP is vulnerable to NTLM relay attacks — a coerced or intercepted authentication can be relayed to the DC's LDAP service to make arbitrary directory changes (including granting DCSync rights) as the relayed identity. Microsoft's 2020 hardening guidance (and later default) is to require LDAP signing on all DCs.
required_log_sources: Windows Directory Service Diagnostics Event Log

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Directory Service
data_sources.description: Directory Service diagnostics log, Event ID 2889 (unsigned LDAP bind was performed).

detection_logic: Event ID 2889 on a domain controller (requires the 'LDAP Interface Events' diagnostic logging level to be enabled).
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Directory Service" EventCode=2889
| table _time, dvc, Client_IP_Address, Bind_Type
tuning_guidance: Requires enabling the '16 LDAP Interface Events' diagnostic logging level (registry) on each DC — not on by default. Once enabled, this can be noisy in environments with legacy applications; use volume/source review to drive an LDAP-signing enforcement project rather than per-event triage.
investigation_steps: Identify the source application/host performing unsigned binds.
Prioritize remediating (upgrading or reconfiguring) the identified legacy application to support signed/encrypted LDAP.
Track progress toward eventually enforcing LDAP signing domain-wide (LDAPServerIntegrity=2).
response_guidance: Migrate identified sources to signed LDAP/LDAPS; this detection's primary value is driving the migration project that closes the underlying relay exposure, since the individual events themselves are not necessarily malicious.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires enabling the LDAP Interface Events diagnostic logging level on domain controllers, which is not on by default and is separate from standard Security-log auditing.

title: LDAP Channel Binding Not Enforced (Simple Bind Over LDAPS Without Channel Binding)
description: Detects LDAPS binds that succeed without channel binding tokens (CBT), meaning the encrypted session is not cryptographically bound to the outer TLS channel. Without channel binding, an attacker positioned to intercept traffic can potentially relay LDAPS authentication similarly to unsigned LDAP, defeating the protection TLS was expected to provide.
required_log_sources: Windows Directory Service Diagnostics Event Log

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Directory Service
data_sources.description: Directory Service diagnostics log, Event ID 3039/3040 (channel binding token check results) when LdapEnforceChannelBinding is set to audit/compatibility mode.

detection_logic: Event ID 3039 (channel binding token missing) or 3040 (channel binding token incorrect) on a domain controller running in audit mode for LdapEnforceChannelBinding.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Directory Service" (EventCode=3039 OR EventCode=3040)
| table _time, dvc, Client_IP_Address, EventCode
tuning_guidance: Requires setting LdapEnforceChannelBinding to audit mode (value 1) on each DC to generate these events before moving to full enforcement (value 2). Use findings to drive a remediation project for identified legacy clients.
investigation_steps: Identify the source client/application missing channel binding support.
Prioritize upgrading or reconfiguring the client.
Track progress toward full LdapEnforceChannelBinding enforcement.
response_guidance: Remediate identified clients and move to full enforcement once compatibility is confirmed domain-wide.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires enabling LdapEnforceChannelBinding in audit mode on domain controllers, a non-default diagnostic setting distinct from standard Security-log auditing.

title: Anonymous LDAP Bind Accepted
description: Detects an anonymous (unauthenticated) LDAP bind being accepted by a domain controller. While a small subset of directory information (rootDSE, certain legacy-compatible attributes) may be exposed to anonymous binds under default settings, an anonymous bind that successfully returns broader directory data indicates weaker-than-default anonymous-access permissions and provides attackers a pre-authentication reconnaissance capability.
required_log_sources: Windows Directory Service Diagnostics Event Log

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Directory Service
data_sources.description: Directory Service diagnostics log, Event ID 2889 with Bind_Type reflecting an anonymous/unauthenticated bind.

detection_logic: Event ID 2889 where Bind_Type indicates anonymous/unauthenticated.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Directory Service" EventCode=2889 Bind_Type="anonymous"
| table _time, dvc, Client_IP_Address
tuning_guidance: Requires the LDAP Interface Events diagnostic logging level. Alert on all matches; anonymous LDAP access should be disabled in virtually all modern environments (dsHeuristics fDoNotAllowAnonymousOperation).
investigation_steps: Identify the source and what information was queried.
Verify the dsHeuristics anonymous-access setting on the domain.
response_guidance: Harden the domain to disable anonymous LDAP operations unless a specific, documented legacy application requires it.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires enabling the LDAP Interface Events diagnostic logging level on domain controllers.

title: High-Volume LDAP Search from a Single Source (Directory Enumeration)
description: Detects an unusually high volume of LDAP search operations from a single source within a short window — consistent with automated directory-enumeration tooling (BloodHound/SharpHound, ADRecon, PowerView) performing bulk collection of users, groups, computers, ACLs, and trust relationships to build an attack-path graph.
required_log_sources: Windows Directory Service Diagnostics Event Log

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Directory Service
data_sources.description: Directory Service diagnostics log, Event ID 1644 (expensive/inefficient LDAP search) or search-operation events grouped by client source.

detection_logic: Directory Service diagnostics search-event volume grouped by Client_IP_Address over 15 minutes; alert when count exceeds a per-source baseline threshold.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Directory Service" EventCode=1644
| bucket _time span=15m
| stats count as search_count by _time, Client_IP_Address
| lookup ldap_search_baseline.csv Client_IP_Address OUTPUT baseline_max
| where search_count > baseline_max
tuning_guidance: Requires the 'Field Engineering' diagnostic logging level (or equivalent) for expensive-search logging; alternatively use network-layer LDAP traffic volume from a network monitoring tool if DC-side diagnostics are not enabled. Maintain ldap_search_baseline.csv per known management/monitoring source.
investigation_steps: Identify the source host and account performing the enumeration.
Check for known AD-recon tooling process/command-line indicators on the source (via EDR/Sysmon if available).
Review what specific objects/attributes were queried.
response_guidance: Investigate the source host for compromise; if confirmed reconnaissance tooling, treat as an active attack in the discovery phase and expect follow-on Kerberoasting/ACL-abuse/privilege-escalation activity.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires the Field Engineering (or equivalent expensive-search) diagnostic logging level on domain controllers, not enabled by default.

title: LDAP Query Pattern Consistent with BloodHound/SharpHound Collection
description: Detects a distinctive sequence of LDAP queries from a single source matching the known collection pattern used by BloodHound/SharpHound and similar attack-path-mapping tools: rapid, sequential queries against users, groups, computers, OUs, GPOs, trusts, and object ACLs (nTSecurityDescriptor) covering the full domain within a short time span.
required_log_sources: Windows Directory Service Diagnostics Event Log

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Directory Service
data_sources.description: Directory Service diagnostics log, sequential search events grouped by source touching multiple distinct object classes including nTSecurityDescriptor reads.

detection_logic: Directory Service search events from a single Client_IP_Address within 30 minutes covering at least 4 distinct object classes (user, group, computer, organizationalUnit) plus a security-descriptor (ACL) read.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Directory Service" EventCode=1644
| bucket _time span=30m
| stats dc(Object_Class) as class_variety values(Object_Class) as classes by _time, Client_IP_Address
| where class_variety >= 4
tuning_guidance: Requires the Field Engineering diagnostic logging level. Exclude known, legitimate identity-governance/attack-path-review tooling used defensively (many organizations run BloodHound themselves for purple-team purposes) via a source allowlist.
investigation_steps: Identify the source host and account.
Confirm whether this is authorized defensive BloodHound use versus an attacker.
If unauthorized, expect the resulting attack-path graph to inform subsequent privilege-escalation activity — review the source's follow-on actions closely.
response_guidance: If unauthorized, treat as an active reconnaissance phase and monitor closely for follow-on ACL-abuse, Kerberoasting, or delegation-abuse activity targeting paths the collection would have revealed.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires the Field Engineering (or equivalent expensive-search) diagnostic logging level on domain controllers, not enabled by default.

title: LDAP Bind from a Non-Domain-Joined or Unmanaged Source
description: Detects an LDAP bind against a domain controller from a source IP address that does not correspond to any known managed/domain-joined asset. Legitimate LDAP clients are typically domain-joined servers, workstations, or documented service integrations; a bind from an unrecognized IP can indicate an unmanaged device or an attacker's own infrastructure directly querying the directory.
required_log_sources: Windows Directory Service Diagnostics Event Log

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Directory Service
data_sources.description: Directory Service diagnostics log, Event ID 2889 correlated against a managed-asset inventory.

detection_logic: Event ID 2889 where Client_IP_Address is not present in managed_asset_inventory.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Directory Service" EventCode=2889
| lookup managed_asset_inventory.csv ip_address AS Client_IP_Address OUTPUT is_managed
| where isnull(is_managed)
| table _time, dvc, Client_IP_Address, Bind_Type
tuning_guidance: Requires the LDAP Interface Events diagnostic logging level and a maintained managed_asset_inventory.csv (e.g. sourced from CMDB/DHCP-lease/asset-management data).
investigation_steps: Identify the source device.
Determine whether it is an unmanaged/unauthorized device or a gap in the asset inventory.
response_guidance: Investigate unrecognized sources; update the inventory or block/remediate unauthorized devices.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires the LDAP Interface Events diagnostic logging level on domain controllers plus a maintained managed-asset inventory lookup.

title: LDAP Simple Bind Failure Burst (LDAP-Based Password Spray/Brute Force)
description: Detects a burst of failed LDAP simple bind attempts. Because LDAP simple binds authenticate directly against the directory rather than through the Kerberos or NTLM authentication packages that generate the standard 4625 failed-logon event, brute-force or password-spray activity conducted via LDAP simple binds can bypass detections built solely on 4625/4771, making this a distinct and necessary detection surface.
required_log_sources: Windows Directory Service Diagnostics Event Log

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Directory Service
data_sources.description: Directory Service diagnostics log, Event ID 2889 combined with bind-failure indicators, or LDAP simple-bind failure events from an LDAP-aware network sensor.

detection_logic: LDAP simple-bind failure events grouped by Client_IP_Address over 10 minutes; alert when distinct_count of attempted account names or total failure count exceeds a threshold.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Directory Service" EventCode=2889 bind_result="failed"
| bucket _time span=10m
| stats count as failure_count, dc(bind_account) as distinct_accounts by _time, Client_IP_Address
| where failure_count >= 10 OR distinct_accounts >= 5
tuning_guidance: Requires the LDAP Interface Events diagnostic logging level exposing bind failure results, which may require supplementing with a network-layer LDAP-aware sensor in environments where DC diagnostic logging cannot capture the bind_result field directly — validate field availability against the actual DC diagnostic log schema before deployment.
investigation_steps: Identify the source and targeted accounts.
Cross-reference with AD-AUTH-002/003 (Kerberos/NTLM-based spray detections) to confirm whether this is a distinct LDAP-specific attack vector.
Check for any resulting successful bind.
response_guidance: Block the source and investigate for successful compromise as with any password-spray finding; treat LDAP-based spray with equal urgency to Kerberos-based spray since it targets the same credential space.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires the LDAP Interface Events diagnostic logging level; the specific bind-result/failure-reason field availability should be validated against the deployed DC diagnostic logging configuration before relying on this detection.

title: LDAP Query Filtering Specifically for Kerberoastable Accounts
description: Detects an LDAP search filter matching the well-known pattern used by Kerberoasting reconnaissance tools to enumerate accounts with a servicePrincipalName set (e.g. filters resembling '(&(objectCategory=person)(objectClass=user)(servicePrincipalName=*))', as used by PowerView's Get-DomainUser -SPN and similar tooling). This is a precursor reconnaissance step that typically precedes the actual Kerberoasting ticket-request activity covered by the AD-KRB namespace.
required_log_sources: Windows Directory Service Diagnostics Event Log

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Directory Service
data_sources.description: Directory Service diagnostics log, Event ID 1644 with the LDAP filter text captured (requires expensive/inefficient search logging or a network LDAP-aware sensor).

detection_logic: Directory Service diagnostics search event where ldap_filter contains 'servicePrincipalName=*'.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Directory Service" EventCode=1644
| search ldap_filter="*servicePrincipalName=\**"
| table _time, dvc, Client_IP_Address, ldap_filter
tuning_guidance: Requires diagnostic logging that captures the actual LDAP filter text — this level of detail typically requires a network-layer LDAP-parsing sensor rather than native DC event logs, which is an explicit telemetry dependency to validate. Exclude known legitimate SPN-inventory/audit tooling.
investigation_steps: Identify the source and correlate with subsequent Kerberos ticket-request volume (AD-KRB-008/009/010) from the same source/account.
Treat as a strong precursor signal.
response_guidance: Monitor the source closely for follow-on Kerberoasting activity; investigate as reconnaissance if the pattern is unauthorized.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Capturing the actual LDAP filter text generally requires network-layer LDAP protocol parsing rather than native Windows DC event logging; validate this capability against the deployed telemetry stack before relying on this detection.

title: LDAP Query Enumerating Membership of Tier-0 Privileged Groups
description: Detects an LDAP query specifically targeting the membership of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, or other Tier-0 groups from a source outside expected identity-administration tooling. While querying group membership is routine for many legitimate purposes, a source with no other administrative activity specifically enumerating privileged-group membership is a reconnaissance indicator worth tracking.
required_log_sources: Windows Directory Service Diagnostics Event Log

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Directory Service
data_sources.description: Directory Service diagnostics log, search events with a base DN or filter referencing a Tier-0 group's distinguishedName.

detection_logic: Directory Service diagnostics search event where base_dn matches an entry in tier0_privileged_groups.csv, from a source not in authorized_identity_admins.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Directory Service" EventCode=1644
| lookup tier0_privileged_groups.csv object_dn AS base_dn OUTPUT is_tier0_group
| where is_tier0_group=1
| lookup authorized_identity_admins.csv Client_IP_Address OUTPUT is_admin_source
| where isnull(is_admin_source)
| table _time, dvc, Client_IP_Address, base_dn
tuning_guidance: Requires the Field Engineering diagnostic logging level. Route to a lower-priority discovery-review queue; use primarily as supporting context for other findings from the same source.
investigation_steps: Identify the source and confirm authorization.
Correlate with other discovery/reconnaissance activity from the same source.
response_guidance: Not independently high-urgency; use as a discovery-phase indicator supporting broader investigation.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires the Field Engineering (or equivalent expensive-search) diagnostic logging level on domain controllers.

title: LDAP Query Against Schema or Configuration Partition by a Non-Administrative Source
description: Detects an LDAP query against the Configuration or Schema naming context by a source outside recognized AD administration/PKI-management tooling. Querying these partitions is a normal part of AD CS attack-path discovery (finding certificate templates, sites, and cross-domain configuration) and general environment reconnaissance beyond the default domain naming context.
required_log_sources: Windows Directory Service Diagnostics Event Log

data_sources.name: WinEventLog:Directory Service
data_sources.description: Directory Service diagnostics log, search events with a base DN under CN=Configuration.

detection_logic: Directory Service diagnostics search event where base_dn contains 'CN=Configuration' or 'CN=Schema', from a source not in authorized_identity_admins.csv or pki_management_principals.csv.
spl:
index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Directory Service" EventCode=1644
| where match(base_dn, "CN=Configuration") OR match(base_dn, "CN=Schema")
| lookup authorized_identity_admins.csv Client_IP_Address OUTPUT is_admin_source
| lookup pki_management_principals.csv Client_IP_Address OUTPUT is_pki_source
| where isnull(is_admin_source) AND isnull(is_pki_source)
| table _time, dvc, Client_IP_Address, base_dn
tuning_guidance: Requires the Field Engineering diagnostic logging level. Route to discovery-review queue; correlate with subsequent AD CS-related findings (AD-ACL-018) for higher-confidence prioritization.
investigation_steps: Identify the source and confirm authorization.
Correlate with subsequent certificate-template or trust-related findings.
response_guidance: Not independently high-urgency; monitor for follow-on activity.
author: Threat Detection Library
attack_mapping_note: Requires the Field Engineering (or equivalent expensive-search) diagnostic logging level on domain controllers.

title: Full-Directory Paged LDAP Export from a Single Source
description: Detects a single source performing a paged LDAP search that iterates through an unusually large number of result pages against a broad base DN (e.g. the domain root), consistent with a bulk export of most or all directory objects — a common precursor to offline attack-path analysis or data exfiltration targeting PII/organizational data stored in AD user attributes.
